abstract: MOS charge storage has been demonstrated as an effective method to store the weights in VLSI implementations of neural network models by several workers 2 . However, to achieve the full power of a VLSI implementation of an adaptive algorithm, the learning operation must built into the circuit. We have fabricated and tested a circuit ideal for this purpose by connecting a pair of capacitors with a CCD like structure, allowing for variable size weight changes as well as a weight decay operation. A 2.51-' CMOS version achieves better than 10 bits of dynamic range in a 140/' X 3501-' area. A 1.25/' chip based upon the same cell has 1104 weights on a 3.5mm x 6.0mm die and is capable of peak learning rates of at least 2 x 109 weight changes per second. 1 Adaptive Networks Much of the recent excitement about neural network models of computation has been driven by the prospect of new architectures for fine grained parallel compu(cid:173) tation using analog VLSI. Adaptive systems are espescially good targets for analog VLSI because the ada.ptive process can compensate for the inaccuracy of individual devices as easily as for the variability of the signal. However, silicon VLSI does not provide us with an ideal solution for weight storage. Among the properties of an ideal storage technology for analog VLSI adaptive systems are: • The minimum available weight change ~w must be small. The simplest adap(cid:173) tive algorithms optimize the weights by minimizing the output error with a steepest descent search in weight space [1]. Iterative improvement algorithms such as steepest descent are based on the heuristic assumption of 'better' weights being found in the neighborhood of 'good' ones; a heuristic that fails when the granularity of the weights is not fine enough. In the worst case, the resolution required just to represent a function can grow exponentially in the dimension of the input space . • The weights must be able to represent both positive and negative values and the changes must be easily reversible. Frequently, the weights may cycle up and down while the adaptive process is converging and millions of incremental changes during a single training session is not unreasonable. paragraphs: The paper addresses a hardware requirement for adaptive neural networks: stored weights must be easy to change during learning. MOS charge storage already offered a way to represent weights in integrated circuits, but storage alone did not provide an on-chip learning mechanism. The authors develop and test a circuit that supports the updates themselves.

The circuit connects two capacitors through a structure resembling a charge-coupled device. It allows weight changes of variable size and provides a weight-decay operation. These capabilities address the need for fine adjustments during iterative learning, when weights may repeatedly increase and decrease. The supplied discussion explains that coarse weight resolution can undermine the search for better settings near existing ones.

One fabricated CMOS implementation achieves more than 10 bits of dynamic range. A smaller-process chip based on the same cell contains 1,104 weights and supports peak learning rates of at least two billion weight changes per second. These results make the contribution concrete: a weight-storage cell designed to participate directly in rapid, repeated adaptation.
summary.tldr: A fabricated charge-storage circuit supports fine, variable-sized weight updates and decay for learning directly in neural hardware.

title: Adaptive Neural Networks Using MOS Charge Storage

paragraphs: EMPATH concerns face, emotion, and gender recognition using features called holons. The readable portions of the abstract describe reducing the dimensionality of facial data with a network. The identifiable methodological focus is therefore the representation of faces: transforming the supplied facial information into a smaller set of extracted features.

The text contrasts these extracted features with features used in previous face-recognition systems and mentions distances between facial elements. However, corruption interrupts the explanation of that contrast and the definition of holons. It supports identifying holons as the paper's named features, but does not support a precise account of how each feature is constructed or what facial information it captures.

The title places this representation in the context of three recognition tasks. Those tasks give the feature-extraction work its purpose, but the damaged abstract does not preserve dependable recognition results. The supported takeaway is that EMPATH explores a network-based reduction of facial data using holons; stronger claims about the representation or its performance would require readable evidence.
summary.tldr: EMPATH explores facial recognition through network-extracted features called holons, though the damaged abstract prevents a precise account of their construction.

title: EMPATH: Face, Emotion, and Gender Recognition Using Holons

abstract: The KBANN approach uses neural networks to refine knowledge that can be written in the form of simple propositional rules. We extend this idea further by presenting the MANNCON algorithm by which the mathematical equations governing a PID controller determine the topology and initial weights of a network, which is further trained using backpropagation. We apply this method to the task of controlling the outflow and temperature of a water tank, producing statistically-significant gains in accuracy over both a standard neural network approach and a non-learning PID con(cid:173) troller. Furthermore, using the PID knowledge to initialize the weights of the network produces statistically less variation in testset accuracy when compared to networks initialized with small random numbers.

We extend this idea further by presenting the MANNCON algorithm by which the mathematical equations governing a PID controller determine the topology and initial weights of a network, which is further trained using backpropagation. We apply this method to the task of controlling the outflow and temperature of a water tank, producing statistically-significant gains in accuracy over both a standard neural network approach and a non-learning PID con(cid:173) troller. Furthermore, using the PID knowledge to initialize the weights of the network produces statistically less variation in testset accuracy when compared to networks initialized with small random numbers.

paragraphs: This paper develops MANNCON, an algorithm that turns the equations of a PID controller into a neural network's topology and initial weights. The network then undergoes further training through backpropagation. Existing controller knowledge therefore supplies a concrete starting structure and behavior that learning can refine.

The approach extends the idea behind KBANN, which uses networks to refine knowledge expressed as simple propositional rules. Here the starting knowledge is mathematical control equations. Encoding those equations into the network connects an established controller design with a trainable representation, allowing the initial control policy to shape both the network's organization and its starting parameters.

The authors apply the method to controlling water-tank outflow and temperature. They report statistically significant accuracy gains over both a standard neural-network approach and a PID controller that does not learn. They also find significantly less variation in test accuracy when weights are initialized from PID knowledge rather than small random values. In this application, informed initialization improves both accuracy and consistency.
summary.tldr: Initializing a trainable network from PID equations improves water-tank control accuracy and reduces variation in test performance.

title: Refining PID Controllers using Neural Networks

Experiments with models of auditory localization and pitch perception also suggest temporal adaptation is an important ele(cid:173) ment of practical auditory processing. I have designed, fabricated, and successfully tested an analog integrated circuit that models many aspects of auditory nerve response, including temporal adap(cid:173) tation.
originalAbstract: Many auditory theorists consider the temporal adaptation of the auditory nerve a key aspect of speech coding in the auditory periph(cid:173) ery. Experiments with models of auditory localization and pitch perception also suggest temporal adaptation is an important ele(cid:173) ment of practical auditory processing. I have designed, fabricated, and successfully tested an analog integrated circuit that models many aspects of auditory nerve response, including temporal adap(cid:173) tation.

paragraphs: The paper describes an analog integrated circuit that models several aspects of auditory-nerve responses, including temporal adaptation. Temporal adaptation concerns how a response changes over time. Incorporating it makes the model sensitive to the time course of neural response, a feature the paper identifies as relevant to auditory processing.

The motivation comes from two related lines of work. Auditory theorists regard adaptation as an important part of speech coding in the auditory periphery. Experiments with models of sound localization and pitch perception also suggest that it matters for practical auditory processing. These observations motivate giving adaptation an explicit role in the circuit.

The author reports designing, fabricating, and successfully testing the integrated circuit. The stated achievement is therefore a physical implementation of an auditory-nerve response model that includes adaptation. Its significance is that a biologically motivated temporal property is realized in analog hardware, providing a concrete circuit model for a response characteristic implicated in several kinds of hearing-related computation.
summary.tldr: A fabricated and tested analog circuit models auditory-nerve responses, including temporal adaptation.

title: Temporal Adaptation in a Silicon Auditory Nerve

abstract: Sparse coding is a method for finding a representation of data in which each of the components of the representation is only rarely significantly active. Such a representation is closely related to re(cid:173) dundancy reduction and independent component analysis, and has some neurophysiological plausibility. In this paper, we show how sparse coding can be used for denoising. Using maximum likelihood estimation of nongaussian variables corrupted by gaussian noise, we show how to apply a shrinkage nonlinearity on the components of sparse coding so as to reduce noise. Furthermore, we show how to choose the optimal sparse coding basis for denoising. Our method is closely related to the method of wavelet shrinkage, but has the important benefit over wavelet methods that both the features and the shrinkage parameters are estimated directly from the data.

Such a representation is closely related to re(cid:173) dundancy reduction and independent component analysis, and has some neurophysiological plausibility. In this paper, we show how sparse coding can be used for denoising. Using maximum likelihood estimation of nongaussian variables corrupted by gaussian noise, we show how to apply a shrinkage nonlinearity on the components of sparse coding so as to reduce noise. paragraphs: Sparse coding represents data using components that are strongly active only rarely. This paper uses that property to separate meaningful structure from noise. The starting assumption is that the underlying components have non-Gaussian distributions and are observed after contamination by Gaussian noise, giving denoising a statistical estimation formulation.

The authors derive a nonlinear shrinkage operation through maximum-likelihood estimation. Applied to the sparse representation, this operation reduces noise in the component values. They also show how to choose a sparse coding basis specifically for denoising, so the method addresses both the representation of the data and the transformation applied within that representation.

The approach is closely related to wavelet shrinkage, but learns both its features and its shrinkage parameters directly from the data. That combination is the principal stated benefit over wavelet methods. The contribution connects sparse representation learning with a noise-removal rule derived from probability models, allowing the denoising procedure to adapt its components and their treatment together.
summary.tldr: Sparse-code denoising learns both a representation and nonlinear shrinkage parameters from data using a probabilistic noise model.

title: Sparse Code Shrinkage: Denoising by Nonlinear Maximum Likelihood Estimation

abstract: N wideband sources recorded using N closely spaced receivers can feasibly be separated based only on second order statistics when using a physical model of the mixing process. In this case we show that the parameter estimation problem can be essentially reduced to considering directions of arrival and attenuations of each signal. The paper presents two demixing methods operating in the time and frequency domain and experimentally shows that it is always possible to demix signals arriving at different angles. Moreover, one can use spatial cues to solve the channel selection problem and a post-processing Wiener filter to ameliorate the artifacts caused by demixing.
originalAbstract: N wideband sources recorded using N closely spaced receivers can feasibly be separated based only on second order statistics when using a physical model of the mixing process. In this case we show that the parameter estimation problem can be essentially reduced to considering directions of arrival and attenuations of each signal. The paper presents two demixing methods operating in the time and frequency domain and experimentally shows that it is always possible to demix signals arriving at different angles. Moreover, one can use spatial cues to solve the channel selection problem and a post-processing Wiener filter to ameliorate the artifacts caused by demixing.

paragraphs: The paper studies separating multiple wideband sources recorded by an equal number of closely spaced receivers. It shows that separation can be feasible using second-order statistics when a physical model of signal mixing is incorporated. That physical description supplies structure to the problem of identifying which contributions belong to which source.

Under the considered model, parameter estimation can be reduced essentially to each signal's arrival direction and attenuation. The authors present two demixing methods, one operating in time and the other in frequency. Their experiments report successful demixing for signals arriving at different angles, supporting angular separation as a useful basis for the proposed methods.

The paper also addresses how to handle the separated outputs. Spatial information can resolve channel selection, and a Wiener filter applied afterward can reduce artifacts introduced by demixing. The overall approach connects a physical description of propagation with statistical separation and output refinement. Its feasibility claim is tied to the modeled mixing setting and the stated relationship between source and receiver counts.
summary.tldr: A physical mixing model enables broadband source separation through arrival directions, attenuations, and second-order statistics.

title: Broadband Direction-Of-Arrival Estimation Based on Second Order Statistics

abstract: Recently, sample complexity bounds have been derived for problems in(cid:173) volving linear functions such as neural networks and support vector ma(cid:173) chines. In this paper, we extend some theoretical results in this area by deriving dimensional independent covering number bounds for regular(cid:173) ized linear functions under certain regularization conditions. We show that such bounds lead to a class of new methods for training linear clas(cid:173) sifiers with similar theoretical advantages of the support vector machine. Furthermore, we also present a theoretical analysis for these new meth(cid:173) ods from the asymptotic statistical point of view. This technique provides better description for large sample behaviors of these algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper extends theoretical work on learning with linear functions, including settings connected to neural networks and support vector machines. Its central result is a set of dimension-independent covering-number bounds for regularized linear functions. A covering number measures how many representative functions are needed to approximate a function class at a chosen resolution.

The bounds hold under particular regularization conditions. Their significance is that the stated complexity control does not depend on dimension, provided those conditions apply. The authors show that the bounds lead to a class of methods for training linear classifiers with theoretical advantages similar to those of support vector machines.

The paper also analyzes these methods from an asymptotic statistical perspective, examining their behavior as sample sizes become large. This complements the covering-number approach with a description of large-sample behavior. The contribution links conditional complexity bounds to new training methods and then studies those methods through a second theoretical lens; the abstract's comparison with support vector machines concerns theoretical advantages.
summary.tldr: Conditional dimension-independent complexity bounds motivate new regularized linear classifiers and an analysis of their large-sample behavior.

title: Some Theoretical Results Concerning the Convergence of Compositions of Regularized Linear Functions

abstract: We present an algorithm to extract features from high-dimensional gene expression proﬁles, based on the knowledge of a graph which links to- gether genes known to participate to successive reactions in metabolic pathways. Motivated by the intuition that biologically relevant features are likely to exhibit smoothness with respect to the graph topology, the algorithm involves encoding the graph and the set of expression pro- ﬁles into kernel functions, and performing a generalized form of canoni- cal correlation analysis in the corresponding reproducible kernel Hilbert spaces. Function prediction experiments for the genes of the yeast S. Cerevisiae validate this approach by showing a consistent increase in performance when a state-of-the-art classiﬁer uses the vector of features instead of the original expression proﬁle to predict the functional class of a gene.

Motivated by the intuition that biologically relevant features are likely to exhibit smoothness with respect to the graph topology, the algorithm involves encoding the graph and the set of expression pro- ﬁles into kernel functions, and performing a generalized form of canoni- cal correlation analysis in the corresponding reproducible kernel Hilbert spaces. paragraphs: Gene expression profiles contain many measurements, while biological knowledge supplies relationships between genes. This paper combines those sources to extract useful features. Its graph connects genes known to take part in successive reactions in metabolic pathways, giving the algorithm information about biological relationships beyond the expression measurements themselves.

The motivating intuition is that biologically relevant features are likely to vary smoothly across the graph. In plain terms, relationships in the pathway graph should help organize the extracted representation. The method encodes both the graph and expression profiles as kernels, then applies a generalized form of canonical correlation analysis in the associated feature spaces.

The authors test the resulting features by predicting functional classes of genes in the yeast S. cerevisiae. A state-of-the-art classifier performs consistently better when given the extracted feature vectors than when given the original expression profiles. The reported result supports the usefulness of incorporating pathway structure into feature extraction for this prediction task.
summary.tldr: Combining pathway graphs with gene expression data produces features that improve gene-function prediction in the reported yeast experiments.

title: Graph-Driven Feature Extraction From Microarray Data Using Diffusion Kernels and Kernel CCA

abstract: Forward decoding kernel machines (FDKM) combine large-margin clas(cid:173) sifiers with hidden Markov models (HMM) for maximum a posteriori (MAP) adaptive sequence estimation. State transitions in the sequence are conditioned on observed data using a kernel-based probability model trained with a recursive scheme that deals effectively with noisy and par(cid:173) tially labeled data. Training over very large data sets is accomplished us(cid:173) ing a sparse probabilistic support vector machine (SVM) model based on quadratic entropy, and an on-line stochastic steepest descent algorithm. For speaker-independent continuous phone recognition, FDKM trained over 177 ,080 samples of the TlMIT database achieves 80.6% recognition accuracy over the full test set, without use of a prior phonetic language model.

State transitions in the sequence are conditioned on observed data using a kernel-based probability model trained with a recursive scheme that deals effectively with noisy and par(cid:173) tially labeled data. Training over very large data sets is accomplished us(cid:173) ing a sparse probabilistic support vector machine (SVM) model based on quadratic entropy, and an on-line stochastic steepest descent algorithm. paragraphs: The paper introduces forward decoding kernel machines for estimating sequences, with continuous phone recognition as the application. The method combines large-margin classifiers with hidden Markov models. It performs adaptive maximum a posteriori sequence estimation, bringing a kernel-based probability model into the process of deciding how hidden states change over time.

A central feature is that state transitions depend on the observed data. The probability model is trained recursively using a scheme designed to handle noisy and partially labeled observations. For large training sets, the authors use a sparse probabilistic support vector machine based on quadratic entropy, together with an online stochastic steepest descent algorithm.

In speaker-independent continuous phone recognition, the system was trained on 177,080 TIMIT samples and achieved 80.6% recognition accuracy across the full test set. This result was obtained without a prior phonetic language model. The finding demonstrates the combined sequence and kernel approach in the stated recognition setting, while the training design addresses the practical demands of large, imperfectly labeled datasets.
summary.tldr: Forward decoding kernel machines combine kernel classifiers and hidden Markov models, achieving 80.6% TIMIT phone recognition accuracy without a prior phonetic language model.

title: Forward-Decoding Kernel-Based Phone Recognition

abstract: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) has enabled scientists to look into the active brain. However, interactivity between functional brain regions, is still little studied. In this paper, we contribute a novel framework for modeling the interactions between multiple active brain regions, using Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) as generative mod- els for brain activation patterns. This framework is applied to modeling of neuronal circuits associated with reward. The novelty of our frame- work from a Machine Learning perspective lies in the use of DBNs to reveal the brain connectivity and interactivity. Such interactivity mod- els which are derived from fMRI data are then validated through a group classiﬁcation task. We employ and compare four different types of DBNs: Parallel Hidden Markov Models, Coupled Hidden Markov Models, Fully-linked Hidden Markov Models and Dynamically Multi- Linked HMMs (DML-HMM). Moreover, we propose and compare two schemes of learning DML-HMMs. Experimental results show that by using DBNs, group classiﬁcation can be performed even if the DBNs are constructed from as few as 5 brain regions. We also demonstrate that, by using the proposed learning algorithms, different DBN structures charac- terize drug addicted subjects vs. control subjects. This ﬁnding provides an independent test for the effect of psychopathology on brain function. In general, we demonstrate that incorporation of computer science prin- ciples into functional neuroimaging clinical studies provides a novel ap- proach for probing human brain function.

paragraphs: This paper uses dynamic Bayesian networks to model interactions among active brain regions measured with fMRI. The networks serve as generative models of brain activation patterns, with an application to neuronal circuits associated with reward. The objective is to study how regions interact through time, extending the analysis beyond which regions are active.

The authors compare four model types: parallel, coupled, fully linked, and dynamically multi-linked hidden Markov models. They also propose and compare two learning schemes for the dynamically multi-linked version. Models inferred from fMRI data are evaluated through a group classification task, testing whether their interaction patterns carry information that distinguishes the studied groups.

The experiments show that classification can be performed using networks constructed from as few as five brain regions. The proposed learning methods also produce different network structures for drug-addicted and control subjects. The authors present these differences as an independent test of psychopathology's relationship with brain function, grounding their interpretation in modeled interactions and the reported group-level classification results.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Bayesian networks model reward-related fMRI interactions and reveal structures that distinguish drug-addicted subjects from controls in a group classification task.

title: Modeling Neuronal Interactivity using Dynamic Bayesian Networks

abstract: In previous work we presented an efﬁcient approach to computing ker- nel summations which arise in many machine learning methods such as kernel density estimation. This approach, dual-tree recursion with ﬁnite- difference approximation, generalized existing methods for similar prob- lems arising in computational physics in two ways appropriate for sta- tistical problems: toward distribution sensitivity and general dimension, partly by avoiding series expansions. While this proved to be the fastest practical method for multivariate kernel density estimation at the optimal bandwidth, it is much less efﬁcient at larger-than-optimal bandwidths. In this work, we explore the extent to which the dual-tree approach can be integrated with multipole-like Hermite expansions in order to achieve reasonable efﬁciency across all bandwidth scales, though only for low di- mensionalities. In the process, we derive and demonstrate the ﬁrst truly hierarchical fast Gauss transforms, effectively combining the best tools from discrete algorithms and continuous approximation theory. 1 Fast Gaussian Summation Kernel summations are fundamental in both statistics/learning and computational physics.

This approach, dual-tree recursion with ﬁnite- difference approximation, generalized existing methods for similar prob- lems arising in computational physics in two ways appropriate for sta- tistical problems: toward distribution sensitivity and general dimension, partly by avoiding series expansions. While this proved to be the fastest practical method for multivariate kernel density estimation at the optimal bandwidth, it is much less efﬁcient at larger-than-optimal bandwidths. In this work, we explore the extent to which the dual-tree approach can be integrated with multipole-like Hermite expansions in order to achieve reasonable efﬁciency across all bandwidth scales, though only for low di- mensionalities. paragraphs: The paper develops faster ways to compute Gaussian kernel sums, calculations that occur in methods such as kernel density estimation. Earlier work combined dual-tree recursion with finite-difference approximation and avoided series expansions in part to accommodate data distributions and general dimensionality. That approach was practically fast at the optimal bandwidth but became much less efficient at larger bandwidths.

The new work investigates combining dual-tree methods with multipole-like Hermite expansions. Bandwidth controls the scale of the kernel, so efficiency across bandwidths matters when the same type of calculation must be performed at different scales. The proposed combination aims to retain useful tree-based organization while adding a different continuous approximation tool.

The authors derive and demonstrate what they describe as the first fully hierarchical fast Gauss transforms. Their stated aim is reasonable efficiency across all bandwidth scales, with the important restriction to low-dimensional settings. The contribution addresses a scale-dependent weakness of the earlier method by integrating discrete algorithmic structure with series-based approximation, rather than claiming the same benefit in arbitrary dimensions.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Gaussian summation combines dual-tree methods with Hermite expansions to address bandwidth-dependent inefficiency in low dimensions.

title: Dual-Tree Fast Gauss Transforms

abstract: This paper develops a multi-frame image super-resolution approach from a Bayesian view-point by marginalizing over the unknown registration parameters relating the set of input low-resolution views. In Tipping and Bishop’s Bayesian image super-resolution approach [16], the marginalization was over the super- resolution image, necessitating the use of an unfavorable image prior. By inte- grating over the registration parameters rather than the high-resolution image, our method allows for more realistic prior distributions, and also reduces the dimen- sion of the integral considerably, removing the main computational bottleneck of the other algorithm. In addition to the motion model used by Tipping and Bishop, illumination components are introduced into the generative model, allowing us to handle changes in lighting as well as motion. We show results on real and synthetic datasets to illustrate the efﬁcacy of this approach.
originalAbstract: This paper develops a multi-frame image super-resolution approach from a Bayesian view-point by marginalizing over the unknown registration parameters relating the set of input low-resolution views. In Tipping and Bishop’s Bayesian image super-resolution approach [16], the marginalization was over the super- resolution image, necessitating the use of an unfavorable image prior. By inte- grating over the registration parameters rather than the high-resolution image, our method allows for more realistic prior distributions, and also reduces the dimen- sion of the integral considerably, removing the main computational bottleneck of the other algorithm. In addition to the motion model used by Tipping and Bishop, illumination components are introduced into the generative model, allowing us to handle changes in lighting as well as motion. We show results on real and synthetic datasets to illustrate the efﬁcacy of this approach.

paragraphs: Multi-frame super-resolution combines several low-resolution views to estimate a higher-resolution image. A central difficulty is that the alignment between those views is unknown. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that accounts for uncertainty in the registration parameters by integrating over them when reconstructing the image.

The choice of what to integrate over is the key contribution. The earlier Bayesian approach discussed in the abstract integrated over the high-resolution image, which required an unfavorable image prior. Integrating over registration parameters instead permits more realistic image priors and substantially reduces the dimension of the integral, removing the earlier method's main computational bottleneck.

The generative model also includes illumination components alongside motion, allowing changes in lighting to be represented together with changes in alignment. Results on real and synthetic datasets illustrate the approach's effectiveness. The paper shows why the organization of Bayesian inference matters practically: choosing different unknowns to average over can improve both the modeling options and the computational burden.
summary.tldr: Integrating over uncertain image alignments makes Bayesian super-resolution more computationally manageable and permits more realistic image priors.

title: Bayesian Image Super-resolution, Continued

abstract: Correspondence algorithms typically struggle with shapes that display part-based variation. We present a probabilistic approach that matches shapes using independent part transformations, where the parts themselves are learnt during matching. Ideas from semi-supervised learning are used to bias the algorithm towards finding `perceptually valid' part structures. Shapes are represented by unlabeled point sets of arbitrary size and a background component is used to handle occlusion, local dissimilarity and clutter. Thus, unlike many shape matching techniques, our approach can be applied to shapes extracted from real images. Model parameters are estimated using an EM algorithm that alternates between finding a soft correspondence and computing the optimal part transformations using Procrustes analysis.

paragraphs: Matching two shapes becomes difficult when their parts vary independently. This paper proposes a probabilistic method that learns the parts while finding correspondences between shapes. Each part receives its own transformation, allowing the match to account for variation at the part level rather than treating the shape as one inseparable object.

Shapes are represented as unlabeled point sets of arbitrary size. Ideas from semi-supervised learning bias the discovered parts toward perceptually meaningful structures. A background component accommodates occlusion, local differences, and clutter, so observations that do not fit the shared part structure can be handled within the model. This supports application to shapes extracted from real images.

An expectation-maximization algorithm alternates between estimating soft correspondences and optimizing the transformations of individual parts through Procrustes analysis. Soft correspondence represents uncertainty about which points should match. Alternating the two steps couples the correspondence problem with the search for appropriate part transformations. The central contribution is that matching and discovering the shape's parts are solved together within a probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic matching method jointly learns shape parts, their independent transformations, and uncertain point correspondences while accommodating clutter and occlusion.

title: Part-based Probabilistic Point Matching using Equivalence Constraints

abstract: Many human interactions involve pieces of information being passed from one person to another, raising the question of how this process of information transmission is affected by the capacities of the agents involved. In the 1930s, Sir Frederic Bartlett explored the influence of memory biases in âserial reproductionâ of information, in which one personâs reconstruction of a stimulus from memory becomes the stimulus seen by the next person. These experiments were done using relatively uncontrolled stimuli such as pictures and stories, but suggested that serial reproduction would transform information in a way that reflected the biases inherent in memory. We formally analyze serial reproduction using a Bayesian model of reconstruction from memory, giving a general result characterizing the effect of memory biases on information transmission. We then test the predictions of this account in two experiments using simple one-dimensional stimuli. Our results provide theoretical and empirical justification for the idea that serial reproduction reflects memory biases.

paragraphs: When information passes from person to person, each recipient may reconstruct it from memory before passing it onward. The paper studies this process, called serial reproduction, to understand how memory biases shape what survives transmission. Earlier work with pictures and stories suggested that repeated reconstruction transforms information in ways that reflect those biases.

The authors give a formal analysis using a Bayesian model of reconstruction from memory. This provides a general result characterizing how memory biases affect transmitted information. The approach turns the broad idea that recollection systematically changes a message into a theoretical account with predictions that can be examined experimentally.

They test those predictions in two experiments using simple one-dimensional stimuli. The results supply both theoretical and empirical support for interpreting serial reproduction as a reflection of memory biases. Using simple stimuli connects the mathematical account to a more controlled test of the transmission process, supporting the claim that its transformations contain information about the reconstructive tendencies of memory.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian analysis and two experiments support the idea that repeated retelling transforms information according to memory biases.

title: How memory biases affect information transmission: A rational analysis of serial reproduction

abstract: Subspace-based learning problems involve data whose elements are linear subspaces of a vector space. To handle such data structures, Grassmann kernels have been proposed and used previously. In this paper, we analyze the relationship between Grassmann kernels and probabilistic similarity measures. Firstly, we show that the KL distance in the limit yields the Projection kernel on the Grassmann manifold, whereas the Bhattacharyya kernel becomes trivial in the limit and is suboptimal for subspace-based problems. Secondly, based on our analysis of the KL distance, we propose extensions of the Projection kernel which can be extended to the set of affine as well as scaled subspaces. We demonstrate the advantages of these extended kernels for classification and recognition tasks with Support Vector Machines and Kernel Discriminant Analysis using synthetic and real image databases.

paragraphs: In subspace-based learning, each data item is an entire linear subspace rather than an individual vector. Learning methods therefore need a way to compare these structured objects. This paper examines Grassmann kernels through their relationship to probabilistic similarity measures, using that connection to explain existing comparisons and construct more flexible ones.

The analysis shows that a limiting form of KL distance yields the Projection kernel on the Grassmann manifold. In the corresponding limit, the Bhattacharyya kernel becomes trivial, making it suboptimal for the subspace-based problems considered. This distinction matters because a similarity measure that loses meaningful distinctions cannot adequately express differences between the objects being learned from.

Building on the KL analysis, the authors extend the Projection kernel to accommodate affine and scaled subspaces. The extensions broaden the types of subspace representations the comparison can handle. Experiments use support vector machines and kernel discriminant analysis for classification and recognition on synthetic and real image databases. The reported advantages connect the theoretical analysis of similarity measures to useful improvements in those learning tasks.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic analysis of subspace similarity motivates extended Projection kernels for affine and scaled subspaces.

title: Extended Grassmann Kernels for Subspace-Based Learning

abstract: Bayesian optimization methods are often used to optimize unknown functions that are costly to evaluate. Typically, these methods sequentially select inputs to be evaluated one at a time based on a posterior over the unknown function that is updated after each evaluation. There are a number of effective sequential policies for selecting the individual inputs. In many applications, however, it is desirable to perform multiple evaluations in parallel, which requires selecting batches of multiple inputs to evaluate at once. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to batch Bayesian optimization, providing a policy for selecting batches of inputs with the goal of optimizing the function as efficiently as possible. The key idea is to exploit the availability of high-quality and efficient sequential policies, by using Monte-Carlo simulation to select input batches that closely match their expected behavior. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first batch selection policy for Bayesian optimization. Our experimental results on six benchmarks show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms two baselines and can lead to large advantages over a top sequential approach in terms of performance per unit time.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to an unknown function whose evaluations are expensive. Sequential methods choose one input, observe its result, and update their beliefs before choosing again. When multiple evaluations can run in parallel, this pattern leaves a scheduling problem: several inputs must be selected before any of their outcomes are available.

The paper proposes a batch-selection policy that builds on effective sequential policies. It uses Monte Carlo simulation to select a collection of inputs whose behavior closely matches what a sequential policy is expected to do. This transfers guidance from sequential decision rules into a setting where evaluations must be committed together.

Across six benchmarks, the proposed approach significantly outperforms two baselines. The authors also find that it can deliver large advantages over a leading sequential approach when performance is measured per unit time. That qualification matters: the reported benefit reflects the opportunity to evaluate inputs in parallel, and the method is designed to make productive use of that opportunity.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo simulation turns effective sequential Bayesian optimization policies into batch choices that can improve performance per unit time.

title: Batch Bayesian Optimization via Simulation Matching

abstract: A common challenge for Bayesian models of perception is the fact that the two fundamental Bayesian components, the prior distribution and the likelihood func- tion, are formally unconstrained. Here we argue that a neural system that emulates Bayesian inference is naturally constrained by the way it represents sensory infor- mation in populations of neurons. More speciﬁcally, we show that an efﬁcient coding principle creates a direct link between prior and likelihood based on the underlying stimulus distribution. The resulting Bayesian estimates can show bi- ases away from the peaks of the prior distribution, a behavior seemingly at odds with the traditional view of Bayesian estimation, yet one that has been reported in human perception. We demonstrate that our framework correctly accounts for the repulsive biases previously reported for the perception of visual orientation, and show that the predicted tuning characteristics of the model neurons match the reported orientation tuning properties of neurons in primary visual cortex. Our results suggest that efﬁcient coding is a promising hypothesis in constrain- ing Bayesian models of perceptual inference.

paragraphs: Bayesian models of perception combine a prior distribution with a likelihood function, but these two ingredients can otherwise be chosen with considerable freedom. The paper argues that the neural representation of sensory information supplies a constraint on both. In particular, efficient coding links them through the distribution of stimuli the system represents.

This connection changes what kinds of perceptual bias the model can produce. Its Bayesian estimates can move away from peaks of the prior, even though Bayesian estimation is often associated with attraction toward more probable values. Such repulsion is a possible consequence of the linked prior and likelihood, rather than evidence that the estimates necessarily abandon Bayesian inference.

The framework accounts for previously reported repulsive biases in visual orientation perception. Its predicted neuronal tuning characteristics also match reported orientation tuning properties in primary visual cortex. These findings connect a behavioral pattern with properties of the sensory representation within one account. The authors present efficient coding as a promising constraint on perceptual Bayesian models, rather than establishing it as the only explanation.
summary.tldr: Efficient sensory coding links Bayesian priors and likelihoods and can explain repulsive biases in visual orientation perception.

title: Efficient coding provides a direct link between prior and likelihood in perceptual Bayesian inference

abstract: We introduce the Multi-Prediction Deep Boltzmann Machine (MP-DBM). The MP-DBM can be seen as a single probabilistic model trained to maximize a variational approximation to the generalized pseudolikelihood, or as a family of recurrent nets that share parameters and approximately solve different inference problems. Prior methods of training DBMs either do not perform well on classification tasks or require an initial learning pass that trains the DBM greedily, one layer at a time. The MP-DBM does not require greedy layerwise pretraining, and outperforms the standard DBM at classification, classification with missing inputs, and mean field prediction tasks.

The MP-DBM does not require greedy layerwise pretraining, and outperforms the standard DBM at classification, classification with missing inputs, and mean field prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Training a deep Boltzmann machine presents difficulties when the model must support useful predictions. Earlier methods either perform poorly on classification or require an initial stage that trains layers greedily, one at a time. This paper introduces the Multi-Prediction Deep Boltzmann Machine as a way to train without that layerwise pretraining stage.

The approach has two complementary interpretations. It is a single probabilistic model trained using a variational approximation to generalized pseudolikelihood. It can also be understood as a family of recurrent networks that share parameters and approximately solve different inference problems. These perspectives connect a probabilistic training objective with several prediction procedures using the same learned parameters.

The authors report better performance than a standard deep Boltzmann machine on classification, classification with missing inputs, and mean-field prediction tasks. The results support the usefulness of training a shared model for multiple inference problems. Alongside those empirical gains, removing greedy pretraining changes the training procedure by eliminating the need for a separate layer-by-layer initialization pass.
summary.tldr: Multi-Prediction Deep Boltzmann Machines avoid greedy layerwise pretraining and improve several prediction tasks over a standard DBM.

title: Multi-Prediction Deep Boltzmann Machines

abstract: We propose an efficient discrete optimization algorithm for selecting a subset of training data to induce sparsity for Gaussian process regression. The algorithm estimates this inducing set and the hyperparameters using a single objective, either the marginal likelihood or a variational free energy. The space and time complexity are linear in the training set size, and the algorithm can be applied to large regression problems on discrete or continuous domains. Empirical evaluation shows state-of-art performance in the discrete case and competitive results in the continuous case.
originalAbstract: We propose an efficient discrete optimization algorithm for selecting a subset of training data to induce sparsity for Gaussian process regression. The algorithm estimates this inducing set and the hyperparameters using a single objective, either the marginal likelihood or a variational free energy. The space and time complexity are linear in the training set size, and the algorithm can be applied to large regression problems on discrete or continuous domains. Empirical evaluation shows state-of-art performance in the discrete case and competitive results in the continuous case.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to make Gaussian process regression more manageable by selecting a subset of training observations. This subset serves as the inducing set that creates a sparse model. The central computational task is deciding which observations to retain while also fitting the model's hyperparameters.

The proposed discrete optimization algorithm handles both decisions through one objective. That objective can be either marginal likelihood or variational free energy. Using a common criterion connects the choice of inducing observations to the fitting of the model, rather than treating subset selection as an unrelated preliminary decision.

The algorithm's time and memory requirements grow linearly with training-set size, making it applicable to large regression problems. It supports both discrete and continuous domains, although the inducing set itself is selected from training data. Empirical evaluation reports state-of-the-art performance in the discrete setting and competitive results in the continuous setting. The findings support a scalable subset-selection approach while distinguishing the stronger reported comparative result for discrete problems from the more qualified result for continuous ones.
summary.tldr: A discrete optimization method jointly selects inducing observations and fits sparse Gaussian process hyperparameters with linear scaling in training-set size.

title: Efficient Optimization for Sparse Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: In sparse principal component analysis we are given noisy observations of a low-rank matrix of dimension $n\times p$ and seek to reconstruct it under additional sparsity assumptions. In particular, we assume here that the principal components $\bv_1,\dots,\bv_r$ have at most $k_1, \cdots, k_q$ non-zero entries respectively, and study the high-dimensional regime in which $p$ is of the same order as $n$. In an influential paper, Johnstone and Lu \cite{johnstone2004sparse} introduced a simple algorithm that estimates the support of the principal vectors $\bv_1,\dots,\bv_r$ by the largest entries in the diagonal of the empirical covariance. This method can be shown to succeed with high probability if $k_q \le C_1\sqrt{n/\log p}$, and to fail with high probability if $k_q\ge C_2 \sqrt{n/\log p}$ for two constants $0 < C_1,C_2 < \infty$. Despite a considerable amount of work over the last ten years, no practical algorithm exists with provably better support recovery guarantees. Here we analyze a covariance thresholding algorithm that was recently proposed by Krauthgamer, Nadler and Vilenchik \cite{KrauthgamerSPCA}. We confirm empirical evidence presented by these authors and rigorously prove that the algorithm succeeds with high probability for $k$ of order $\sqrt{n}$. Recent conditional lower bounds \cite{berthet2013computational} suggest that it might be impossible to do significantly better. The key technical component of our analysis develops new bounds on the norm of kernel random matrices, in regimes that were not considered before.

Conditional lower bounds suggest that substantially better performance might be impossible, but do not establish an unconditional barrier. The contribution is a stronger rigorous recovery guarantee for a practical algorithm, supported by new mathematical tools.
summary.tldr: Covariance thresholding provably recovers sparse PCA supports at sparsity of order square root of n, improving on diagonal thresholding guarantees.

title: Sparse PCA via Covariance Thresholding

abstract: Ensembles of randomized decision trees, usually referred to as random forests, are widely used for classification and regression tasks in machine learning and statistics. Random forests achieve competitive predictive performance and are computationally efficient to train and test, making them excellent candidates for real-world prediction tasks. The most popular random forest variants (such as Breiman's random forest and extremely randomized trees) operate on batches of training data. Online methods are now in greater demand. Existing online random forests, however, require more training data than their batch counterpart to achieve comparable predictive performance. In this work, we use Mondrian processes (Roy and Teh, 2009) to construct ensembles of random decision trees we call Mondrian forests. Mondrian forests can be grown in an incremental/online fashion and remarkably, the distribution of online Mondrian forests is the same as that of batch Mondrian forests. Mondrian forests achieve competitive predictive performance comparable with existing online random forests and periodically re-trained batch random forests, while being more than an order of magnitude faster, thus representing a better computation vs accuracy tradeoff.

paragraphs: Random forests combine randomized decision trees and are attractive for efficient prediction. Popular variants train on batches of data, while online settings require updating a model as observations arrive. The paper identifies a drawback of existing online forests: they can need more training data than batch counterparts to reach comparable predictive performance.

The authors construct Mondrian forests using Mondrian processes. These forests can grow incrementally, and their online construction produces the same distribution over forests as their batch construction. This is a distributional equivalence between the two training procedures; it connects incremental updates to a corresponding batch model in a precise way.

The reported experiments find predictive performance comparable to existing online random forests and periodically retrained batch forests, alongside speed gains exceeding an order of magnitude. The resulting advantage is a better measured balance between computation and accuracy. The paper therefore combines an online tree-building construction with both a theoretical link to batch training and empirical evidence of efficient prediction learning as data arrive.
summary.tldr: Mondrian forests match their batch construction in distribution while delivering competitive online accuracy and reported speed gains exceeding tenfold.

title: Mondrian Forests: Efficient Online Random Forests

abstract: We reduce a broad class of machine learning problems, usually addressed by EM or sampling, to the problem of finding the $k$ extremal rays spanning the conical hull of a data point set. These $k$ ``anchors'' lead to a global solution and a more interpretable model that can even outperform EM and sampling on generalization error. To find the $k$ anchors, we propose a novel divide-and-conquer learning scheme ``DCA'' that distributes the problem to $\mathcal O(k\log k)$ same-type sub-problems on different low-D random hyperplanes, each can be solved by any solver. For the 2D sub-problem, we present a non-iterative solver that only needs to compute an array of cosine values and its max/min entries. DCA also provides a faster subroutine for other methods to check whether a point is covered in a conical hull, which improves algorithm design in multiple dimensions and brings significant speedup to learning. We apply our method to GMM, HMM, LDA, NMF and subspace clustering, then show its competitive performance and scalability over other methods on rich datasets.

paragraphs: This paper gives a geometric formulation for a broad class of learning problems commonly approached through expectation maximization or sampling. It reduces these problems to finding k extreme directions, called anchors, that span the data’s conical hull. Within this formulation, the anchors yield a global solution and a more interpretable model, with the possibility of better generalization.

The proposed divide-and-conquer algorithm, DCA, distributes anchor finding across O(k log k) subproblems on low-dimensional random hyperplanes. Each subproblem retains the same general form and can use an appropriate solver. For two-dimensional subproblems, the authors provide a non-iterative procedure based on computing cosine values and finding their largest and smallest entries.

DCA also accelerates checking whether a point lies within a conical hull, supplying a useful subroutine for other methods. Applications include Gaussian mixtures, hidden Markov models, topic models, nonnegative matrix factorization, and subspace clustering. Experiments report competitive performance and scalability across varied datasets. The contribution is a shared geometric route to solving these problems, with small projected tasks supporting more efficient learning.
summary.tldr: DCA turns a class of learning problems into geometric anchor finding and solves it through many small random-projection subproblems.

title: Divide-and-Conquer Learning by Anchoring a Conical Hull

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a ubiquitous algorithm for a variety of machine learning problems. Researchers and industry have developed several techniques to optimize SGD's runtime performance, including asynchronous execution and reduced precision. Our main result is a martingale-based analysis that enables us to capture the rich noise models that may arise from such techniques. Specifically, we useour new analysis in three ways: (1) we derive convergence rates for the convex case (Hogwild) with relaxed assumptions on the sparsity of the problem; (2) we analyze asynchronous SGD algorithms for non-convex matrix problems including matrix completion; and (3) we design and analyze an asynchronous SGD algorithm, called Buckwild, that uses lower-precision arithmetic. We show experimentally that our algorithms run efficiently for a variety of problems on modern hardware.

Our main result is a martingale-based analysis that enables us to capture the rich noise models that may arise from such techniques. Specifically, we useour new analysis in three ways: (1) we derive convergence rates for the convex case (Hogwild) with relaxed assumptions on the sparsity of the problem; (2) we analyze asynchronous SGD algorithms for non-convex matrix problems including matrix completion; and (3) we design and analyze an asynchronous SGD algorithm, called Buckwild, that uses lower-precision arithmetic. We show experimentally that our algorithms run efficiently for a variety of problems on modern hardware.

paragraphs: Asynchronous execution and reduced-precision arithmetic can accelerate stochastic gradient descent, but they also create noise that complicates convergence analysis. This paper develops a martingale-based framework designed to handle the richer noise patterns introduced by these implementation choices. The aim is to analyze efficient execution strategies within a shared mathematical approach.

The framework is applied in three ways. It gives convergence rates for convex Hogwild-style optimization under relaxed sparsity assumptions. It also analyzes asynchronous stochastic-gradient algorithms for nonconvex matrix problems, including matrix completion. Finally, it supports the design and analysis of Buckwild, an asynchronous algorithm that uses lower-precision arithmetic.

These applications connect theoretical analysis with choices that affect how training runs on hardware. The authors report experiments showing efficient execution across a variety of problems on modern hardware. The results support the practical value of the analyzed algorithms, while the theory provides convergence arguments for the particular convex, matrix, and reduced-precision settings addressed rather than a blanket guarantee for every asynchronous optimization problem.
summary.tldr: A martingale-based analysis supports asynchronous and reduced-precision SGD, including relaxed Hogwild assumptions and the new Buckwild algorithm.

title: Taming the Wild: A Unified Analysis of Hogwild-Style Algorithms

abstract: We consider a crowdsourcing model in which n workers are asked to rate the quality of n items previously generated by other workers. An unknown set of $\alpha n$ workers generate reliable ratings, while the remaining workers may behave arbitrarily and possibly adversarially. The manager of the experiment can also manually evaluate the quality of a small number of items, and wishes to curate together almost all of the high-quality items with at most an fraction of low-quality items. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this is possible with an amount of work required of the manager, and each worker, that does not scale with n: the dataset can be curated with $\tilde{O}(1/\beta\alpha\epsilon^4)$ ratings per worker, and $\tilde{O}(1/\beta\epsilon^2)$ ratings by the manager, where $\beta$ is the fraction of high-quality items. Our results extend to the more general setting of peer prediction, including peer grading in online classrooms.

paragraphs: This paper studies crowdsourcing when workers evaluate items produced by other workers and some ratings may be deliberately misleading. Among n workers, an unknown fraction α supplies reliable ratings; everyone else may behave arbitrarily. A manager can inspect a small number of items directly and wants to recover almost all high-quality items while keeping low-quality inclusions limited.

The main result is that this curation can be achieved without the stated workload for the manager or each individual worker scaling with n. The bounds instead depend on the reliable-worker fraction, the high-quality-item fraction β, and an error parameter ε. The respective bounds are expressed as Õ(1/(βαε⁴)) ratings per worker and Õ(1/(βε²)) ratings by the manager.

The distinction between individual and total effort matters: the result concerns each worker's burden and the manager's burden as the collection grows. It demonstrates how limited direct evaluation can support curation despite an unknown adversarial population. The authors also extend their results to peer prediction, including peer grading in online classrooms.
summary.tldr: With a reliable fraction of workers and limited manager checks, adversarial crowdsourcing permits accurate curation with individual workloads that do not scale with collection size.

title: Avoiding Imposters and Delinquents: Adversarial Crowdsourcing and Peer Prediction

abstract: Matrix completion, where we wish to recover a low rank matrix by observing a few entries from it, is a widely studied problem in both theory and practice with wide applications. Most of the provable algorithms so far on this problem have been restricted to the offline setting where they provide an estimate of the unknown matrix using all observations simultaneously. However, in many applications, the online version, where we observe one entry at a time and dynamically update our estimate, is more appealing. While existing algorithms are efficient for the offline setting, they could be highly inefficient for the online setting. In this paper, we propose the first provable, efficient online algorithm for matrix completion. Our algorithm starts from an initial estimate of the matrix and then performs non-convex stochastic gradient descent (SGD). After every observation, it performs a fast update involving only one row of two tall matrices, giving near linear total runtime. Our algorithm can be naturally used in the offline setting as well, where it gives competitive sample complexity and runtime to state of the art algorithms. Our proofs introduce a general framework to show that SGD updates tend to stay away from saddle surfaces and could be of broader interests to other non-convex problems.

title: Provable Efficient Online Matrix Completion via Non-convex Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art results on many pattern recognition tasks, especially vision classification problems. Understanding the inner workings of such computational brains is both fascinating basic science that is interesting in its own right---similar to why we study the human brain---and will enable researchers to further improve DNNs. One path to understanding how a neural network functions internally is to study what each of its neurons has learned to detect. One such method is called activation maximization, which synthesizes an input (e.g. an image) that highly activates a neuron. Here we dramatically improve the qualitative state of the art of activation maximization by harnessing a powerful, learned prior: a deep generator network. The algorithm (1) generates qualitatively state-of-the-art synthetic images that look almost real, (2) reveals the features learned by each neuron in an interpretable way, (3) generalizes well to new datasets and somewhat well to different network architectures without requiring the prior to be relearned, and (4) can be considered as a high-quality generative method (in this case, by generating novel, creative, interesting, recognizable images).

This technique, activation maximization, aims to reveal what the neuron has learned to detect. The paper improves the interpretability and visual quality of these synthesized inputs by using a deep generator network as a learned prior.

The generator supplies learned image structure to the synthesis process, helping produce recognizable images that still activate the chosen neuron strongly. The authors report a substantial qualitative improvement over earlier activation-maximization results, with synthetic images that appear almost real. The resulting visualizations make learned features easier to interpret.

The prior also transfers well to new datasets and somewhat well to different network architectures without being retrained. That qualified transfer result suggests the learned image prior can be reused across multiple analysis settings. Beyond visualizing neurons, the method can serve as an image generator, producing novel and recognizable images. Its contribution therefore links network interpretation with visually coherent image synthesis.
summary.tldr: A deep generator prior makes activation-maximizing images more realistic and interpretable, helping reveal the features individual neurons respond to.

title: Synthesizing the preferred inputs for neurons in neural networks via deep generator networks

abstract: How does our motor system solve the problem of anticipatory control in spite of a wide spectrum of response dynamics from different musculo-skeletal systems, transport delays as well as response latencies throughout the central nervous system? To a great extent, our highly-skilled motor responses are a result of a reactive feedback system, originating in the brain-stem and spinal cord, combined with a feed-forward anticipatory system, that is adaptively fine-tuned by sensory experience and originates in the cerebellum. Based on that interaction we design the counterfactual predictive control (CFPC) architecture, an anticipatory adaptive motor control scheme in which a feed-forward module, based on the cerebellum, steers an error feedback controller with counterfactual error signals. Those are signals that trigger reactions as actual errors would, but that do not code for any current of forthcoming errors. In order to determine the optimal learning strategy, we derive a novel learning rule for the feed-forward module that involves an eligibility trace and operates at the synaptic level. In particular, our eligibility trace provides a mechanism beyond co-incidence detection in that it convolves a history of prior synaptic inputs with error signals. In the context of cerebellar physiology, this solution implies that Purkinje cell synapses should generate eligibility traces using a forward model of the system being controlled. From an engineering perspective, CFPC provides a general-purpose anticipatory control architecture equipped with a learning rule that exploits the full dynamics of the closed-loop system.

paragraphs: Anticipatory movement control must account for delays and for body systems that respond at different speeds. This paper develops counterfactual predictive control, an architecture inspired by the interaction between reactive motor feedback and the cerebellum’s adaptive anticipatory contribution. Its feed-forward module guides a feedback controller by supplying signals that provoke corrective reactions.

These signals are counterfactual: they act like error signals without representing actual present or future errors. To determine how the anticipatory module should learn, the authors derive a synaptic learning rule involving an eligibility trace. The trace combines a history of earlier synaptic inputs with error signals, extending beyond learning based only on events occurring together.

Applied to cerebellar physiology, the derivation implies that Purkinje cell synapses should construct these traces using a forward model of the controlled system. This is a consequence of the proposed control framework. For engineering, the contribution is an anticipatory architecture whose learning rule incorporates the dynamics of the complete feedback loop, connecting the timing of past inputs to their later control effects.
summary.tldr: A cerebellum-inspired control architecture derives a synaptic learning rule that uses system dynamics to support anticipatory movement.

title: A forward model at Purkinje cell synapses facilitates cerebellar anticipatory control

abstract: We present new practical local differentially private heavy hitters algorithms achieving optimal or near-optimal worst-case error -- TreeHist and Bitstogram. In both algorithms, server running time is $\tilde O(n)$ and user running time is $\tilde O(1)$, hence improving on the prior state-of-the-art result of Bassily and Smith [STOC 2015] requiring $\tilde O(n^{5/2})$ server time and $\tilde O(n^{3/2})$ user time. With a typically large number of participants in local algorithms ($n$ in the millions), this reduction in time complexity, in particular at the user side, is crucial for the use of such algorithms in practice. We implemented Algorithm TreeHist to verify our theoretical analysis and compared its performance with the performance of Google's RAPPOR code.

paragraphs: Finding heavy hitters means identifying frequently occurring values among participants' data. This paper develops two algorithms, TreeHist and Bitstogram, for doing so under local differential privacy. Their main contribution is to combine optimal or nearly optimal worst-case error with substantially lower computation requirements for both the collecting server and individual users.

Ignoring logarithmic factors, server computation grows linearly with the number of participants, while each user's computation is constant. The prior result discussed in the abstract required server time growing as the number of users to the power 2.5 and user time growing to the power 1.5. This changes how the workload scales as participation increases.

The improvement is particularly relevant when local privacy systems involve millions of participants, where expensive processing on every user's side can obstruct deployment. The authors implement TreeHist to check their theoretical analysis and compare it with Google's RAPPOR implementation. The abstract reports this practical evaluation alongside the complexity guarantees without stating a specific numerical outcome for that comparison.
summary.tldr: TreeHist and Bitstogram make locally private heavy-hitter detection computationally practical while retaining optimal or near-optimal worst-case error.

title: Practical Locally Private Heavy Hitters

abstract: Calcium imaging is a prominent technology in neuroscience research which allows for simultaneous recording of large numbers of neurons in awake animals. Automated extraction of neurons and their temporal activity from imaging datasets is an important step in the path to producing neuroscience results. However, nearly all imaging datasets contain gross contaminating sources which could originate from the technology used, or the underlying biological tissue. Although past work has considered the effects of contamination under limited circumstances, there has not been a general framework treating contamination and its effects on the statistical estimation of calcium signals. In this work, we proceed in a new direction and propose to extract cells and their activity using robust statistical estimation. Using the theory of M-estimation, we derive a minimax optimal robust loss, and also find a simple and practical optimization routine for this loss with provably fast convergence. We use our proposed robust loss in a matrix factorization framework to extract the neurons and their temporal activity in calcium imaging datasets. We demonstrate the superiority of our robust estimation approach over existing methods on both simulated and real datasets.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging records activity from many neurons, but extracting cells and their activity traces requires statistical processing. Imaging data commonly contain substantial contamination from the recording technology or biological tissue. This paper treats that contamination as a central estimation problem and develops a robust approach to recovering neural signals.

Using M-estimation theory, the authors derive a robust loss with a minimax optimality property. They also provide a simple, practical routine for optimizing the loss and prove fast convergence. The statistical objective and its optimization procedure are therefore developed together, addressing both resistance to contamination and the practicality of fitting the model.

The robust loss is incorporated into a matrix-factorization framework that extracts neurons and their temporal activity from imaging datasets. Evaluations on simulated and real data show better performance than existing methods. The contribution is a general robust-estimation treatment of contamination in this setting, supported by theoretical properties of the loss and optimization routine as well as empirical improvements in signal extraction.
summary.tldr: A theoretically grounded robust loss improves extraction of neurons and activity traces from contaminated calcium-imaging data.

title: Robust Estimation of Neural Signals in Calcium Imaging

abstract: We study adversarial perturbations when the instances are uniformly distributed over {0,1}^n. We study both "inherent" bounds that apply to any problem and any classifier for such a problem as well as bounds that apply to specific problems and specific hypothesis classes. As the current literature contains multiple definitions of adversarial risk and robustness, we start by giving a taxonomy for these definitions based on their direct goals; we identify one of them as the one guaranteeing misclassification by pushing the instances to the error region. We then study some classic algorithms for learning monotone conjunctions and compare their adversarial risk and robustness under different definitions by attacking the hypotheses using instances drawn from the uniform distribution. We observe that sometimes these definitions lead to significantly different bounds. Thus, this study advocates for the use of the error-region definition, even though other definitions, in other contexts with context-dependent assumptions, may coincide with the error-region definition. Using the error-region definition of adversarial perturbations, we then study inherent bounds on risk and robustness of any classifier for any classification problem whose instances are uniformly distributed over {0,1}^n. Using the isoperimetric inequality for the Boolean hypercube, we show that for initial error 0.01, there always exists an adversarial perturbation that changes O(√n) bits of the instances to increase the risk to 0.5, making classifier's decisions meaningless. Furthermore, by also using the central limit theorem we show that when n→∞, at most c√n bits of perturbations, for a universal constant c<1.17, suffice for increasing the risk to 0.5, and the same c√n bits of perturbations on average suffice to increase the risk to 1, hence bounding the robustness by c√n.

paragraphs: What counts as a successful adversarial attack depends on how robustness is defined. This paper organizes competing definitions by their goals and emphasizes attacks that move inputs into the classifier’s error region, where predictions are actually wrong. Comparisons using algorithms for monotone conjunctions show that different definitions can produce substantially different robustness bounds.

The authors then study inputs drawn uniformly from the set of all binary strings of length n. Under the error-region definition, they establish bounds applying to any classifier with an initial error of 0.01. An attack changing on the order of the square root of n bits can raise the error probability to 0.5.

The asymptotic result sharpens this statement: a budget of c times the square root of n bits suffices, with a universal constant c below 1.17. The same budget on average can raise error to 1. These are distribution-specific mathematical results, showing how both the input distribution and the definition of attack success shape robustness claims.
summary.tldr: For uniformly distributed binary inputs, the paper clarifies adversarial robustness definitions and proves square-root-dimensional perturbation bounds.

title: Adversarial Risk and Robustness: General Definitions and Implications for the Uniform Distribution

abstract: This paper presents a novel method to compute the exact Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance between a pair of $d$-dimensional histograms having $n$ bins each. We prove that this problem is equivalent to an uncapacitated minimum cost flow problem on a $(d+1)$-partite graph with $(d+1)n$ nodes and $dn^{\frac{d+1}{d}}$ arcs, whenever the cost is separable along the principal $d$-dimensional directions. We show numerically the benefits of our approach by computing the Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance of order 2 among two sets of instances: gray scale images and $d$-dimensional biomedical histograms. On these types of instances, our approach is competitive with state-of-the-art optimal transport algorithms.
