We prove that this problem is equivalent to an uncapacitated minimum cost flow problem on a $(d+1)$-partite graph with $(d+1)n$ nodes and $dn^{\frac{d+1}{d}}$ arcs, whenever the cost is separable along the principal $d$-dimensional directions. We show numerically the benefits of our approach by computing the Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance of order 2 among two sets of instances: gray scale images and $d$-dimensional biomedical histograms. On these types of instances, our approach is competitive with state-of-the-art optimal transport algorithms.

paragraphs: The Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance compares histograms through the cost of transporting mass between their bins. Computing this distance exactly requires finding a least-cost transportation arrangement. This paper develops an alternative formulation for pairs of d-dimensional histograms, each containing n bins, that represents the computation as a structured graph problem.

The central result proves equivalence to an uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem on a graph with d+1 parts. The graph contains (d+1)n nodes and d times n raised to the power (d+1)/d arcs. This equivalence holds when transportation cost separates along the principal coordinate directions. That condition is essential to the stated result: it enables the graph formulation to preserve the exact distance.

The authors evaluate the approach by computing order-two Kantorovich-Wasserstein distances for grayscale images and multidimensional biomedical histograms. On these instances, the method is competitive with leading optimal transport algorithms. The contribution therefore combines an exact mathematical reformulation with numerical evidence that its graph structure can be computationally useful for the tested histogram problems.
summary.tldr: For coordinate-separable costs, exact histogram transport distances can be computed through a structured minimum-cost flow problem.

title: Computing Kantorovich-Wasserstein Distances on $d$-dimensional histograms using $(d+1)$-partite graphs

abstract: This paper proposes REFUEL, a reinforcement learning method with two techniques: {\em reward shaping} and {\em feature rebuilding}, to improve the performance of online symptom checking for disease diagnosis. Reward shaping can guide the search of policy towards better directions. Feature rebuilding can guide the agent to learn correlations between features. Together, they can find symptom queries that can yield positive responses from a patient with high probability. Experimental results justify that the two techniques in REFUEL allows the symptom checker to identify the disease more rapidly and accurately.

Together, they can find symptom queries that can yield positive responses from a patient with high probability. Experimental results justify that the two techniques in REFUEL allows the symptom checker to identify the disease more rapidly and accurately.

paragraphs: REFUEL addresses online symptom checking as a reinforcement learning problem. The system must choose symptom questions that help it identify a disease efficiently. The paper focuses on improving those choices through two techniques, reward shaping and feature rebuilding, so that the learned policy can make better use of sparse symptom information.

Reward shaping guides the search for a policy toward more useful directions. Feature rebuilding encourages the agent to learn correlations among features. The two mechanisms therefore contribute different kinds of guidance: one shapes policy learning, while the other develops knowledge of relationships among symptoms. Together, they can identify questions that a patient is likely to answer positively.

The reported experiments show that combining these techniques lets the symptom checker identify disease more rapidly and accurately. This connects the quality of question selection with the effectiveness of the overall diagnostic interaction. The stated result is an experimental improvement for the symptom-checking method, with the contribution centered on how reward design and feature relationships support learning which questions to ask.
summary.tldr: REFUEL combines reward shaping and feature rebuilding to learn symptom queries that improve diagnostic speed and accuracy in experiments.

title: REFUEL: Exploring Sparse Features in Deep Reinforcement Learning for Fast Disease Diagnosis

abstract: The last decade has witnessed an explosion in the development of models, theory and computational algorithms for ``big data'' analysis. In particular, distributed inference has served as a natural and dominating paradigm for statistical inference. However, the existing literature on parallel inference almost exclusively focuses on Euclidean data and parameters. While this assumption is valid for many applications, it is increasingly more common to encounter problems where the data or the parameters lie on a non-Euclidean space, like a manifold for example. Our work aims to fill a critical gap in the literature by generalizing parallel inference algorithms to optimization on manifolds. We show that our proposed algorithm is both communication efficient and carries theoretical convergence guarantees. In addition, we demonstrate the performance of our algorithm to the estimation of Fr\'echet means on simulated spherical data and the low-rank matrix completion problem over Grassmann manifolds applied to the Netflix prize data set.

paragraphs: Parallel statistical inference distributes computational work, but much of its existing theory assumes that data and parameters occupy ordinary Euclidean spaces. Some problems instead place them on manifolds, where the relevant geometry differs. The paper addresses this gap by extending parallel inference algorithms to optimization in these non-Euclidean settings.

The proposed algorithm combines communication efficiency with theoretical convergence guarantees. Both properties matter for distributed optimization: dividing computation across machines is useful only if exchanging information remains manageable and the combined procedure still progresses toward its optimization objective. The contribution brings these concerns together for problems whose geometry must be respected.

The authors demonstrate the method in two distinct settings. They estimate Fréchet means on simulated spherical data, providing an example of averaging in a curved space. They also apply low-rank matrix completion over Grassmann manifolds to the Netflix prize dataset. These applications show how the framework can address both explicitly geometric data and a matrix estimation problem represented through manifold optimization.
summary.tldr: The paper extends parallel inference to manifold optimization with communication efficiency and theoretical convergence guarantees.

title: Communication Efficient Parallel Algorithms for Optimization on Manifolds

abstract: In collective decision making, members of a group need to coordinate their actions in order to achieve a desirable outcome. When there is no direct communication between group members, one should decide based on inferring others' intentions from their actions. The inference of others' intentions is called "theory of mind" and can involve different levels of reasoning, from a single inference on a hidden variable to considering others partially or fully optimal and reasoning about their actions conditioned on one's own actions (levels of “theory of mind”). In this paper, we present a new Bayesian theory of collective decision making based on a simple yet most commonly observed behavior: conformity. We show that such a Bayesian framework allows one to achieve any level of theory of mind in collective decision making. The viability of our framework is demonstrated on two different experiments, a consensus task with 120 subjects and a volunteer's dilemma task with 29 subjects, each with multiple conditions.

The inference of others' intentions is called "theory of mind" and can involve different levels of reasoning, from a single inference on a hidden variable to considering others partially or fully optimal and reasoning about their actions conditioned on one's own actions (levels of “theory of mind”). paragraphs: Group decisions require people to coordinate, even when they cannot directly communicate. In that situation, someone’s actions become evidence about what they intend to do. The paper develops a Bayesian account of this process around conformity: the commonly observed tendency for group members to align their behavior. Its goal is to explain collective decision making through probabilistic reasoning about others.

The framework accommodates different levels of theory of mind. At a simpler level, a person infers another person’s hidden intention. More elaborate reasoning considers how capable others are of choosing good actions and how their choices might depend on one’s own behavior. The authors show that their conformity-based framework can express any level of this reasoning.

They demonstrate the framework’s viability in two human experiments: a consensus task involving 120 participants and a volunteer’s dilemma involving 29, each under multiple conditions. These demonstrations support its usefulness for studying distinct coordination problems. The contribution connects conformity with increasingly elaborate reasoning about other people within a single Bayesian framework.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian framework uses conformity to model different levels of reasoning about others in collective decisions.

title: A Bayesian Theory of Conformity in Collective Decision Making

abstract: The vast majority of successful deep neural networks are trained using variants of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithms. Recent attempts to improve SGD can be broadly categorized into two approaches: (1) adaptive learning rate schemes, such as AdaGrad and Adam and (2) accelerated schemes, such as heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum. In this paper, we propose a new optimization algorithm, Lookahead, that is orthogonal to these previous approaches and iteratively updates two sets of weights. Intuitively, the algorithm chooses a search direction by looking ahead at the sequence of ``fast weights" generated by another optimizer. We show that Lookahead improves the learning stability and lowers the variance of its inner optimizer with negligible computation and memory cost. We empirically demonstrate Lookahead can significantly improve the performance of SGD and Adam, even with their default hyperparameter settings on ImageNet, CIFAR-10/100, neural machine translation, and Penn Treebank.

In this paper, we propose a new optimization algorithm, Lookahead, that is orthogonal to these previous approaches and iteratively updates two sets of weights. Intuitively, the algorithm chooses a search direction by looking ahead at the sequence of ``fast weights" generated by another optimizer. We show that Lookahead improves the learning stability and lowers the variance of its inner optimizer with negligible computation and memory cost. We empirically demonstrate Lookahead can significantly improve the performance of SGD and Adam, even with their default hyperparameter settings on ImageNet, CIFAR-10/100, neural machine translation, and Penn Treebank.

paragraphs: Training a neural network involves repeatedly adjusting its weights to reduce prediction error. Many improvements to this process change learning rates or add momentum. Lookahead introduces a complementary mechanism that uses another optimizer's sequence of updates to guide its own movement through the space of possible weights.

The algorithm maintains two sets of weights. One set consists of fast weights updated by an inner optimizer, such as SGD or Adam. Lookahead uses the trajectory of these fast weights to choose a search direction for the other set. Its contribution therefore concerns how a sequence of optimization steps informs a broader update, rather than requiring a replacement for the inner optimizer.

The authors show improved learning stability and lower variance for the inner optimizer, with negligible additional computation and memory. Experiments demonstrate that Lookahead can substantially improve SGD and Adam, even with default hyperparameters, on image classification, neural machine translation, and Penn Treebank tasks. These findings support its use as a lightweight addition to established training methods.
summary.tldr: Lookahead uses two sets of weights to stabilize an existing optimizer and improve training with little added cost.

title: Lookahead Optimizer: k steps forward, 1 step back

abstract: Imitation learning (IL) aims to mimic the behavior of an expert policy in a sequential decision-making problem given only demonstrations. In this paper, we focus on understanding the minimax statistical limits of IL in episodic Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). We first consider the setting where the learner is provided a dataset of $N$ expert trajectories ahead of time, and cannot interact with the MDP. Here, we show that the policy which mimics the expert whenever possible is in expectation $\lesssim \frac{|\mathcal{S}| H^2 \log (N)}{N}$ suboptimal compared to the value of the expert, even when the expert plays a stochastic policy. Here $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space and $H$ is the length of the episode. Furthermore, we establish a suboptimality lower bound of $\gtrsim |\mathcal{S}| H^2 / N$ which applies even if the expert is constrained to be deterministic, or if the learner is allowed to actively query the expert at visited states while interacting with the MDP for $N$ episodes. To our knowledge, this is the first algorithm with suboptimality having no dependence on the number of actions, under no additional assumptions. We then propose a novel algorithm based on minimum-distance functionals in the setting where the transition model is given and the expert is deterministic. The algorithm is suboptimal by $\lesssim |\mathcal{S}| H^{3/2} / N$, matching our lower bound up to a $\sqrt{H}$ factor, and breaks the $\mathcal{O}(H^2)$ error compounding barrier of IL.

title: Toward the Fundamental Limits of Imitation Learning

abstract: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis is a conjecture that every large neural network contains a subnetwork that, when trained in isolation, achieves comparable performance to the large network. An even stronger conjecture has been proven recently: Every sufficiently overparameterized network contains a subnetwork that, even without training, achieves comparable accuracy to the trained large network. This theorem, however, relies on a number of strong assumptions and guarantees a polynomial factor on the size of the large network compared to the target function. In this work, we remove the most limiting assumptions of this previous work while providing significantly tighter bounds: the overparameterized network only needs a logarithmic factor (in all variables but depth) number of neurons per weight of the target subnetwork.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that a large neural network contains a smaller network that can match its performance after being trained separately. This paper concerns a stronger result: sufficiently overparameterized networks can contain subnetworks that already achieve comparable accuracy without training. The question is how much extra network size is needed to guarantee such a subnetwork exists.

Previous theory established this stronger claim under restrictive assumptions and required a polynomial size overhead relative to the target function. The authors remove what they describe as the most limiting assumptions and substantially tighten the size guarantee. Their bound requires a number of neurons per target-subnetwork weight that grows only logarithmically in the relevant variables other than depth.

The significance is a sharper theoretical relationship between overparameterization and what pruning can uncover. A smaller guaranteed overhead strengthens the claim that an untrained large network can already contain useful computational structure. The depth exception remains part of the result: the abstract does not claim logarithmic dependence on every aspect of network size. The contribution is specifically an improved existence and size guarantee for suitable subnetworks.
summary.tldr: Improved pruning theory reduces the overparameterization needed to contain an accurate untrained subnetwork to a logarithmic factor in variables other than depth.

title: Logarithmic Pruning is All You Need

abstract: Differential equations parameterized by neural networks become expensive to solve numerically as training progresses. We propose a remedy that encourages learned dynamics to be easier to solve. Specifically, we introduce a differentiable surrogate for the time cost of standard numerical solvers, using higher-order derivatives of solution trajectories. These derivatives are efficient to compute with Taylor-mode automatic differentiation. Optimizing this additional objective trades model performance against the time cost of solving the learned dynamics. We demonstrate our approach by training substantially faster, while nearly as accurate, models in supervised classification, density estimation, and time-series modelling tasks.

paragraphs: When neural networks parameterize differential equations, the learned dynamics can become increasingly expensive for numerical solvers during training. This paper makes that computational burden part of the learning objective. It encourages dynamics that remain easier to solve, alongside the objective associated with the model's prediction task.

The method introduces a differentiable proxy for the time required by standard numerical solvers. This proxy uses higher-order derivatives of solution trajectories, computed efficiently through Taylor-mode automatic differentiation. Because the proxy is differentiable, training can optimize it directly and influence the dynamics toward behavior associated with cheaper numerical solution.

Adding this objective creates an explicit tradeoff between model performance and solving time. Across supervised classification, density estimation, and time-series modelling, the authors demonstrate substantially faster models that remain nearly as accurate. The findings show that the difficulty of numerical solution can be addressed through what the model learns. Computational cost becomes a property to shape during training, alongside the quality of the model's outputs.
summary.tldr: A differentiable solver-cost objective trains neural differential equations that run substantially faster while remaining nearly as accurate.

title: Learning Differential Equations that are Easy to Solve

abstract: We investigate the problem of testing the global null in the high-dimensional regression models when the feature dimension $p$ grows proportionally to the number of observations $n$. Despite a number of prior work studying this problem, whether there exists a test that is model-agnostic, efficient to compute and enjoys a high power, still remains unsettled. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative by leveraging the random projection techniques, and propose a testing procedure that blends the classical $F$-test with a random projection step. When combined with a systematic choice of the projection dimension, the proposed procedure is proved to be minimax optimal and, meanwhile, reduces the computation and data storage requirements. We illustrate our results in various scenarios when the underlying feature matrix exhibits an intrinsic lower dimensional structure (such as approximate low-rank or has exponential/polynomial eigen-decay), and it turns out that the proposed test achieves sharp adaptive rates. Our theoretical findings are further validated by comparisons to other state-of-the-art tests on synthetic data.

paragraphs: This paper studies testing the global null in regression when the number of features grows proportionally with the number of observations. The aim is a test that combines broad applicability, computational efficiency, and strong statistical power. High dimensionality makes achieving these properties together a central challenge.

The proposed procedure combines random projection with the classical F-test. Projection reduces the dimension of the problem before testing, and the authors provide a systematic way to choose the projection dimension. With that choice, they prove minimax optimality while reducing computation and data-storage requirements. The dimension selection is therefore part of the statistical guarantee, not just an implementation choice.

The analysis also considers feature matrices with intrinsic lower-dimensional structure, including approximate low rank and particular patterns of eigenvalue decay. In these settings, the test achieves sharp adaptive rates. Comparisons with other state-of-the-art tests on synthetic data support the theoretical findings. The results connect dimension reduction to efficient hypothesis testing while showing how the guarantees respond to structure in the feature matrix.
summary.tldr: A randomly projected F-test combines reduced computation and storage with minimax-optimal testing under a systematic projection-dimension choice.

title: Randomized tests for high-dimensional regression: A more efficient and powerful solution

abstract: The classical analysis of online algorithms, due to its worst-case nature, can be quite pessimistic when the input instance at hand is far from worst-case. Often this is not an issue with machine learning approaches, which shine in exploiting patterns in past inputs in order to predict the future. However, such predictions, although usually accurate, can be arbitrarily poor. Inspired by a recent line of work, we augment three well-known online settings with machine learned predictions about the future, and develop algorithms that take them into account. In particular, we study the following online selection problems: (i) the classical secretary problem, (ii) online bipartite matching and (iii) the graphic matroid secretary problem. Our algorithms still come with a worst-case performance guarantee in the case that predictions are subpar while obtaining an improved competitive ratio (over the best-known classical online algorithm for each problem) when the predictions are sufficiently accurate. For each algorithm, we establish a trade-off between the competitive ratios obtained in the two respective cases.

paragraphs: Worst-case analysis can make online decision problems look pessimistic when actual inputs contain useful patterns. Predictions learned from past inputs may exploit those patterns, but they can also be arbitrarily poor. This paper develops algorithms that use predictions about the future while preserving a performance guarantee when that advice is unreliable.

The authors address three settings: the classical secretary problem, online bipartite matching, and the graphic matroid secretary problem. For each, they incorporate machine-learned predictions into the online selection process. Their guarantees distinguish between the case of sufficiently accurate predictions and the case of subpar predictions, making the role of advice explicit in the analysis.

With sufficiently accurate predictions, the algorithms improve the competitive ratio over the best-known classical online algorithm for each problem. They still retain a worst-case guarantee when predictions are poor. The paper establishes a trade-off between these two competitive ratios for each algorithm. Its contribution is a quantified way to balance the benefits of accurate forecasts against protection from unreliable ones across several selection problems.
summary.tldr: Prediction-assisted secretary and matching algorithms improve guarantees with sufficiently accurate advice while retaining worst-case protection when advice is poor.

title: Secretary and Online Matching Problems with Machine Learned Advice

abstract: Human reasoning involves recognising common underlying principles across many examples. The by-products of such reasoning are invariants that capture patterns such as "if someone went somewhere then they are there", expressed using variables "someone" and "somewhere" instead of mentioning specific people or places. Humans learn what variables are and how to use them at a young age. This paper explores whether machines can also learn and use variables solely from examples without requiring human pre-engineering. We propose Unification Networks, an end-to-end differentiable neural network approach capable of lifting examples into invariants and using those invariants to solve a given task. The core characteristic of our architecture is soft unification between examples that enables the network to generalise parts of the input into variables, thereby learning invariants. We evaluate our approach on five datasets to demonstrate that learning invariants captures patterns in the data and can improve performance over baselines.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a machine can learn reusable patterns expressed through variables directly from examples. A rule about a person moving to a place can apply across many people and places if those particulars are treated as variables. The aim is to learn this abstraction without requiring humans to pre-engineer the variables.

Unification Networks implement the idea in an end-to-end differentiable neural architecture. Their central mechanism is soft unification between examples, which lets the network generalize parts of an input into variables. The resulting invariants capture shared patterns across examples, and the network uses those patterns to solve the task. Learning the abstraction and applying it are therefore parts of the same trainable approach.

The authors evaluate the method on five datasets and show that learned invariants capture patterns in the data and can improve performance over baselines. The stated finding supports learning variable-based abstractions as a useful ingredient in neural reasoning. It does not claim that such abstractions improve every task, but demonstrates their potential through the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Unification Networks learn variable-based patterns from examples through soft unification and can use those patterns to improve task performance.

title: Learning Invariants through Soft Unification

abstract: We study the cluster recovery problem in the semi-supervised active clustering framework. Given a finite set of input points, and an oracle revealing whether any two points lie in the same cluster, our goal is to recover all clusters exactly using as few queries as possible. To this end, we relax the spherical $k$-means cluster assumption of Ashtiani et al.\ to allow for arbitrary ellipsoidal clusters with margin. This removes the assumption that the clustering is center-based (i.e., defined through an optimization problem), and includes all those cases where spherical clusters are individually transformed by any combination of rotations, axis scalings, and point deletions. We show that, even in this much more general setting, it is still possible to recover the latent clustering exactly using a number of queries that scales only logarithmically with the number of input points. More precisely, we design an algorithm that, given $n$ points to be partitioned into $k$ clusters, uses $O(k^3 \ln k \ln n)$ oracle queries and $\widetilde{O}(kn + k^3)$ time to recover the clustering with zero misclassification error. The $O(\cdot)$ notation hides an exponential dependence on the dimensionality of the clusters, which we show to be necessary thus characterizing the query complexity of the problem. Our algorithm is simple, easy to implement, and can also learn the clusters using low-stretch separators, a class of ellipsoids with additional theoretical guarantees. Experiments on large synthetic datasets confirm that we can reconstruct clusterings exactly and efficiently.

The objective is to recover every cluster exactly while asking few questions. It expands earlier spherical cluster assumptions to ellipsoidal clusters with a margin, accommodating rotations, unequal axis scaling, and deleted points.

summary.tldr: An active clustering algorithm exactly recovers separated ellipsoidal clusters with logarithmically many queries in dataset size, but exponential dependence on dimension.

title: Exact Recovery of Mangled Clusters with Same-Cluster Queries

abstract: A core problem in cognitive science and machine learning is to understand how humans derive semantic representations from perceptual objects, such as color from an apple, pleasantness from a musical chord, or seriousness from a face. Markov Chain Monte Carlo with People (MCMCP) is a prominent method for studying such representations, in which participants are presented with binary choice trials constructed such that the decisions follow a Markov Chain Monte Carlo acceptance rule. However, while MCMCP has strong asymptotic properties, its binary choice paradigm generates relatively little information per trial, and its local proposal function makes it slow to explore the parameter space and find the modes of the distribution. Here we therefore generalize MCMCP to a continuous-sampling paradigm, where in each iteration the participant uses a slider to continuously manipulate a single stimulus dimension to optimize a given criterion such as ‘pleasantness’. We formulate both methods from a utility-theory perspective, and show that the new method can be interpreted as ‘Gibbs Sampling with People’ (GSP). Further, we introduce an aggregation parameter to the transition step, and show that this parameter can be manipulated to flexibly shift between Gibbs sampling and deterministic optimization. In an initial study, we show GSP clearly outperforming MCMCP; we then show that GSP provides novel and interpretable results in three other domains, namely musical chords, vocal emotions, and faces. We validate these results through large-scale perceptual rating experiments. The final experiments use GSP to navigate the latent space of a state-of-the-art image synthesis network (StyleGAN), a promising approach for applying GSP to high-dimensional perceptual spaces. We conclude by discussing future cognitive applications and ethical implications.

title: Gibbs Sampling with People

abstract: Pre-trained language models like BERT and its variants have recently achieved impressive performance in various natural language understanding tasks. However, BERT heavily relies on the global self-attention block and thus suffers large memory footprint and computation cost. Although all its attention heads query on the whole input sequence for generating the attention map from a global perspective, we observe some heads only need to learn local dependencies, which means existence of computation redundancy. We therefore propose a novel span-based dynamic convolution to replace these self-attention heads to directly model local dependencies. The novel convolution heads, together with the rest self-attention heads, form a new mixed attention block that is more efficient at both global and local context learning. We equip BERT with this mixed attention design and build a ConvBERT model. Experiments have shown that ConvBERT significantly outperforms BERT and its variants in various downstream tasks, with lower training cost and fewer model parameters. Remarkably, ConvBERTbase model achieves 86.4 GLUE score, 0.7 higher than ELECTRAbase, using less than 1/4 training cost. Code and pre-trained models will be released.

paragraphs: BERT’s global self-attention is expensive, yet some attention heads mainly learn local dependencies. This paper treats that behavior as computational redundancy and proposes replacing those heads with span-based dynamic convolutions that directly model local context.

The remaining self-attention heads and new convolutional heads form a mixed attention block. ConvBERT incorporates this block into a BERT-style model, combining mechanisms for global and local information rather than making every head inspect the full sequence in the same way.

These figures describe the stated model comparison; the abstract does not provide a general cost bound or per-task results for every language-understanding application.
summary.tldr: ConvBERT combines local dynamic convolutions with global attention to reduce language-model training cost.

title: ConvBERT: Improving BERT with Span-based Dynamic Convolution

abstract: Feature attributions are a popular tool for explaining the behavior of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), but have recently been shown to be vulnerable to attacks that produce divergent explanations for nearby inputs. This lack of robustness is especially problematic in high-stakes applications where adversarially-manipulated explanations could impair safety and trustworthiness. Building on a geometric understanding of these attacks presented in recent work, we identify Lipschitz continuity conditions on models' gradient that lead to robust gradient-based attributions, and observe that smoothness may also be related to the ability of an attack to transfer across multiple attribution methods. To mitigate these attacks in practice, we propose an inexpensive regularization method that promotes these conditions in DNNs, as well as a stochastic smoothing technique that does not require re-training. Our experiments on a range of image models demonstrate that both of these mitigations consistently improve attribution robustness, and confirm the role that smooth geometry plays in these attacks on real, large-scale models.

paragraphs: Feature-attribution methods explain a network by assigning importance to parts of an input. Attacks can make those explanations differ sharply between nearby inputs, undermining their reliability. This paper studies that vulnerability through the geometry of the model, focusing on how rapidly its gradients change as inputs move.

The authors identify Lipschitz continuity conditions on model gradients that lead to robust gradient-based attributions. These conditions place bounds on gradient variation, linking smoother behavior to more stable explanations. They also observe that smoothness may help explain whether an attack transfers between attribution methods; that connection is presented as a possibility rather than a universal conclusion.

The paper proposes two mitigations: an inexpensive training regularizer that promotes the identified conditions, and stochastic smoothing that can be used without retraining. Experiments on multiple image models show that both consistently improve attribution robustness. The results connect a geometric explanation of the attacks with practical ways to reduce their effects on real, large-scale networks.
summary.tldr: Gradient-smoothness conditions motivate training regularization and retraining-free smoothing that improve attribution robustness in image-model experiments.

title: Smoothed Geometry for Robust Attribution

abstract: Although many fairness criteria have been proposed for decision making, their long-term impact on the well-being of a population remains unclear. In this work, we study the dynamics of population qualification and algorithmic decisions under a partially observed Markov decision problem setting. By characterizing the equilibrium of such dynamics, we analyze the long-term impact of static fairness constraints on the equality and improvement of group well-being. Our results show that static fairness constraints can either promote equality or exacerbate disparity depending on the driving factor of qualification transitions and the effect of sensitive attributes on feature distributions. We also consider possible interventions that can effectively improve group qualification or promote equality of group qualification. Our theoretical results and experiments on static real-world datasets with simulated dynamics show that our framework can be used to facilitate social science studies.

paragraphs: A fairness rule applied to decisions today does not by itself explain how a population will fare over time. This paper studies the interaction between algorithmic decisions and changes in group qualification. It uses a partially observed Markov decision framework to represent dynamics in which relevant population states are not fully observed.

The authors characterize equilibria of these dynamics to examine whether static fairness constraints improve group well-being and reduce inequality over the long term. Their results are conditional: the same broad type of constraint can promote equality or worsen disparities. The outcome depends on what drives qualification transitions and how sensitive attributes influence feature distributions.

The paper also considers interventions that can improve group qualification or promote equality between groups. Its evidence combines theoretical analysis with experiments using static real-world datasets and simulated dynamics. This makes the framework a tool for studying possible long-term effects, rather than direct evidence of observed population trajectories. The central lesson is that evaluating fairness over time requires modeling the processes through which qualification changes.
summary.tldr: A dynamic model shows that static fairness constraints can improve or worsen long-term group equality depending on qualification transitions and feature distributions.

title: How do fair decisions fare in long-term qualification?

abstract: Recent results in the ML community have revealed that learning algorithms used to compute the optimal strategy for the leader to commit to in a Stackelberg game, are susceptible to manipulation by the follower. Such a learning algorithm operates by querying the best responses or the payoffs of the follower, who consequently can deceive the algorithm by responding as if their payoffs were much different than what they actually are. For this strategic behavior to be successful, the main challenge faced by the follower is to pinpoint the payoffs that would make the learning algorithm compute a commitment so that best responding to it maximizes the follower's utility, according to the true payoffs. While this problem has been considered before, the related literature only focused on the simplified scenario in which the payoff space is finite, thus leaving the general version of the problem unanswered. In this paper, we fill this gap by showing that it is always possible for the follower to efficiently compute (near-)optimal payoffs for various scenarios of learning interaction between the leader and the follower.

paragraphs: In a Stackelberg game, a leader commits to a strategy and a follower responds. A learning leader may query the follower's payoffs or best responses to determine its commitment. Those queries create an opportunity for manipulation: the follower can answer as though it had different payoffs, influencing the strategy the leader chooses.

The follower's challenge is to select deceptive payoffs that induce a favorable commitment. Its eventual benefit must be evaluated using its true payoffs, after it best responds to that commitment. Finding suitable reported payoffs is therefore an optimization problem involving both the leader's learning process and the follower's actual preferences.

Earlier work considered a simplified version with a finite payoff space. This paper addresses the more general problem and shows that the follower can efficiently compute optimal or near-optimal deceptive payoffs in various learning-interaction scenarios. The result establishes that, within those scenarios, effective manipulation is computationally attainable and need not depend on restricting the possible payoffs to a finite set.
summary.tldr: Followers can efficiently compute optimal or near-optimal deceptive payoffs in several Stackelberg learning scenarios beyond finite payoff spaces.

title: Optimally Deceiving a Learning Leader in Stackelberg Games

abstract: Given taxi-ride counts information between departure and destination locations, how can we forecast their future demands? In general, given a data stream of events with seasonal patterns that innovate over time, how can we effectively and efficiently forecast future events? In this paper, we propose Shifting Seasonal Matrix Factorization approach, namely SSMF, that can adaptively learn multiple seasonal patterns (called regimes), as well as switching between them. Our proposed method has the following properties: (a) it accurately forecasts future events by detecting regime shifts in seasonal patterns as the data stream evolves; (b) it works in an online setting, i.e., processes each observation in constant time and memory; (c) it effectively realizes regime shifts without human intervention by using a lossless data compression scheme. We demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods by accurately forecasting upcoming events on three real-world data streams.

paragraphs: Seasonal patterns in a data stream can change over time, making forecasting harder than simply learning one repeating cycle. This paper proposes Shifting Seasonal Matrix Factorization, or SSMF, to learn multiple seasonal patterns and switch between them as observations arrive. Forecasting taxi trips between departure and destination locations is one motivating example.

The method calls these different seasonal patterns regimes. It detects changes between regimes as the stream evolves and adapts its forecasts accordingly. A lossless data compression scheme supports the switching process without human intervention, making regime changes part of the automatic forecasting procedure rather than something an operator must specify.

SSMF operates online, with constant time and memory per observation as stated in the abstract. This makes its adaptation relevant to continuing streams rather than only fixed historical datasets. Experiments on three real-world streams show more accurate forecasts than the state-of-the-art baseline methods considered. The contribution combines multiple seasonal regimes, automatic switching, and bounded per-observation processing into one forecasting approach for evolving event data.
summary.tldr: SSMF forecasts evolving data streams by automatically learning and switching seasonal regimes with constant per-observation time and memory.

title: SSMF: Shifting Seasonal Matrix Factorization

abstract: The fine-tuning of pre-trained language models has a great success in many NLP fields. Yet, it is strikingly vulnerable to adversarial examples, e.g., word substitution attacks using only synonyms can easily fool a BERT-based sentiment analysis model. In this paper, we demonstrate that adversarial training, the prevalent defense technique, does not directly fit a conventional fine-tuning scenario, because it suffers severely from catastrophic forgetting: failing to retain the generic and robust linguistic features that have already been captured by the pre-trained model. In this light, we propose Robust Informative Fine-Tuning (RIFT), a novel adversarial fine-tuning method from an information-theoretical perspective. In particular, RIFT encourages an objective model to retain the features learned from the pre-trained model throughout the entire fine-tuning process, whereas a conventional one only uses the pre-trained weights for initialization. Experimental results show that RIFT consistently outperforms the state-of-the-arts on two popular NLP tasks: sentiment analysis and natural language inference, under different attacks across various pre-trained language models.

paragraphs: Fine-tuned language models can be fooled by small wording changes, including substitutions with synonyms. Although adversarial training is a common defense, this paper finds that applying it in the conventional fine-tuning setup can cause catastrophic forgetting. The model loses generic, robust linguistic features that it had already acquired during pre-training.

The proposed method, Robust Informative Fine-Tuning, or RIFT, addresses that loss using an information-theoretic perspective. It encourages the task model to preserve features from its pre-trained counterpart throughout fine-tuning. This gives the pre-trained representation an ongoing role in learning, extending its contribution beyond supplying the initial weights.

Experiments cover sentiment analysis and natural language inference, using different attacks and several pre-trained language models. RIFT consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in those reported evaluations. The findings support the paper's diagnosis that retaining useful pre-trained features is relevant to adversarial robustness. They also motivate treating robustness-oriented fine-tuning as a problem of preserving existing knowledge while adapting it to a task.
summary.tldr: RIFT improves adversarial fine-tuning by encouraging language models to retain robust features learned during pre-training.

title: How Should Pre-Trained Language Models Be Fine-Tuned Towards Adversarial Robustness?

abstract: We consider the problem of searching an input maximizing a black-box objective function given a static dataset of input-output queries. A popular approach to solving this problem is maintaining a proxy model, e.g., a deep neural network (DNN), that approximates the true objective function. Here, the main challenge is how to avoid adversarially optimized inputs during the search, i.e., the inputs where the DNN highly overestimates the true objective function. To handle the issue, we propose a new framework, coined robust model adaptation (RoMA), based on gradient-based optimization of inputs over the DNN. Specifically, it consists of two steps: (a) a pre-training strategy to robustly train the proxy model and (b) a novel adaptation procedure of the proxy model to have robust estimates for a specific set of candidate solutions. At a high level, our scheme utilizes the local smoothness prior to overcome the brittleness of the DNN. Experiments under various tasks show the effectiveness of RoMA compared with previous methods, obtaining state-of-the-art results, e.g., RoMA outperforms all at 4 out of 6 tasks and achieves runner-up results at the remaining tasks.

paragraphs: Offline model-based optimization seeks a high-scoring input using only a fixed dataset of previous input-output measurements. A neural proxy can approximate the unknown objective, but optimizing inputs against it creates a problem: the search may discover inputs for which the proxy badly overestimates the true score. Apparent progress can therefore reflect model error.

RoMA addresses this issue with two stages. It first trains the proxy using a strategy intended to improve robustness. It then adapts the proxy to produce robust estimates for a particular set of candidate solutions while using gradients to optimize inputs. The framework relies on a local smoothness prior to reduce the neural model's brittleness.

Across six reported tasks, RoMA achieves the best results on four and the second-best results on the remaining two. These experiments support combining robust initial training with adaptation around candidate solutions. The practical idea is to improve the model precisely where its predictions guide the search, reducing the opportunity for optimization to exploit exaggerated estimates.
summary.tldr: RoMA combines robust proxy training and candidate-specific adaptation to reduce overestimation during offline input optimization.

title: RoMA: Robust Model Adaptation for Offline Model-based Optimization

abstract: Language models can generate harmful and biased outputs and exhibit undesirable behavior according to a given cultural context. We propose a Process for Adapting Language Models to Society (PALMS) with Values-Targeted Datasets, an iterative process to significantly change model behavior by crafting and fine-tuning on a dataset that reflects a predetermined set of target values. We evaluate our process using three metrics: quantitative metrics with human evaluations that score output adherence to a target value, toxicity scoring on outputs; and qualitative metrics analyzing the most common word associated with a given social category. Through each iteration, we add additional training dataset examples based on observed shortcomings from evaluations. PALMS performs significantly better on all metrics compared to baseline and control models for a broad range of GPT-3 language model sizes without compromising capability integrity. We find that the effectiveness of PALMS increases with model size. We show that significantly adjusting language model behavior is feasible with a small, hand-curated dataset.

paragraphs: PALMS studies how to adjust a language model's behavior toward a predetermined set of values. The motivation is that generated language can be harmful, biased, or undesirable within a particular cultural context. The proposed process uses a small, manually curated dataset whose examples reflect the chosen behavioral targets.

The process alternates fine-tuning with evaluation. Human judgments assess whether outputs follow the target values, toxicity scoring measures another aspect of output behavior, and qualitative analysis examines words commonly associated with social categories. Shortcomings found through these evaluations guide the addition of further training examples. The dataset therefore develops in response to observed model behavior.

Across a broad range of GPT-3 model sizes, PALMS performs significantly better than baseline and control models on all reported evaluation measures without compromising capability integrity. Its effectiveness increases with model size in the reported study. These findings show that a small curated dataset can substantially change behavior toward specified values; the targets remain those selected for the process and its cultural context.
summary.tldr: PALMS iteratively curates fine-tuning examples to move language-model behavior toward specified values, with stronger reported effects in larger models.

title: Process for Adapting Language Models to Society (PALMS) with Values-Targeted Datasets

abstract: The world provides us with data of multiple modalities. Intuitively, models fusing data from different modalities outperform their uni-modal counterparts, since more information is aggregated. Recently, joining the success of deep learning, there is an influential line of work on deep multi-modal learning, which has remarkable empirical results on various applications. However, theoretical justifications in this field are notably lacking. Can multi-modal learning provably perform better than uni-modal?In this paper, we answer this question under a most popular multi-modal fusion framework, which firstly encodes features from different modalities into a common latent space and seamlessly maps the latent representations into the task space. We prove that learning with multiple modalities achieves a smaller population risk than only using its subset of modalities. The main intuition is that the former has a more accurate estimate of the latent space representation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical treatment to capture important qualitative phenomena observed in real multi-modal applications from the generalization perspective. Combining with experiment results, we show that multi-modal learning does possess an appealing formal guarantee.

paragraphs: Combining several data modalities often improves empirical performance, but an intuitive appeal to additional information does not by itself explain when learning should improve. This paper develops a theoretical account within a common fusion framework: features from different modalities enter a shared latent representation, which is then mapped to the task output.

Within the framework studied, the authors prove that learning with multiple modalities achieves lower population risk than learning with only a subset. The explanation centers on the quality of the latent representation: the additional modalities allow it to be estimated more accurately. This links the benefit of fusion to representation learning and performance on the underlying data population.

The paper combines its analysis with experimental results to support the formal account. Its contribution is a generalization-based explanation for qualitative behavior observed in multimodal applications. The guarantee belongs to the analyzed fusion setting; it should not be read as saying that adding any modality to any system must improve predictions. The result clarifies how better shared representations can support a multimodal advantage.
summary.tldr: Within a shared-latent-space fusion framework, the paper proves a multimodal population-risk advantage through more accurate latent representations.

title: What Makes Multi-Modal Learning Better than Single (Provably)

abstract: The ability to train complex and highly effective models often requires an abundance of training data, which can easily become a bottleneck in cost, time, and computational resources. Batch active learning, which adaptively issues batched queries to a labeling oracle, is a common approach for addressing this problem. The practical benefits of batch sampling come with the downside of less adaptivity and the risk of sampling redundant examples within a batch -- a risk that grows with the batch size. In this work, we analyze an efficient active learning algorithm, which focuses on the large batch setting. In particular, we show that our sampling method, which combines notions of uncertainty and diversity, easily scales to batch sizes (100K-1M) several orders of magnitude larger than used in previous studies and provides significant improvements in model training efficiency compared to recent baselines. Finally, we provide an initial theoretical analysis, proving label complexity guarantees for a related sampling method, which we show is approximately equivalent to our sampling method in specific settings.

paragraphs: Active learning selects examples to send for labeling, aiming to make model training more efficient. Requesting labels in batches is convenient at scale, but it reduces opportunities to adapt between selections. Large batches also risk containing many redundant examples, so increasing batch size can weaken the value of each labeling request.

This paper analyzes an efficient selection algorithm designed specifically for large batches. The method combines uncertainty with diversity: it considers both which examples the model is unsure about and how much variety the selected batch contains. This combination addresses the possibility that many individually informative examples convey much the same information when selected together.

The reported experiments scale to batches of 100,000 to one million examples, several orders of magnitude beyond earlier studies, and show significant training-efficiency improvements over recent baselines. The theoretical contribution is more qualified: label-complexity guarantees apply to a related sampling method that is approximately equivalent to the proposed method in specific settings. Together, the results provide practical evidence at large scale and an initial theoretical account of why the sampling strategy can help.
summary.tldr: Combining uncertainty and diversity enables active learning with very large labeling batches while improving reported training efficiency.

title: Batch Active Learning at Scale

abstract: Empowered by neural networks, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) achieves tremendous empirical success. However, DRL requires a large dataset by interacting with the environment, which is unrealistic in critical scenarios such as autonomous driving and personalized medicine. In this paper, we study how to incorporate the dataset collected in the offline setting to improve the sample efficiency in the online setting. To incorporate the observational data, we face two challenges. (a) The behavior policy that generates the observational data may depend on unobserved random variables (confounders), which affect the received rewards and transition dynamics. (b) Exploration in the online setting requires quantifying the uncertainty given both the observational and interventional data. To tackle such challenges, we propose the deconfounded optimistic value iteration (DOVI) algorithm, which incorporates the confounded observational data in a provably efficient manner. DOVI explicitly adjusts for the confounding bias in the observational data, where the confounders are partially observed or unobserved. In both cases, such adjustments allow us to construct the bonus based on a notion of information gain, which takes into account the amount of information acquired from the offline setting. In particular, we prove that the regret of DOVI is smaller than the optimal regret achievable in the pure online setting when the confounded observational data are informative upon the adjustments.

paragraphs: This paper asks how previously collected observational data can reduce the amount of new interaction required for reinforcement learning. A central difficulty is confounding: unobserved variables may influence both the behavior policy that collected the data and the rewards or transitions. Online exploration must also account for uncertainty using both old observations and new interventions.

The authors consider cases with partially observed confounders and cases with unobserved confounders. These adjustments support an exploration bonus based on information gain that accounts for information already obtained from the offline dataset.

Thus, the benefit depends on what useful information survives correction for confounding. The contribution connects causal adjustment with exploration incentives, showing how appropriately handled offline evidence can provably improve online learning efficiency.
summary.tldr: DOVI provably improves online reinforcement-learning regret when confounded offline data are informative after causal adjustment.

title: Provably Efficient Causal Reinforcement Learning with Confounded Observational Data

abstract: Empirically it has been observed that the performance of deep neural networks steadily improves with increased model size, contradicting the classical view on overfitting and generalization. Recently, the double descent phenomenon has been proposed to reconcile this observation with theory, suggesting that the test error has a second descent when the model becomes sufficiently overparameterized, as the model size itself acts as an implicit regularizer. In this paper we add to the growing body of work in this space, providing a careful study of learning dynamics as a function of model size for the least squares scenario. We show an excess risk bound for the gradient descent solution of the least squares objective. The bound depends on the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the sample covariance matrix of the input features, via a functional form that has the double descent behaviour. This gives a new perspective on the double descent curves reported in the literature, as our analysis of the excess risk allows to decouple the effect of optimization and generalization error. In particular, we find that in the case of noiseless regression, double descent is explained solely by optimization-related quantities, which was missed in studies focusing on the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse solution. We believe that our derivation provides an alternative view compared to existing works, shedding some light on a possible cause of this phenomenon, at least in the considered least squares setting. We empirically explore if our predictions hold for neural networks, in particular whether the spectrum of the sample covariance of features at intermediary hidden layers has a similar behaviour as the one predicted by our derivations in the least squares setting.

This paper investigates how optimization contributes to that pattern in least-squares regression. Instead of analyzing only a final algebraic solution, it studies gradient descent and how its learning dynamics change with model size.

That exploration asks whether the spectral behavior predicted in the simpler setting appears in learned neural representations.
summary.tldr: A least-squares analysis separates optimization from generalization and attributes noiseless double descent to optimization-related spectral quantities.

title: On the Role of Optimization in Double Descent: A Least Squares Study

abstract: We present 360-MLC, a self-training method based on multi-view layout consistency for finetuning monocular room-layout models using unlabeled 360-images only. This can be valuable in practical scenarios where a pre-trained model needs to be adapted to a new data domain without using any ground truth annotations. Our simple yet effective assumption is that multiple layout estimations in the same scene must define a consistent geometry regardless of their camera positions. Based on this idea, we leverage a pre-trained model to project estimated layout boundaries from several camera views into the 3D world coordinate. Then, we re-project them back to the spherical coordinate and build a probability function, from which we sample the pseudo-labels for self-training. To handle unconfident pseudo-labels, we evaluate the variance in the re-projected boundaries as an uncertainty value to weight each pseudo-label in our loss function during training. In addition, since ground truth annotations are not available during training nor in testing, we leverage the entropy information in multiple layout estimations as a quantitative metric to measure the geometry consistency of the scene, allowing us to evaluate any layout estimator for hyper-parameter tuning, including model selection without ground truth annotations. Experimental results show that our solution achieves favorable performance against state-of-the-art methods when self-training from three publicly available source datasets to a unique, newly labeled dataset consisting of multi-view images of the same scenes.

paragraphs: 360-MLC adapts a pretrained room-layout predictor to a new domain using unlabeled panoramic images. Its central assumption is geometric: predictions made from different camera positions in the same room should describe a consistent layout. Agreement across views therefore provides a learning signal when annotated room boundaries are unavailable.

The method projects predicted boundaries from several views into shared three-dimensional coordinates, then projects them back into spherical image coordinates. It constructs a probability function from these predictions and samples pseudo-labels for training. Where the projected boundaries disagree, their variance serves as an uncertainty estimate, reducing the influence of less confident pseudo-labels.

The paper also uses entropy across layout estimates to measure geometric consistency. This gives a way to tune hyperparameters and select models without ground-truth annotations. Experiments adapting from three public source datasets to a newly labeled dataset of multiple views per scene report favorable performance against leading methods. The contribution connects adaptation and model selection through the same cross-view consistency principle.
summary.tldr: 360-MLC uses agreement across panoramic views to adapt room-layout models and select hyperparameters without ground-truth annotations.

title: 360-MLC: Multi-view Layout Consistency for Self-training and Hyper-parameter Tuning

abstract: Recent work has seen the development of general purpose neural architectures that can be trained to perform tasks across diverse data modalities. General purpose models typically make few assumptions about the underlying data-structure and are known to perform well in the large-data regime. At the same time, there has been growing interest in modular neural architectures that represent the data using sparsely interacting modules. These models can be more robust out-of-distribution, computationally efficient, and capable of sample-efficient adaptation to new data. However, they tend to make domain-specific assumptions about the data, and present challenges in how module behavior (i.e., parameterization) and connectivity (i.e., their layout) can be jointly learned. In this work, we introduce a general purpose, yet modular neural architecture called Neural Attentive Circuits (NACs) that jointly learns the parameterization and a sparse connectivity of neural modules without using domain knowledge. NACs are best understood as the combination of two systems that are jointly trained end-to-end: one that determines the module configuration and the other that executes it on an input. We demonstrate qualitatively that NACs learn diverse and meaningful module configurations on the Natural Language and Visual Reasoning for Real (NLVR2) dataset without additional supervision. Quantitatively, we show that by incorporating modularity in this way, NACs improve upon a strong non-modular baseline in terms of low-shot adaptation on CIFAR and Caltech-UCSD Birds dataset (CUB) by about 10 percent, and OOD robustness on Tiny ImageNet-R by about 2.5 percent. Further, we find that NACs can achieve an 8x speedup at inference time while losing less than 3 percent performance. Finally, we find NACs to yield competitive results on diverse data modalities spanning point-cloud classification, symbolic processing and text-classification from ASCII bytes, thereby confirming its general purpose nature.

title: Neural Attentive Circuits

abstract: Succinct representation of complex signals using coordinate-based neural representations (CNRs) has seen great progress, and several recent efforts focus on extending them for handling videos. Here, the main challenge is how to (a) alleviate a compute-inefficiency in training CNRs to (b) achieve high-quality video encoding while (c) maintaining the parameter-efficiency. To meet all requirements (a), (b), and (c) simultaneously, we propose neural video representations with learnable positional features (NVP), a novel CNR by introducing "learnable positional features" that effectively amortize a video as latent codes. Specifically, we first present a CNR architecture based on designing 2D latent keyframes to learn the common video contents across each spatio-temporal axis, which dramatically improves all of those three requirements. Then, we propose to utilize existing powerful image and video codecs as a compute-/memory-efficient compression procedure of latent codes. We demonstrate the superiority of NVP on the popular UVG benchmark; compared with prior arts, NVP not only trains 2 times faster (less than 5 minutes) but also exceeds their encoding quality as 34.07$\rightarrow$34.57 (measured with the PSNR metric), even using $>$8 times fewer parameters. We also show intriguing properties of NVP, e.g., video inpainting, video frame interpolation, etc.

paragraphs: Representing a video with a coordinate-based neural network requires balancing training cost, reconstruction quality, and parameter count. Improving one can make another less attractive. Neural Video Representations with Learnable Positional Features, or NVP, addresses these objectives together by storing shared video content in learned latent features.

The architecture uses two-dimensional latent keyframes designed to capture common content across spatial and temporal axes. These learnable positional features encode information that the coordinate-based representation can reuse. The authors also compress the latent codes with existing image and video codecs, connecting the neural representation to established compression tools for computational and memory efficiency.

On the UVG benchmark, NVP trains twice as fast as prior approaches, taking less than five minutes, while using more than eight times fewer parameters. Reported reconstruction quality rises from 34.07 to 34.57 in PSNR. The paper also demonstrates video inpainting and frame interpolation. Together, the findings show that learned latent positional information can improve the reported quality, training-speed, and parameter-efficiency tradeoff while supporting additional video operations.
summary.tldr: NVP uses learned latent keyframes to improve neural video encoding quality while reducing training time and parameter count.

title: Scalable Neural Video Representations with Learnable Positional Features

abstract: Differentially private mechanisms protect privacy by introducing additional randomness into the data. Restricting access to only the privatized data makes it challenging to perform valid statistical inference on parameters underlying the confidential data. Specifically, the likelihood function of the privatized data requires integrating over the large space of confidential databases and is typically intractable. For Bayesian analysis, this results in a posterior distribution that is doubly intractable, rendering traditional MCMC techniques inapplicable. We propose an MCMC framework to perform Bayesian inference from the privatized data, which is applicable to a wide range of statistical models and privacy mechanisms. Our MCMC algorithm augments the model parameters with the unobserved confidential data, and alternately updates each one. For the potentially challenging step of updating the confidential data, we propose a generic approach that exploits the privacy guarantee of the mechanism to ensure efficiency. We give results on the computational complexity, acceptance rate, and mixing properties of our MCMC. We illustrate the efficacy and applicability of our methods on a naïve-Bayes log-linear model and on a linear regression model.

paragraphs: Differential privacy adds randomness to released data, which complicates statistical inference about the confidential data that generated it. Computing the likelihood of a private release can require integrating over a huge space of possible confidential databases. For Bayesian analysis, the resulting posterior is doubly intractable, making traditional MCMC techniques inapplicable in the setting described.

The proposed framework introduces the unobserved confidential data as additional variables alongside the model parameters. Its sampling algorithm alternates between updating these two groups. This turns the hidden database into part of the inference procedure. For the difficult confidential-data update, the authors develop a generic approach that uses the privacy mechanism’s guarantee to support efficient sampling.

The paper provides results on computational complexity, acceptance rates, and mixing, addressing both the cost of sampling and how the chain explores its target distribution. Demonstrations use a naïve-Bayes log-linear model and linear regression. The framework is intended to cover a broad range of statistical models and privacy mechanisms, providing a route to Bayesian inference that explicitly accounts for the privatization process.
summary.tldr: The framework alternates between hidden confidential data and model parameters to make Bayesian inference from privatized releases tractable.

title: Data Augmentation MCMC for Bayesian Inference from Privatized Data

abstract: We study envy-free policy teaching. A number of agents independently explore a common Markov decision process (MDP), but each with their own reward function and discounting rate. A teacher wants to teach a target policy to this diverse group of agents, by means of modifying the agents' reward functions: providing additional bonuses to certain actions, or penalizing them. When personalized reward modification programs are used, an important question is how to design the programs so that the agents think they are treated fairly. We adopt the notion of envy-freeness (EF) from the literature on fair division to formalize this problem and investigate several fundamental questions about the existence of EF solutions in our setting, the computation of cost-minimizing solutions, as well as the price of fairness (PoF), which measures the increase of cost due to the consideration of fairness. We show that 1) an EF solution may not exist if penalties are not allowed in the modifications, but otherwise always exists. 2) Computing a cost-minimizing EF solution can be formulated as convex optimization and hence solved efficiently. 3) The PoF increases but at most quadratically with the geometric sum of the discount factor, and at most linearly with the size of the MDP and the number of agents involved; we present tight asymptotic bounds on the PoF. These results indicate that fairness can be incorporated in multi-agent teaching without significant computational or PoF burdens.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a teacher can encourage several agents to follow a target policy while treating them fairly. The agents explore the same Markov decision process independently, but have different rewards and discounting rates. The teacher can personalize incentives by adding bonuses or penalties to particular actions, raising the question of whether agents prefer someone else's incentive program.

The authors formalize fairness through envy-freeness and examine whether fair teaching programs exist, how to minimize their cost, and how much extra cost fairness imposes. They show that an envy-free solution may fail to exist when only bonuses are permitted. Allowing penalties restores existence in their setting. Finding a minimum-cost envy-free solution can be expressed as convex optimization and solved efficiently.

The analysis also bounds the price of fairness. It grows at most quadratically with the geometric sum associated with discounting, and at most linearly with the size of the decision process and number of agents. Tight asymptotic bounds characterize this growth, showing how fairness costs scale with the teaching problem.
summary.tldr: Fair personalized incentives can efficiently teach a shared policy, with existence guaranteed when penalties are allowed.

title: Envy-free Policy Teaching to Multiple Agents

abstract: Stochastic Programming is a powerful modeling framework for decision-making under uncertainty. In this work, we tackle two-stage stochastic programs (2SPs), the most widely used class of stochastic programming models. Solving 2SPs exactly requires optimizing over an expected value function that is computationally intractable. Having a mixed-integer linear program (MIP) or a nonlinear program (NLP) in the second stage further aggravates the intractability, even when specialized algorithms that exploit problem structure are employed.Finding high-quality (first-stage) solutions -- without leveraging problem structure -- can be crucial in such settings. We develop Neur2SP, a new method that approximates the expected value function via a neural network to obtain a surrogate model that can be solved more efficiently than the traditional extensive formulation approach. Neur2SP makes no assumptions about the problem structure, in particular about the second-stage problem, and can be implemented using an off-the-shelf MIP solver. Our extensive computational experiments on four benchmark 2SP problem classes with different structures (containing MIP and NLP second-stage problems) demonstrate the efficiency (time) and efficacy (solution quality) of Neur2SP. In under 1.66 seconds, Neur2SP finds high-quality solutions across all problems even as the number of scenarios increases, an ideal property that is difficult to have for traditional 2SP solution techniques. Namely, the most generic baseline method typically requires minutes to hours to find solutions of comparable quality.

Mixed-integer or nonlinear second-stage problems make this challenge more severe, including when specialized algorithms exploit available structure.

The authors report high-quality solutions in under 1.66 seconds across the tested problems, even as scenario counts increase. The most generic baseline typically takes minutes to hours for comparable quality. These results support the surrogate’s efficiency and solution quality in the evaluated settings, with approximate modeling central to the approach.
summary.tldr: Neur2SP replaces an expensive expected-value function with a neural surrogate to efficiently find high-quality two-stage stochastic decisions.

title: Neur2SP: Neural Two-Stage Stochastic Programming

abstract: Sketching is an important tool for dealing with high-dimensional vectors that are sparse (or well-approximated by a sparse vector), especially useful in distributed, parallel, and streaming settings.It is known that sketches can be made differentially private by adding noise according to the sensitivity of the sketch, and this has been used in private analytics and federated learning settings.The post-processing property of differential privacy implies that \emph{all} estimates computed from the sketch can be released within the given privacy budget.In this paper we consider the classical CountSketch, made differentially private with the Gaussian mechanism, and give an improved analysis of its estimation error.Perhaps surprisingly, the privacy-utility trade-off is essentially the best one could hope for, independent of the number of repetitions in CountSketch:The error is almost identical to the error from non-private CountSketch plus the noise needed to make the vector private in the original, high-dimensional domain.
