paragraphs: Sketches compress high-dimensional vectors into smaller representations that still support useful estimates, particularly when the vectors are sparse or nearly sparse. They are valuable in distributed and streaming computation. Differential privacy can be added by introducing noise calibrated to the sketch's sensitivity, but the resulting estimation error determines how useful the private sketch remains.

This paper gives an improved error analysis for CountSketch made private with Gaussian noise. Its main finding is that the privacy-utility tradeoff is essentially as favorable as one could hope for. The estimation error is almost the same as ordinary CountSketch error plus the noise needed to privatize the original high-dimensional vector.

Crucially, this near-ideal tradeoff is independent of CountSketch's number of repetitions. The result sharpens the understanding of an existing private sketch construction rather than introducing a different compression method. Differential privacy's post-processing property also means that all estimates derived from the private sketch can be released within its privacy budget, making the accuracy analysis relevant to multiple downstream uses.
summary.tldr: An improved analysis shows Gaussian-private CountSketch achieves a near-ideal privacy-accuracy tradeoff independent of its number of repetitions.

title: Improved Utility Analysis of Private CountSketch

abstract: Training and evaluating language models increasingly requires the construction of meta-datasets -- diverse collections of curated data with clear provenance. Natural language prompting has recently lead to improved zero-shot generalization by transforming existing, supervised datasets into a variety of novel instruction tuning tasks, highlighting the benefits of meta-dataset curation. While successful in general-domain text, translating these data-centric approaches to biomedical language modeling remains challenging, as labeled biomedical datasets are significantly underrepresented in popular data hubs. To address this challenge, we introduce BigBio a community library of 126+ biomedical NLP datasets, currently covering 13 task categories and 10+ languages. BigBio facilitates reproducible meta-dataset curation via programmatic access to datasets and their metadata, and is compatible with current platforms for prompt engineering and end-to-end few/zero shot language model evaluation. We discuss our process for task schema harmonization, data auditing, contribution guidelines, and outline two illustrative use cases: zero-shot evaluation of biomedical prompts and large-scale, multi-task learning. BigBio is an ongoing community effort and is available at https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/biomedical

paragraphs: Building and evaluating language models increasingly involves combining many curated datasets whose origins are clearly documented. Biomedical datasets are underrepresented in popular data hubs, making this approach harder to apply to biomedical language. BigBio addresses that infrastructure problem through a community library containing more than 126 datasets across 13 task categories and more than 10 languages.

The framework provides programmatic access to both datasets and their metadata, helping researchers assemble collections reproducibly. It also works with platforms for creating prompts and evaluating language models with few examples or no task-specific examples. The paper describes how task schemas are harmonized, how data is audited, and how community contributions are organized.

Two illustrative uses connect this infrastructure to research practice: evaluating biomedical prompts in a zero-shot setting and conducting large-scale learning across multiple tasks. The contribution is a shared foundation for those activities. By making diverse biomedical resources easier to access and combine, BigBio supports systematic data-centered experimentation as an ongoing community effort.
summary.tldr: BigBio organizes biomedical language datasets and metadata into a reproducible community framework for prompting, evaluation, and multitask learning.

title: BigBio: A Framework for Data-Centric Biomedical Natural Language Processing

abstract: Most cross-device federated learning (FL) studies focus on the model-homogeneous setting where the global server model and local client models are identical. However, such constraint not only excludes low-end clients who would otherwise make unique contributions to model training but also restrains clients from training large models due to on-device resource bottlenecks. In this work, we propose FedRolex, a partial training (PT)-based approach that enables model-heterogeneous FL and can train a global server model larger than the largest client model. At its core, FedRolex employs a rolling sub-model extraction scheme that allows different parts of the global server model to be evenly trained, which mitigates the client drift induced by the inconsistency between individual client models and server model architectures. Empirically, we show that FedRolex outperforms state-of-the-art PT-based model-heterogeneous FL methods (e.g. Federated Dropout) and reduces the gap between model-heterogeneous and model-homogeneous FL, especially under the large-model large-dataset regime. In addition, we provide theoretical statistical analysis on its advantage over Federated Dropout. Lastly, we evaluate FedRolex on an emulated real-world device distribution to show that FedRolex can enhance the inclusiveness of FL and boost the performance of low-end devices that would otherwise not benefit from FL. Our code is available at: https://github.com/AIoT-MLSys-Lab/FedRolex.

paragraphs: Federated learning often assumes that every participating device trains the same model as the server. That requirement can exclude devices with limited resources and constrain the size of the shared model. FedRolex allows clients to train smaller models, including a setting where the server model exceeds the size of every individual client model.

Its central mechanism is rolling sub-model extraction. Different portions of the server model are selected over time so that its parts receive even training. This partial-training approach addresses client drift associated with mismatches between client and server architectures. It lets devices contribute within their own resource limits while collectively training a larger model.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art partial-training approaches, including Federated Dropout, and a smaller gap from model-homogeneous learning, especially with large models and datasets. A theoretical statistical analysis also supports its advantage over Federated Dropout. Under an emulated real-world device distribution, FedRolex improves participation and performance for low-end devices that otherwise would not benefit from federated learning.
summary.tldr: FedRolex rotates client sub-models to train a larger shared model while improving participation by resource-limited devices.

title: FedRolex: Model-Heterogeneous Federated Learning with Rolling Sub-Model Extraction

abstract: Branch-and-bound approaches in integer programming require ordering portions of the space to explore next, a problem known as node comparison. We propose a new siamese graph neural network model to tackle this problem, where the nodes are represented as bipartite graphs with attributes. Similar to prior work, we train our model to imitate a diving oracle that plunges towards the optimal solution. We evaluate our method by solving the instances in a plain framework where the nodes are explored according to their rank. On three NP-hard benchmarks chosen to be particularly primal-difficult, our approach leads to faster solving and smaller branch- and-bound trees than the default ranking function of the open-source solver SCIP, as well as competing machine learning methods. Moreover, these results generalize to instances larger than used for training. Code for reproducing the experiments can be found at https://github.com/ds4dm/learn2comparenodes.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solves integer programming problems by exploring portions of a search space. Its node-comparison rule determines which portion to investigate next, so that ordering influences how the search proceeds. This paper learns the comparison rule with a graph neural network, using structured representations of the candidate search nodes.

Each search node is represented as a bipartite graph carrying attributes. A siamese graph neural network compares these representations, and training imitates a diving oracle that heads toward an optimal solution. The learned comparisons then determine node ranks in a plain evaluation framework where exploration follows that ranking.

On three NP-hard benchmarks selected to be particularly difficult for finding feasible solutions, the method solves instances faster and produces smaller search trees than SCIP's default ranking rule and competing machine learning approaches. The reported advantages also extend to instances larger than those used in training. These results support learned graph-based comparisons as a way to improve search ordering in the tested setting, including beyond the training instance sizes.
summary.tldr: A siamese graph neural network learns branch-and-bound node rankings that yield faster solving and smaller search trees on three challenging benchmarks.

title: Learning to Compare Nodes in Branch and Bound with Graph Neural Networks

abstract: 3D segmentation of nuclei images is a fundamental task for many biological studies. Despite the rapid advances of large-volume 3D imaging acquisition methods and the emergence of sophisticated algorithms to segment the nuclei in recent years, a benchmark with all cells completely annotated is still missing, making it hard to accurately assess and further improve the performance of the algorithms. The existing nuclei segmentation benchmarks either worked on 2D only or annotated a small number of 3D cells, perhaps due to the high cost of 3D annotation for large-scale data. To fulfill the critical need, we constructed NIS3D, a 3D, high cell density, large-volume, and completely annotated Nuclei Image Segmentation benchmark, assisted by our newly designed semi-automatic annotation software. NIS3D provides more than 22,000 cells across multiple most-used species in this area. Each cell is labeled by three independent annotators, so we can measure the variability of each annotation. A confidence score is computed for each cell, allowing more nuanced testing and performance comparison. A comprehensive review on the methods of segmenting 3D dense nuclei was conducted. The benchmark was used to evaluate the performance of several selected state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. The best of current methods is still far away from human-level accuracy, corroborating the necessity of generating such a benchmark. The testing results also demonstrated the strength and weakness of each method and pointed out the directions of further methodological development. The dataset can be downloaded here: https://github.com/yu-lab-vt/NIS3D.

paragraphs: Separating individual nuclei in three-dimensional images is important for biological research, but evaluating these algorithms requires extensive annotations. Earlier benchmarks either focused on two-dimensional images or labeled only a small number of three-dimensional cells. NIS3D addresses this gap with a large-volume, densely populated, completely annotated benchmark.

The dataset contains more than 22,000 cells from multiple commonly studied species. The authors developed semi-automatic annotation software to help construct it. Each cell receives labels from three independent annotators, enabling measurement of annotation variability. A confidence score for each cell supports comparisons that account for differences in annotation certainty.

Alongside a review of methods for segmenting dense three-dimensional nuclei, the authors evaluate selected state-of-the-art algorithms on NIS3D. Even the best evaluated methods remain far from human-level accuracy. The results also expose different methods' strengths and weaknesses, suggesting directions for further development. The benchmark's value comes from combining complete annotation with information about annotation variability, providing a more informative basis for assessing progress on a difficult segmentation task.
summary.tldr: NIS3D provides complete annotations for more than 22,000 cells and reveals a substantial gap between evaluated 3D nuclei segmentation methods and human accuracy.

title: NIS3D: A Completely Annotated Benchmark for Dense 3D Nuclei Image Segmentation

abstract: In reinforcement learning, robust policies for high-stakes decision-making problems with limited data are usually computed by optimizing the percentile criterion. The percentile criterion is optimized by constructing an uncertainty set that contains the true model with high probability and optimizing the policy for the worst model in the set. Since the percentile criterion is non-convex, constructing these sets itself is challenging. Existing works use Bayesian credible regions as uncertainty sets, but they are often unnecessarily large and result in learning overly conservative policies. To overcome these shortcomings, we propose a novel Value-at-Risk based dynamic programming algorithm to optimize the percentile criterion without explicitly constructing any uncertainty sets. Our theoretical and empirical results show that our algorithm implicitly constructs much smaller uncertainty sets and learns less-conservative robust policies.

paragraphs: With limited data, a reinforcement learning policy may need protection against uncertainty about the environment. One approach optimizes a percentile criterion by building a set of plausible models that contains the true model with high probability, then choosing a policy for the worst model in that set. Constructing a useful set is challenging because the criterion is non-convex.

Existing methods use Bayesian credible regions as uncertainty sets, but these can be unnecessarily large. Protecting against every model in an oversized set can make the resulting policy overly conservative. The paper proposes a Value-at-Risk-based dynamic programming algorithm that optimizes the percentile criterion without explicitly constructing uncertainty sets.

The theoretical and empirical results show that the algorithm implicitly produces much smaller uncertainty sets and learns less-conservative robust policies. The contribution is not simply to discard uncertainty: it changes how uncertainty enters the optimization. This matters because excessive conservatism can come from the construction of the uncertainty set itself, rather than from the amount of protection the decision problem actually calls for.
summary.tldr: A Value-at-Risk-based dynamic programming method optimizes the percentile criterion without explicit uncertainty sets and yields less-conservative robust policies.

title: Percentile Criterion Optimization in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome in linear structural causal models (SCM) with latent confounders when we have access to a single proxy variable.Several methods (such as difference-in-difference (DiD) estimator or negative outcome control) have been proposed in this setting in the literature. However, these approaches require either restrictive assumptions on the data generating model or having access to at least two proxy variables.We propose a method to estimate the causal effect using cross moments between the treatment, the outcome, and the proxy variable. In particular, we show that the causal effect can be identified with simple arithmetic operations on the cross moments if the latent confounder in linear SCM is non-Gaussian.In this setting, DiD estimator provides an unbiased estimate only in the special case where the latent confounder has exactly the same direct causal effects on the outcomes in the pre-treatment and post-treatment phases. This translates to the common trend assumption in DiD, which we effectively relax.Additionally, we provide an impossibility result that shows the causal effect cannot be identified if the observational distribution over the treatment, the outcome, and the proxy is jointly Gaussian. Our experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets showcase the effectivenessof the proposed approach in estimating the causal effect.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a treatment’s causal effect when an unobserved factor influences both treatment and outcome. It considers linear structural causal models with access to just one proxy variable. Such a proxy provides indirect information about the hidden confounder, but existing approaches can require restrictive assumptions or additional proxies.

The proposed method uses cross moments: quantities that summarize how treatment, outcome, and proxy values vary together through products of their values. The authors show that, in their setting, a non-Gaussian latent confounder allows the causal effect to be identified through simple arithmetic on these quantities. This relaxes the equal-effect condition underlying the difference-in-differences comparison discussed in the paper.

The distributional condition matters. The authors also prove that identification is impossible when the observed treatment, outcome, and proxy are jointly Gaussian. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the approach’s effectiveness. Together, the results explain both an opportunity for estimation with one proxy and a setting where observational information cannot identify the effect.
summary.tldr: Cross moments can identify causal effects with one proxy in the studied linear models when the latent confounder is non-Gaussian.

title: A Cross-Moment Approach for Causal Effect Estimation

abstract: The two-hand interaction is one of the most challenging signals to analyze due to the self-similarity, complicated articulations, and occlusions of hands. Although several datasets have been proposed for the two-hand interaction analysis, all of them do not achieve 1) diverse and realistic image appearances and 2) diverse and large-scale groundtruth (GT) 3D poses at the same time. In this work, we propose Re:InterHand, a dataset of relighted 3D interacting hands that achieve the two goals. To this end, we employ a state-of-the-art hand relighting network with our accurately tracked two-hand 3D poses. We compare our Re:InterHand with existing 3D interacting hands datasets and show the benefit of it. Our Re:InterHand is available in https://mks0601.github.io/ReInterHand/

paragraphs: Understanding how two hands interact is difficult because the hands look similar, bend into complicated configurations, and hide parts of one another. A useful dataset must therefore provide both varied images and reliable three-dimensional pose labels. The paper identifies a gap in earlier datasets: they did not simultaneously offer realistic, diverse appearances and large-scale, diverse ground-truth poses.

Re:InterHand addresses these requirements by combining accurately tracked three-dimensional poses of interacting hands with a hand relighting network. The tracked poses supply the geometric supervision, while relighting supports variation in image appearance. This combination connects the appearance of the hands with known pose information within the same dataset.

The authors compare Re:InterHand with existing datasets for three-dimensional interacting hands and report benefits from their approach. The contribution is a data resource that brings appearance diversity and pose diversity together, rather than treating either as sufficient on its own. It supports research on a visual problem where realistic images and dependable geometric labels are both central.
summary.tldr: Re:InterHand combines hand relighting with accurately tracked poses to provide diverse, realistic images of interacting hands with three-dimensional labels.

title: A Dataset of Relighted 3D Interacting Hands

abstract: We propose the Thinker algorithm, a novel approach that enables reinforcement learning agents to autonomously interact with and utilize a learned world model. The Thinker algorithm wraps the environment with a world model and introduces new actions designed for interacting with the world model. These model-interaction actions enable agents to perform planning by proposing alternative plans to the world model before selecting a final action to execute in the environment. This approach eliminates the need for handcrafted planning algorithms by enabling the agent to learn how to plan autonomously and allows for easy interpretation of the agent's plan with visualization. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through experimental results in the game of Sokoban and the Atari 2600 benchmark, where the Thinker algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance and competitive results, respectively. Visualizations of agents trained with the Thinker algorithm demonstrate that they have learned to plan effectively with the world model to select better actions. Thinker is the first work showing that an RL agent can learn to plan with a learned world model in complex environments.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can use a world model to consider possible actions before acting in its environment. Thinker makes those interactions part of what the agent learns. It wraps the environment with a learned world model and introduces additional actions specifically for interacting with that model.

Through these actions, the agent proposes alternative plans before selecting a final action to execute in the environment. This removes the need to supply a handcrafted planning algorithm: the agent learns how to use the model for planning. The resulting planning activity can also be visualized, making the agent’s considered plans easier to interpret.

Experiments show state-of-the-art performance in Sokoban and competitive results on the Atari 2600 benchmark. Visualizations indicate that trained agents learn to use the world model effectively when selecting actions. The authors identify this as the first demonstration of an RL agent learning to plan with a learned world model in complex environments. The central contribution is making planning behavior itself learnable through the agent’s action interface.
summary.tldr: Thinker gives reinforcement learning agents actions for interacting with a learned world model, enabling them to learn how to plan.

title: Thinker: Learning to Plan and Act

abstract: Training Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a challenging problem. The discriminator trains the generator by learning the distribution of real/generated data. However, the distribution of generated data changes throughout the training process, which is difficult for the discriminator to learn. In this paper, we propose a novel method for GANs from the viewpoint of online continual learning. We observe that the discriminator model, trained on historically generated data, often slows down its adaptation to the changes in the new arrival generated data, which accordingly decreases the quality of generated results. By treating the generated data in training as a stream, we propose to detect whether the discriminator slows down the learning of new knowledge in generated data. Therefore, we can explicitly enforce the discriminator to learn new knowledge fast. Particularly, we propose a new discriminator, which automatically detects its retardation and then dynamically masks its features, such that the discriminator can adaptively learn the temporally-vary distribution of generated data. Experimental results show our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: In a generative adversarial network, the discriminator helps train the generator by learning to distinguish real and generated data. The generated distribution changes throughout training, creating a moving target. This paper examines that difficulty through online continual learning, treating generated examples as an evolving stream that the discriminator must keep learning from.

The authors observe that learning from earlier generated data can slow the discriminator’s adaptation to newly generated data. That slowdown can reduce the quality of generated outputs. Their method detects when the discriminator is becoming slow to learn new information and responds by dynamically masking its features, explicitly encouraging faster adaptation.

The resulting discriminator adjusts its feature masking as training progresses so that it can track the changing generated distribution. Experiments report better performance than the state-of-the-art approaches considered. The contribution is a mechanism for responding to an observed learning slowdown inside GAN training. Its motivation connects the quality of generated results to how well the discriminator keeps up with the generator’s changing behavior.
summary.tldr: A discriminator that detects adaptation slowdowns and dynamically masks features improves GAN results in the reported experiments.

title: Dynamically Masked Discriminator for GANs

abstract: Model selection in the context of bandit optimization is a challenging problem, as it requires balancing exploration and exploitation not only for action selection, but also for model selection. One natural approach is to rely on online learning algorithms that treat different models as experts. Existing methods, however, scale poorly ($\mathrm{poly}M$) with the number of models $M$ in terms of their regret.Our key insight is that, for model selection in linear bandits, we can emulate full-information feedback to the online learner with a favorable bias-variance trade-off. This allows us to develop ALEXP, which has an exponentially improved ($\log M$) dependence on $M$ for its regret.ALEXP has anytime guarantees on its regret, and neither requires knowledge of the horizon $n$, nor relies on an initial purely exploratory stage.Our approach utilizes a novel time-uniform analysis of the Lasso, establishing a new connection between online learning and high-dimensional statistics.

paragraphs: In linear bandits, a learner must choose actions while learning from limited feedback. Selecting among several candidate models introduces another exploration problem: the learner must also decide which model to trust. Treating models as competing experts is a natural strategy, but existing approaches have regret that grows polynomially with the number of models.

The paper introduces ALEXP, which emulates full-information feedback for the online learner. This means constructing feedback that supports comparisons across models despite the limited observations available from bandit interaction. The construction manages a bias-variance trade-off and improves the regret dependence on the number of models from polynomial to logarithmic.

ALEXP also provides anytime guarantees: it does not need to know the eventual number of rounds and requires no initial phase devoted exclusively to exploration. Its analysis uses a new time-uniform treatment of the Lasso, linking model selection in online learning with high-dimensional statistics. The improvement concerns dependence on model count, making that aspect of the guarantee substantially more favorable as the candidate collection grows.
summary.tldr: ALEXP achieves logarithmic regret dependence on the number of candidate linear-bandit models without requiring a known time horizon.

title: Anytime Model Selection in Linear Bandits

abstract: Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) achieve remarkable visual quality when synthesizing novel views of time-evolving 3D scenes. However, the common reliance on backward deformation fields makes reanimation of the captured object poses challenging. Moreover, the state of the art dynamic models are often limited by low visual fidelity, long reconstruction time or specificity to narrow application domains. In this paper, we present a novel method utilizing a point-based representation and Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) to jointly learn a Dynamic NeRF and an associated skeletal model from even sparse multi-view video. Our forward-warping approach achieves state-of-the-art visual fidelity when synthesizing novel views and poses while significantly reducing the necessary learning time when compared to existing work. We demonstrate the versatility of our representation on a variety of articulated objects from common datasets and obtain reposable 3D reconstructions without the need of object-specific skeletal templates.

paragraphs: A dynamic neural radiance field can render new views of a moving object, but changing that object's pose after reconstruction remains challenging. The paper links this difficulty to the backward deformation fields commonly used in dynamic models. It proposes learning a representation that combines visual reconstruction with an explicit skeletal model.

The method uses a point-based representation and linear blend skinning to learn the dynamic radiance field and skeleton jointly, even from sparse multi-view video. Its forward-warping approach supports moving the representation into new poses. Learning the skeleton alongside appearance removes the need to supply an object-specific skeletal template beforehand.

Across articulated objects from common datasets, the authors demonstrate reconstructions that can be reposed and viewed from new directions. They report state-of-the-art visual fidelity for new views and poses, together with significantly shorter learning time than existing work. These findings connect rendering quality, reconstruction efficiency, and pose control in one representation, extending the usefulness of a captured dynamic object beyond replaying the motion originally observed.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning neural points and a skeleton produces high-quality, reposable reconstructions without object-specific skeletal templates.

title: Template-free Articulated Neural Point Clouds for Reposable View Synthesis

abstract: Causal inference from observational data is crucial for many disciplines such as medicine and economics. However, sharp bounds for causal effects under relaxations of the unconfoundedness assumption (causal sensitivity analysis) are subject to ongoing research. So far, works with sharp bounds are restricted to fairly simple settings (e.g., a single binary treatment). In this paper, we propose a unified framework for causal sensitivity analysis under unobserved confounding in various settings. For this, we propose a flexible generalization of the marginal sensitivity model (MSM) and then derive sharp bounds for a large class of causal effects. This includes (conditional) average treatment effects, effects for mediation analysis and path analysis, and distributional effects. Furthermore, our sensitivity model is applicable to discrete, continuous, and time-varying treatments. It allows us to interpret the partial identification problem under unobserved confounding as a distribution shift in the latent confounders while evaluating the causal effect of interest. In the special case of a single binary treatment, our bounds for (conditional) average treatment effects coincide with recent optimality results for causal sensitivity analysis. Finally, we propose a scalable algorithm to estimate our sharp bounds from observational data.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave causal effects uncertain when unmeasured factors influence both treatment and outcome. Sensitivity analysis asks how conclusions change when the assumption of no unobserved confounding is relaxed. This paper develops a unified framework for calculating sharp bounds: ranges that tightly describe the causal effects compatible with the chosen sensitivity model.

The authors generalize the marginal sensitivity model to cover a broad set of effects and treatments. The framework includes average and conditional average treatment effects, mediation and path effects, and distributional effects. It also handles discrete, continuous, and time-varying treatments. This expands sharp-bound analysis beyond simpler settings such as a single binary treatment.

The key interpretation treats uncertainty from hidden confounding as a distribution shift in latent confounders when evaluating a causal effect. For a single binary treatment, the resulting average-effect bounds agree with recent optimality results. A scalable estimation algorithm brings the framework to observational data. The bounds quantify what remains identifiable under the specified sensitivity model rather than assuming hidden confounding has disappeared.
summary.tldr: A generalized sensitivity framework derives sharp causal-effect bounds under unobserved confounding across varied treatments and causal questions.

title: Sharp Bounds for Generalized Causal Sensitivity Analysis

abstract: Sketching algorithms have recently proven to be a powerful approach both for designing low-space streaming algorithms as well as fast polynomial time approximation schemes (PTAS). In this work, we develop new techniques to extend the applicability of sketching-based approaches to the sparse dictionary learning and the Euclidean $k$-means clustering problems. In particular, we initiate the study of the challenging setting where the dictionary/clustering assignment for each of the $n$ input points must be output, which has surprisingly received little attention in prior work. On the fast algorithms front, we obtain a new approach for designing PTAS's for the $k$-means clustering problem, which generalizes to the first PTAS for the sparse dictionary learning problem. On the streaming algorithms front, we obtain new upper bounds and lower bounds for dictionary learning and $k$-means clustering. In particular, given a design matrix $\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ in a turnstile stream, we show an $\tilde O(nr/\epsilon^2 + dk/\epsilon)$ space upper bound for $r$-sparse dictionary learning of size $k$, an $\tilde O(n/\epsilon^2 + dk/\epsilon)$ space upper bound for $k$-means clustering, as well as an $\tilde O(n)$ space upper bound for $k$-means clustering on random order row insertion streams with a natural "bounded sensitivity" assumption. On the lower bounds side, we obtain a general $\tilde\Omega(n/\epsilon + dk/\epsilon)$ lower bound for $k$-means clustering, as well as an $\tilde\Omega(n/\epsilon^2)$ lower bound for algorithms which can estimate the cost of a single fixed set of candidate centers.

paragraphs: Sketching compresses information so algorithms can use less memory or compute approximations efficiently. This paper develops sketching techniques for sparse dictionary learning and Euclidean k-means, emphasizing the requirement to output an assignment for every input point. That output requirement is central to the memory questions it studies.

The authors obtain a new route to polynomial-time approximation schemes for k-means and extend it to the first such scheme for sparse dictionary learning. They also analyze turnstile streams, where matrix entries receive updates. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the space upper bounds are nr/epsilon² + dk/epsilon for an r-sparse dictionary of size k, and n/epsilon² + dk/epsilon for k-means on n points with d dimensions.

For randomly ordered row insertions, k-means needs roughly linear space in n under a bounded-sensitivity assumption. Lower bounds establish unavoidable memory requirements, including a stronger requirement for algorithms estimating the cost of a fixed candidate center set. Together, these results characterize both achievable compression and limits on streaming solutions.
summary.tldr: New sketching techniques yield approximation schemes and streaming memory bounds for sparse dictionary learning and k-means with per-point outputs.

title: Sketching Algorithms for Sparse Dictionary Learning: PTAS and Turnstile Streaming

abstract: We propose a new family of label randomizers for training _regression_ models under the constraint of label differential privacy (DP). In particular, we leverage the trade-offs between bias and variance to construct better label randomizers depending on a privately estimated prior distribution over the labels. We demonstrate that these randomizers achieve state-of-the-art privacy-utility trade-offs on several datasets, highlighting the importance of reducing bias when training neural networks with label DP. We also provide theoretical results shedding light on the structural properties of the optimal unbiased randomizers.

In particular, we leverage the trade-offs between bias and variance to construct better label randomizers depending on a privately estimated prior distribution over the labels. We demonstrate that these randomizers achieve state-of-the-art privacy-utility trade-offs on several datasets, highlighting the importance of reducing bias when training neural networks with label DP. We also provide theoretical results shedding light on the structural properties of the optimal unbiased randomizers.

paragraphs: Regression models predict numerical labels, and those labels may need privacy protection during training. This paper develops a family of label randomizers for regression under label differential privacy. The design problem is to alter labels enough to satisfy the privacy requirement while preserving information useful for learning the prediction task.

The authors use the tradeoff between bias and variance to construct the randomizers. Bias concerns systematic distortion, while variance concerns the spread introduced by randomness. Their construction depends on a prior distribution over labels that is itself estimated privately. This allows the randomization procedure to respond to the label distribution while accounting for privacy in estimating that distribution.

Across several datasets, the randomizers achieve state-of-the-art privacy–utility tradeoffs. The results highlight the importance of reducing bias when neural networks learn under label privacy constraints. Alongside the experiments, the paper provides theoretical results about the structural properties of optimal unbiased randomizers. Together, the findings connect useful private regression performance to deliberate control of the statistical distortion introduced into labels.
summary.tldr: Privately estimated label distributions guide regression randomizers that improve privacy–utility tradeoffs by managing bias and variance.

title: Optimal Unbiased Randomizers for Regression with Label Differential Privacy

abstract: This paper presents ClusterFormer, a universal vision model that is based on the Clustering paradigm with TransFormer. It comprises two novel designs: 1) recurrent cross-attention clustering, which reformulates the cross-attention mechanism in Transformer and enables recursive updates of cluster centers to facilitate strong representation learning; and 2) feature dispatching, which uses the updated cluster centers to redistribute image features through similarity-based metrics, resulting in a transparent pipeline. This elegant design streamlines an explainable and transferable workflow, capable of tackling heterogeneous vision tasks (i.e., image classification, object detection, and image segmentation) with varying levels of clustering granularity (i.e., image-, box-, and pixel-level). Empirical results demonstrate that ClusterFormer outperforms various well-known specialized architectures, achieving 83.41% top-1 acc. over ImageNet-1K for image classification, 54.2% and 47.0% mAP over MS COCO for object detection and instance segmentation, 52.4% mIoU over ADE20K for semantic segmentation, and 55.8% PQ over COCO Panoptic for panoptic segmentation. This work aims to initiate a paradigm shift in universal visual understanding and to benefit the broader field.

This work aims to initiate a paradigm shift in universal visual understanding and to benefit the broader field.

paragraphs: ClusterFormer explores clustering as a shared organizing mechanism for several computer vision tasks. Classification, object detection, and segmentation require predictions at different levels of detail. The paper builds a Transformer-based model that addresses these differences through clustering at image, box, and pixel granularity, connecting multiple tasks through a common representation-learning process.

Its first component reformulates cross-attention as recurrent clustering. Cluster centers are updated repeatedly, allowing the model to refine the information they represent. A second component, feature dispatching, redistributes image features using their similarity to the updated centers. Together, these steps create an explicit process of forming groups and using those groups to reorganize features.

The reported experiments outperform various established specialized architectures across classification, detection, and several segmentation tasks. Evaluations cover ImageNet-1K, MS COCO, ADE20K, and COCO Panoptic. These results support the claim that clustering can provide a transferable visual-learning framework across heterogeneous tasks. The paper's broader ambition is universal visual understanding, while its concrete evidence concerns the tasks and benchmarks evaluated.
summary.tldr: ClusterFormer repeatedly updates cluster centers and redistributes visual features to support classification, detection, and segmentation within a shared framework.

title: ClusterFomer: Clustering As A Universal Visual Learner

abstract: Transformer architecture has shown impressive performance in multiple research domains and has become the backbone of many neural network models. However, there is limited understanding on how it works. In particular, with a simple predictive loss, how the representation emerges from the gradient \emph{training dynamics} remains a mystery. In this paper, for 1-layer transformer with one self-attention layer plus one decoder layer, we analyze its SGD training dynamics for the task of next token prediction in a mathematically rigorous manner. We open the black box of the dynamic process of how the self-attention layer combines input tokens, and reveal the nature of underlying inductive bias. More specifically, with the assumption (a) no positional encoding, (b) long input sequence, and (c) the decoder layer learns faster than the self-attention layer, we prove that self-attention acts as a \emph{discriminative scanning algorithm}: starting from uniform attention, it gradually attends more to distinct key tokens for a specific next token to be predicted, and pays less attention to common key tokens that occur across different next tokens. Among distinct tokens, it progressively drops attention weights, following the order of low to high co-occurrence between the key and the query token in the training set. Interestingly, this procedure does not lead to winner-takes-all, but stops due to a \emph{phase transition} that is controllable by the learning rate of the decoder layer, leaving (almost) fixed token combination. We verify this \textbf{\emph{scan and snap}} dynamics on synthetic and real-world data (WikiText-103).

paragraphs: This paper studies how attention patterns emerge during next-token training in a transformer with one self-attention layer and one decoder layer. It analyzes stochastic gradient descent directly, asking how a simple predictive objective leads the model to combine input tokens in a particular way.

The proof assumes no positional encoding, long input sequences, and a decoder that learns faster than the attention layer. It emphasizes key tokens that distinguish a particular predicted next token and downweights tokens shared across different predictions. This pruning does not continue to a single winning token. A phase transition, controlled by the decoder's learning rate, stops the process and leaves an almost fixed combination of tokens. The authors verify this scan-and-snap pattern on synthetic data and WikiText-103, connecting a conditional mathematical account of training to observed representation formation.
summary.tldr: Under explicit assumptions, a one-layer transformer's attention scans for discriminative tokens before a learning-rate-dependent transition fixes their combination.

title: Scan and Snap: Understanding Training Dynamics and Token Composition in 1-layer Transformer

abstract: Current post-training quantization methods for LLMs compress the weights down to 4-bits, with moderate to low degradation in accuracy. However, further reducing the number of bits or accelerating the network while avoiding large accuracy drops, especially for smaller, sub 7B models, remains an actively researched and open problem. To address this, in this work, we introduce Quantization with Binary Bases (QBB), a new approach for low-bit quantization that effectively removes (nearly) all multiplications, reducing the implementation to summations. Our novel approach works by decomposing the original weights into a set of binary (1-bit) matrices using an iterative process. For a given layer, starting from a weight matrix, we first construct an initial approximation using an analytical solution, where each new binary matrix, paired with a scaling vector, approximates the residual error of the previous estimation. Secondly, using gradient descent and a progressive learning curriculum, we find the optimal set of binary matrices and scaling vectors that minimize the $\ell_2$ distance between the produced approximation and original weights. Thirdly, as previous steps are input agnostic, we holistically optimize the scaling vectors alone, calibrating them in student-teacher fashion, with the teacher providing both the data, by autoregressive generation starting from a random token, and the target logits. When evaluated across multiple LLM families, our approach matches and outperforms all prior works, setting a new state-of-the-art result using a summation-only based approach.

Across multiple model families, the authors report results matching or surpassing prior work, establishing strong performance for their summation-based approach.

title: QBB: Quantization with Binary Bases for LLMs

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is crucial for ensuring reliable deployment of machine learning models. Recent advancements focus on utilizing easily accessible auxiliary outliers (e.g., data from the web or other datasets) in training. However, we experimentally reveal that these methods still struggle to generalize their detection capabilities to unknown OOD data, due to the limited diversity of the auxiliary outliers collected. Therefore, we thoroughly examine this problem from the generalization perspective and demonstrate that a more diverse set of auxiliary outliers is essential for enhancing the detection capabilities. However, in practice, it is difficult and costly to collect sufficiently diverse auxiliary outlier data. Therefore, we propose a simple yet practical approach with a theoretical guarantee, termed Diversity-induced Mixup for OOD detection (diverseMix), which enhances the diversity of auxiliary outlier set for training in an efficient way. Extensive experiments show that diverseMix achieves superior performance on commonly used and recent challenging large-scale benchmarks, which further confirm the importance of the diversity of auxiliary outliers.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection aims to recognize inputs outside the data a model is intended to handle. One approach trains with auxiliary outliers gathered from other datasets or the web. This paper shows experimentally that such training can still generalize poorly to unknown outliers when the auxiliary examples lack sufficient diversity.

The authors examine this failure from a generalization perspective and establish the importance of a more diverse auxiliary outlier set. Collecting that diversity directly can be expensive and difficult. Their proposed method, Diversity-induced Mixup, or diverseMix, instead increases the diversity of the auxiliary set used during training through an efficient approach with a theoretical guarantee.

Experiments report superior performance on both commonly used benchmarks and newer challenging large-scale benchmarks. Those results support the paper's central explanation: exposure to auxiliary outliers is less useful when that exposure covers too narrow a range. The contribution ties a generalization analysis to a practical training method, making diversity of the available outlier data an explicit design consideration for improving detection of unfamiliar inputs.
summary.tldr: diverseMix improves out-of-distribution detection by efficiently increasing auxiliary-outlier diversity, supported by theoretical analysis and benchmark results.

title: Out-Of-Distribution Detection with Diversification (Provably)

abstract: The problem of heterogeneous clients in federated learning has recently drawn a lot of attention. Spectral model sharding, i.e., partitioning the model parameters into low-rank matrices based on the singular value decomposition, has been one of the proposed solutions for more efficient on-device training in such settings. In this work we present two sampling strategies for such sharding, obtained as solutions to specific optimization problems. The first produces unbiased estimators of the original weights, while the second aims to minimize the squared approximation error. We discuss how both of these estimators can be incorporated in the federated learning loop and practical considerations that arise during local training. Empirically, we demonstrate that both of these methods can lead to improved performance in various commonly used datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning must often accommodate clients with different computational capabilities. Spectral model sharding addresses this by splitting model parameters into low-rank matrices obtained through singular value decomposition. This gives a basis for distributing smaller pieces of a model for more efficient training on individual devices.

The paper develops two sampling strategies for deciding which spectral components to use. Each follows from a different optimization objective. One produces weight estimates that are unbiased, meaning their average agrees with the original weights. The other targets the squared error between an approximation and the original weights, emphasizing the quality of the reconstructed approximation.

The authors explain how both estimators can fit into the federated learning process and discuss practical issues arising during local training. Experiments on commonly used datasets show that either strategy can improve performance. The contribution is therefore both a principled derivation of sampling rules and an examination of their use in training, with the two objectives offering distinct ways to judge a sampled model representation.
summary.tldr: Two optimization-derived sampling strategies improve spectral model sharding by targeting unbiased weights or low squared approximation error.

title: On Sampling Strategies for Spectral Model Sharding

abstract: Goal misalignment, reward sparsity and difficult credit assignment are only a few of the many issues that make it difficult for deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents to learn optimal policies. Unfortunately, the black-box nature of deep neural networks impedes the inclusion of domain experts for inspecting the model and revising suboptimal policies.To this end, we introduce Successive Concept Bottleneck Agents (SCoBots), that integrate consecutive concept bottleneck (CB) layers. In contrast to current CB models, SCoBots do not just represent concepts as properties of individual objects, but also as relations between objects which is crucial for many RL tasks. Our experimental results provide evidence of SCoBots' competitive performances, but also of their potential for domain experts to understand and regularize their behavior. Among other things, SCoBots enabled us to identify a previously unknown misalignment problem in the iconic video game, Pong, and resolve it. Overall, SCoBots thus result in more human-aligned RL agents.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can learn undesirable behavior because their goals are misaligned, rewards are scarce, or it is difficult to determine which actions deserve credit. Deep neural networks make these problems harder for domain experts to inspect. This paper introduces Successive Concept Bottleneck Agents, or SCoBots, to make an agent's decision process more accessible to human understanding and revision.

SCoBots use consecutive concept bottleneck layers that represent information through interpretable concepts. Their representation includes both properties of individual objects and relationships between objects. This matters because many reinforcement learning tasks depend on how objects relate to one another. The successive layers provide a structured representation through which experts can examine behavior and guide its regularization.

Experiments provide evidence that SCoBots achieve competitive performance while offering opportunities for expert inspection and intervention. In Pong, the approach exposed a previously unknown misalignment problem and enabled the authors to resolve it. This example supports the practical value of interpretable internal representations for improving alignment, alongside the reported evidence that transparency can coexist with competitive task performance.
summary.tldr: SCoBots use interpretable object and relationship concepts to help experts inspect and correct reinforcement-learning behavior.

title: Interpretable Concept Bottlenecks to Align Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: In recent years, deep neural networks (DNNs) have witnessed extensive applications, and protecting their intellectual property (IP) is thus crucial. As a non-invasive way for model IP protection, model fingerprinting has become popular. However, existing single-point based fingerprinting methods are highly sensitive to the changes in the decision boundary, and may suffer from the misjudgment of the resemblance of sparse fingerprinting, yielding high false positives of innocent models. In this paper, we propose ADV-TRA, a more robust fingerprinting scheme that utilizes adversarial trajectories to verify the ownership of DNN models. Benefited from the intrinsic progressively adversarial level, the trajectory is capable of tolerating greater degree of alteration in decision boundaries. We further design novel schemes to generate a surface trajectory that involves a series of fixed-length trajectories with dynamically adjusted step sizes. Such a design enables a more unique and reliable fingerprinting with relatively low querying costs. Experiments on three datasets against four types of removal attacks show that ADV-TRA exhibits superior performance in distinguishing between infringing and innocent models, outperforming the state-of-the-art comparisons.

paragraphs: Model fingerprinting seeks to identify copied neural networks without modifying them. Fingerprints based on isolated inputs can be fragile when decision boundaries change and may falsely resemble unrelated models. ADV-TRA uses sequences of progressively adversarial inputs to capture a richer behavioral signature.

The trajectory design tolerates larger changes in the decision boundary. A surface-trajectory construction combines fixed-length trajectories with dynamically adjusted step sizes, aiming to make fingerprints distinctive while keeping query costs relatively low.

Experiments on three datasets against four types of removal attack distinguish copied and unrelated models better than state-of-the-art comparisons. The abstract does not provide false-positive rates or query counts. The contribution is a more robust behavioral identification scheme; a fingerprint match is evidence within the tested threat model, not by itself a complete legal determination of ownership or infringement.
summary.tldr: ADV-TRA uses adversarial trajectories as more robust fingerprints of neural-network behavior.

title: United We Stand, Divided We Fall: Fingerprinting Deep Neural Networks via Adversarial Trajectories

abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in recent years. Interestingly, transformers have shown particularly strong in-context learning capability -- even without fine-tuning, they are still able to solve unseen tasks well purely based on task-specific prompts. In this paper, we study the capability of one-layer transformers in learning the one-nearest neighbor prediction rule. Under a theoretical framework where the prompt contains a sequence of labeled training data and unlabeled test data, we show that, although the loss function is nonconvex, when trained with gradient descent, a single softmax attention layer can successfully learn to behave like a one-nearest neighbor classifier. Our result gives a concrete example on how transformers can be trained to implement nonparametric machine learning algorithms, and sheds light on the role of softmax attention in transformer models.

paragraphs: This paper studies a concrete form of in-context learning: predicting a test example's label by finding its nearest labeled example in the prompt. The prompt contains labeled training data together with unlabeled test data. The question is whether training can make a very small transformer learn this one-nearest-neighbor rule and then apply it through its context.

Under the paper's theoretical framework, gradient descent can train a single softmax attention layer to behave like a one-nearest-neighbor classifier. The result concerns successful learning despite a nonconvex loss function, meaning the training objective does not have a simple globally bowl-shaped geometry. It therefore addresses the optimization process as well as the behavior the trained layer can express.

The finding gives a concrete example of a transformer learning to implement a nonparametric prediction algorithm. Task-specific examples supplied in the prompt provide the information used for prediction, which helps explain how context can support new tasks without further fine-tuning. The result also clarifies a role for softmax attention within this particular theoretical setting.
summary.tldr: Under a theoretical framework, gradient descent trains one softmax attention layer to perform one-nearest-neighbor classification from examples in its prompt.

title: One-Layer Transformer Provably Learns One-Nearest Neighbor In Context

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning (RL), addressing the out-of-distribution (OOD) action issue has been a focus, but we argue that there exists an OOD state issue that also impairs performance yet has been underexplored. Such an issue describes the scenario when the agent encounters states out of the offline dataset during the test phase, leading to uncontrolled behavior and performance degradation. To this end, we propose SCAS, a simple yet effective approach that unifies OOD state correction and OOD action suppression in offline RL. Technically, SCAS achieves value-aware OOD state correction, capable of correcting the agent from OOD states to high-value in-distribution states. Theoretical and empirical results show that SCAS also exhibits the effect of suppressing OOD actions. On standard offline RL benchmarks, SCAS achieves excellent performance without additional hyperparameter tuning. Moreover, benefiting from its OOD state correction feature, SCAS demonstrates enhanced robustness against environmental perturbations.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains an agent from an existing dataset. Much attention has focused on avoiding actions poorly represented in that data, but this paper highlights a related problem: at test time, the agent can encounter unfamiliar states. These out-of-distribution states can lead to uncontrolled behavior and degraded performance even when action selection has received attention.

The proposed method, SCAS, combines state correction with action suppression. Its state correction is value-aware, aiming to guide the agent from unfamiliar states toward high-value states represented in the training distribution. The authors also provide theoretical and empirical results showing that the method has the effect of suppressing out-of-distribution actions.

On standard offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks, SCAS achieves strong performance without additional hyperparameter tuning. It also shows improved robustness to environmental perturbations, which the authors connect to its state-correction capability. The contribution is a unified approach that addresses both where the agent finds itself and what it chooses to do when operating beyond its offline experience.
summary.tldr: SCAS improves offline reinforcement learning by guiding unfamiliar states toward valuable familiar states while suppressing out-of-distribution actions.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning with OOD State Correction and OOD Action Suppression

abstract: The rapid progress in generative models has resulted in impressive leaps in generation quality, blurring the lines between synthetic and real data. Web-scale datasets are now prone to the inevitable contamination by synthetic data, directly impacting the training of future generated models. Already, some theoretical results on self-consuming generative models (a.k.a., iterative retraining) have emerged in the literature, showcasing that either model collapse or stability could be possible depending on the fraction of generated data used at each retraining step. However, in practice, synthetic data is often subject to human feedback and curated by users before being used and uploaded online. For instance, many interfaces of popular text-to-image generative models, such as Stable Diffusion or Midjourney, produce several variations of an image for a given query which can eventually be curated by the users. In this paper, we theoretically study the impact of data curation on iterated retraining of generative models and show that it can be seen as an implicit preference optimization mechanism. However, unlike standard preference optimization, the generative model does not have access to the reward function or negative samples needed for pairwise comparisons. Moreover, our study doesn't require access to the density function, only to samples. We prove that, if the data is curated according to a reward model, then the expected reward of the iterative retraining procedure is maximized. We further provide theoretical results on the stability of the retraining loop when using a positive fraction of real data at each step. Finally, we conduct illustrative experiments on both synthetic datasets and on CIFAR10 showing that such a procedure amplifies biases of the reward model.

summary.tldr: Reward-based curation can make iterative generative-model retraining implicitly optimize preferences while amplifying the reward model's biases.

title: Self-Consuming Generative Models with Curated Data Provably Optimize Human Preferences

abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry has played a pivotal role in advancing proteomics, enabling the analysis of protein composition in biological tissues. Many deep learning methods have been developed for \emph{de novo} peptide sequencing task, i.e., predicting the peptide sequence for the observed mass spectrum. However, two key challenges seriously hinder the further research of this important task. Firstly, since there is no consensus for the evaluation datasets, the empirical results in different research papers are often not comparable, leading to unfair comparison. Secondly, the current methods are usually limited to amino acid-level or peptide-level precision and recall metrics. In this work, we present the first unified benchmark NovoBench for \emph{de novo} peptide sequencing, which comprises diverse mass spectrum data, integrated models, and comprehensive evaluation metrics. Recent impressive methods, including DeepNovo, PointNovo, Casanovo, InstaNovo, AdaNovo and $\pi$-HelixNovo are integrated into our framework. In addition to amino acid-level and peptide-level precision and recall, we also evaluate the models' performance in terms of identifying post-tranlational modifications (PTMs), efficiency and robustness to peptide length, noise peaks and missing fragment ratio, which are important influencing factors while seldom be considered. Leveraging this benchmark, we conduct a large-scale study of current methods, report many insightful findings that open up new possibilities for future development. The benchmark is open-sourced to facilitate future research and application. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/Westlake-OmicsAI/NovoBench}.

Common precision and recall measures also give a limited view of how systems behave under important variations in the sequencing problem.

NovoBench brings diverse mass-spectrum data, existing models, and broader evaluation criteria into one framework. It integrates DeepNovo, PointNovo, Casanovo, InstaNovo, AdaNovo, and π-HelixNovo. Alongside amino-acid and peptide precision and recall, it evaluates detection of post-translational modifications, efficiency, and robustness to peptide length, noise peaks, and missing fragments.

The authors use the benchmark for a large-scale study of current methods and release it openly to support further research and applications. Its central contribution is a shared basis for assessing methods across more dimensions of practical performance. By evaluating accuracy together with robustness and efficiency, NovoBench makes comparisons more informative than results obtained from disconnected datasets and a narrow set of metrics.
summary.tldr: NovoBench unifies peptide-sequencing datasets, models, and metrics to compare accuracy, modification detection, efficiency, and robustness.

title: NovoBench: Benchmarking Deep Learning-based \emph{De Novo} Sequencing Methods in Proteomics

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated competitive performance in missing data imputation (MDI) task. However, directly applying diffusion models to MDI produces suboptimal performance due to two primary defects. First, the sample diversity promoted by diffusion models hinders the accurate inference of missing values. Second, data masking reduces observable indices for model training, obstructing imputation performance. To address these challenges, we introduce $\underline{\text{N}}$egative $\underline{\text{E}}$ntropy-regularized $\underline{\text{W}}$asserstein gradient flow for $\underline{\text{Imp}}$utation (NewImp), enhancing diffusion models for MDI from a gradient flow perspective. To handle the first defect, we incorporate a negative entropy regularization term into the cost functional to suppress diversity and improve accuracy. To handle the second defect, we demonstrate that the imputation procedure of NewImp, induced by the conditional distribution-related cost functional, can equivalently be replaced by that induced by the joint distribution, thereby naturally eliminating the need for data masking. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our method. Code is available at [https://github.com/JustusvLiebig/NewImp](https://github.com/JustusvLiebig/NewImp).

paragraphs: Diffusion models can fill missing data, but the paper identifies two tensions with using them directly. Their emphasis on producing diverse samples can work against accurate recovery of missing values. Training with data masking also reduces the entries available for learning. NewImp addresses both issues by reformulating imputation through a Wasserstein gradient-flow perspective.

The first change adds negative-entropy regularization to the cost functional. This term suppresses diversity to improve imputation accuracy, aligning the objective with the recovery task. The second change concerns how the imputation procedure is expressed: the authors show that the procedure induced by a conditional-distribution cost can equivalently be replaced by one induced by the joint distribution.

That equivalence removes the need for data masking within the proposed formulation. The two changes therefore address separate obstacles: the diversity encouraged by the objective and the observable information used during training. Extensive experiments support the method's effectiveness, showing the practical value of adapting diffusion-based learning to the particular requirements of missing-data inference.
summary.tldr: NewImp adapts diffusion-based imputation by suppressing sample diversity and using a joint-distribution formulation that eliminates training-time data masking.

title: Rethinking the Diffusion Models for Missing Data Imputation: A Gradient Flow Perspective

abstract: Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering (HOBRE) lies at the intersection of binary and source code, aiming to lift binary code to human-readable content relevant to source code, thereby bridging the binary-source semantic gap. Recent advancements in uni-modal code model pre-training, particularly in generative Source Code Foundation Models (SCFMs) and binary understanding models, have laid the groundwork for transfer learning applicable to HOBRE. However, existing approaches for HOBRE rely heavily on uni-modal models like SCFMs for supervised fine-tuning or general LLMs for prompting, resulting in sub-optimal performance. Inspired by recent progress in large multi-modal models, we propose that it is possible to harness the strengths of uni-modal code models from both sides to bridge the semantic gap effectively. In this paper, we introduce a novel probe-and-recover framework that incorporates a binary-source encoder-decoder model and black-box LLMs for binary analysis. Our approach leverages the pre-trained knowledge within SCFMs to synthesize relevant, symbol-rich code fragments as context. This additional context enables black-box LLMs to enhance recovery accuracy. We demonstrate significant improvements in zero-shot binary summarization and binary function name recovery, with a 10.3% relative gain in CHRF and a 16.7% relative gain in a GPT4-based metric for summarization, as well as a 6.7% and 7.4% absolute increase in token-level precision and recall for name recovery, respectively. These results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in automating and improving binary code analysis.

summary.tldr: A probe-and-recover framework turns source-code model knowledge into context that improves binary summaries and function-name recovery.

title: Source Code Foundation Models are Transferable Binary Analysis Knowledge Bases

abstract: Floods are among the most common and devastating natural hazards, imposing immense costs on our society and economy due to their disastrous consequences. Recent progress in weather prediction and spaceborne flood mapping demonstrated the feasibility of anticipating extreme events and reliably detecting their catastrophic effects afterwards. However, these efforts are rarely linked to one another and there is a critical lack of datasets and benchmarks to enable the direct forecasting of flood extent. To resolve this issue, we curate a novel dataset enabling a timely prediction of flood extent. Furthermore, we provide a representative evaluation of state-of-the-art methods, structured into two benchmark tracks for forecasting flood inundation maps i) in general and ii) focused on coastal regions. Altogether, our dataset and benchmark provide a comprehensive platform for evaluating flood forecasts, enabling future solutions for this critical challenge. Data, code \& models are shared at https://github.com/Multihuntr/GFF under a CC0 license.

paragraphs: Weather prediction can help anticipate extreme events, while satellite-based flood mapping can reveal their consequences afterward. This paper identifies a gap between those capabilities: datasets and benchmarks for directly predicting where flooding will spread are scarce. Its focus is flood extent, the geographic area covered by floodwater, rather than weather prediction or retrospective detection alone.

The authors curate a dataset intended to support timely forecasts of flood extent. They also evaluate state-of-the-art methods through two benchmark tracks. One covers flood inundation mapping in general, and the other focuses on coastal regions. This structure gives researchers a shared basis for studying both the broader prediction problem and its coastal setting.

The contribution is a dataset and evaluation platform for comparing flood forecasts and developing future methods. The abstract does not present a particular forecasting method as the central advance; it emphasizes making direct flood-extent prediction easier to study systematically. Data, code, and models are shared under a CC0 license, supporting reuse of the platform.
summary.tldr: A new dataset and two benchmark tracks support direct forecasting of flood extent, including a dedicated coastal evaluation.

title: Off to new Shores: A Dataset & Benchmark for (near-)coastal Flood Inundation Forecasting

abstract: We present a computational framework that transforms single images into 3D physical objects. The visual geometry of a physical object in an image is determined by three orthogonal attributes: mechanical properties, external forces, and rest-shape geometry. Existing single-view 3D reconstruction methods often overlook this underlying composition, presuming rigidity or neglecting external forces. Consequently, the reconstructed objects fail to withstand real-world physical forces, resulting in instability or undesirable deformation -- diverging from their intended designs as depicted in the image. Our optimization framework addresses this by embedding physical compatibility into the reconstruction process. We explicitly decompose the three physical attributes and link them through static equilibrium, which serves as a hard constraint, ensuring that the optimized physical shapes exhibit desired physical behaviors. Evaluations on a dataset collected from Objaverse demonstrate that our framework consistently enhances the physical realism of 3D models over existing methods. The utility of our framework extends to practical applications in dynamic simulations and 3D printing, where adherence to physical compatibility is paramount.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a physical object from one image involves more than reproducing its visible shape. The paper describes that shape as the result of mechanical properties, external forces, and the object’s rest geometry. Methods that assume rigidity or ignore forces can produce reconstructions that deform undesirably or become unstable when subjected to physical conditions.

The proposed optimization framework represents those three attributes explicitly and connects them through static equilibrium. Equilibrium is imposed as a hard constraint during reconstruction, making physical compatibility part of the shape-generation process. The framework therefore seeks a physical configuration whose behavior agrees with the intended appearance shown in the image.

Evaluations on a dataset collected from Objaverse show consistent improvements in physical realism over existing methods. The authors also identify dynamic simulation and 3D printing as practical applications, where the interaction between shape and forces matters directly. The main contribution is a reconstruction formulation that incorporates material behavior and loading conditions into the search for a physically compatible object.
summary.tldr: The framework reconstructs objects from single images while enforcing static equilibrium between geometry, mechanical properties, and external forces.

title: Physically Compatible 3D Object Modeling from a Single Image

abstract: Vision Language Models exhibit impressive performance for various tasks, yet they often lack the sophisticated situational reasoning required for complex decision-making. This paper shows that VLMs can achieve surprisingly strong decision-making performance when visual scenes are replaced by textual descriptions, suggesting foundational reasoning can be effectively learned from language. Motivated by this insight, we propose Praxis-VLM, a reasoning VLM for vision-grounded decision-making. Praxis-VLM employs the GRPO algorithm on textual scenarios to instill robust reasoning capabilities, where models learn to evaluate actions and their consequences. These reasoning skills, acquired purely from text, successfully transfer to multimodal inference with visual inputs, significantly reducing reliance on scarce paired image-text training data. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks demonstrate that Praxis-VLM substantially outperforms standard supervised fine-tuning, exhibiting superior performance and generalizability. Further analysis confirms that our models engage in explicit and effective reasoning, underpinning their enhanced performance and adaptability.
