paragraphs: Submodular optimization captures diminishing returns when selecting a set of items. This paper generalizes the problem to several disjoint sets with a shared objective. The formulation can represent allocating resources among multiple agents, where both the allocation and the combined selection matter, and the union of allocated resources must satisfy a feasibility constraint.

For maximization, the authors establish approximation guarantees for practical methods, including accelerated greedy variants and distributed algorithms, over broad constraint families such as matroids and p-systems. They also give a transfer result: an alpha approximation for the corresponding single-set multilinear formulation yields an alpha times (1−1/e) approximation in the monotone multivariate case, or alpha times 0.385 in the nonmonotone case.

For minimization, the paper gives essentially optimal approximation guarantees expressed through the objective's curvature. These results expand the collection of multivariate allocation problems with provable algorithmic treatment. The importance is the connection between a more expressive joint objective and existing optimization machinery, with the quality of the resulting solutions quantified rather than assumed.
summary.tldr: Multivariate submodular optimization extends set selection to joint allocations and provides approximation guarantees for maximization and minimization.

title: Multivariate Submodular Optimization

abstract: We attempt to interpret how adversarially trained convolutional neural networks (AT-CNNs) recognize objects. We design systematic approaches to interpret AT-CNNs in both qualitative and quantitative ways and compare them with normally trained models. Surprisingly, we find that adversarial training alleviates the texture bias of standard CNNs when trained on object recognition tasks, and helps CNNs learn a more shape-biased representation. We validate our hypothesis from two aspects. First, we compare the salience maps of AT-CNNs and standard CNNs on clean images and images under different transformations. The comparison could visually show that the prediction of the two types of CNNs is sensitive to dramatically different types of features. Second, to achieve quantitative verification, we construct additional test datasets that destroy either textures or shapes, such as style-transferred version of clean data, saturated images and patch-shuffled ones, and then evaluate the classification accuracy of AT-CNNs and normal CNNs on these datasets. Our findings shed some light on why AT-CNNs are more robust than those normally trained ones and contribute to a better understanding of adversarial training over CNNs from an interpretation perspective.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how adversarial training changes the visual features convolutional networks use to recognize objects. Its central finding is that adversarially trained networks show less of the texture bias found in normally trained networks and develop representations that rely more on shape. The authors study this shift using both visual interpretation and quantitative testing.

First, they compare salience maps on clean images and on images subjected to different transformations. These comparisons reveal that the two kinds of networks can be sensitive to very different features. Second, they construct test datasets that disrupt texture or shape, including style-transferred images, saturated images, and images with shuffled patches.

Classification accuracy on these altered datasets provides quantitative evidence alongside the salience-map comparisons. The combined approach matters because visual explanations alone are complemented by tests of recognition when particular visual information is disrupted. The findings offer insight into why adversarially trained networks are more robust in the studied setting, connecting that robustness to a change in learned representation rather than treating it solely as a prediction-level outcome.
summary.tldr: Visual and quantitative tests suggest that adversarial training shifts CNN object recognition away from texture and toward shape.

title: Interpreting Adversarially Trained Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) using a fixed offline dataset of logged interactions is an important consideration in real world applications. This paper studies offline RL using the DQN replay dataset comprising the entire replay experience of a DQN agent on 60 Atari 2600 games. We demonstrate that recent off-policy deep RL algorithms, even when trained solely on this fixed dataset, outperform the fully trained DQN agent. To enhance generalization in the offline setting, we present Random Ensemble Mixture (REM), a robust Q-learning algorithm that enforces optimal Bellman consistency on random convex combinations of multiple Q-value estimates. Offline REM trained on the DQN replay dataset surpasses strong RL baselines. Ablation studies highlight the role of offline dataset size and diversity as well as the algorithm choice in our positive results. Overall, the results here present an optimistic view that robust RL algorithms trained on sufficiently large and diverse offline datasets can lead to high quality policies. The DQN replay dataset can serve as an offline RL benchmark and is open-sourced.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning from a fixed collection of previously logged interactions. Its dataset contains the full replay experience of a DQN agent across 60 Atari games. The authors show that recent off-policy deep reinforcement learning algorithms can exceed the fully trained DQN agent's performance while learning exclusively from those stored experiences.

They also introduce Random Ensemble Mixture, or REM, to improve generalization in this offline setting. REM maintains multiple Q-value estimates and enforces optimal Bellman consistency on random convex combinations of them. These combinations are weighted mixtures whose weights sum to one. The training constraint therefore applies across random mixtures of value estimates.

Offline REM outperforms strong reinforcement learning baselines on the DQN replay dataset. Ablation studies connect these positive outcomes to dataset size, dataset diversity, and algorithm choice. The broader conclusion is conditional: robust algorithms can produce high-quality policies from sufficiently large and diverse offline data. The released replay dataset also provides a benchmark for studying that possibility.
summary.tldr: REM and other off-policy algorithms learn strong Atari policies from fixed replay data, with success tied to data size, diversity, and algorithm choice.

title: An Optimistic Perspective on Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce and analyze a class of algorithms, called Mirror Ascent against an Improved Opponent (MAIO), for computing Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games, both in normal form and in sequential form with imperfect information. These algorithms update the policy of each player with a mirror-ascent step to maximize the value of playing against an improved opponent. An improved opponent can be a best response, a greedy policy, a policy improved by policy gradient, or by any other reinforcement learning or search techniques. We establish a convergence result of the last iterate to the set of Nash equilibria and show that the speed of convergence depends on the amount of improvement offered by these improved policies. In addition, we show that under some condition, if we use a best response as improved policy, then an exponential convergence rate is achieved.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Mirror Ascent against an Improved Opponent, or MAIO, for finding Nash equilibria in two-player zero-sum games. It covers both normal-form games and sequential games with imperfect information. The goal is to learn strategies that approach equilibrium even when players do not have complete information during play.

Each player updates its policy using a mirror-ascent step evaluated against an improved opponent. That opponent can be produced through a best response, a greedy policy, policy-gradient improvement, or other reinforcement learning and search techniques. This makes opponent improvement a flexible ingredient of the algorithm, connecting equilibrium computation with several ways of strengthening a policy.

The authors establish convergence of the last iterate to the set of Nash equilibria, so their result concerns the current policies themselves. They also connect convergence speed to how much improvement the opponent policies provide. With a best-response opponent, an exponential convergence rate follows under an additional condition; the rate is therefore a conditional result rather than a guarantee for every MAIO variant.
summary.tldr: MAIO learns equilibrium strategies against improved opponents, with convergence speed linked to the strength of those improvements.

title: Fast computation of Nash Equilibria in Imperfect Information Games

abstract: Reinforcement learning allows solving complex tasks, however, the learning tends to be task-specific and the sample efficiency remains a challenge. We present Plan2Explore, a self-supervised reinforcement learning agent that tackles both these challenges through a new approach to self-supervised exploration and fast adaptation to new tasks, which need not be known during exploration. During exploration, unlike prior methods which retrospectively compute the novelty of observations after the agent has already reached them, our agent acts efficiently by leveraging planning to seek out expected future novelty. After exploration, the agent quickly adapts to multiple downstream tasks in a zero or a few-shot manner. We evaluate on challenging control tasks from high-dimensional image inputs. Without any training supervision or task-specific interaction, Plan2Explore outperforms prior self-supervised exploration methods, and in fact, almost matches the performances oracle which has access to rewards. Videos and code: https://ramanans1.github.io/plan2explore/

paragraphs: Plan2Explore addresses a problem in reinforcement learning: collecting experience efficiently when the tasks that will eventually matter are not yet known. The agent explores through self-supervision and later adapts to multiple downstream tasks. This separates the collection of useful experience from the requirement to specify a particular task during exploration.

Its central idea is to plan for expected future novelty. Methods that assess novelty only after reaching an observation use that information retrospectively; Plan2Explore uses planning to seek informative experiences ahead of time. A self-supervised world model supports this approach, allowing exploration to be guided by what the agent expects to encounter.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging control problems with high-dimensional image inputs. After exploration, the agent adapts in zero-shot or few-shot settings. Without training supervision or task-specific interaction, it outperforms earlier self-supervised exploration methods and nearly matches a reward-informed oracle in the reported evaluation. These findings support planning for novelty as a way to gather experience useful across subsequently specified tasks.
summary.tldr: Plan2Explore plans toward expected novelty during self-supervised exploration, enabling rapid adaptation to tasks that need not be known beforehand.

title: Planning to Explore via Self-Supervised World Models

abstract: Recent work pre-training Transformers with self-supervised objectives on large text corpora has shown great success when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks including text summarization. However, pre-training objectives tailored for abstractive text summarization have not been explored. Furthermore there is a lack of systematic evaluation across diverse domains. In this work, we propose pre-training large Transformer-based encoder-decoder models on massive text corpora with a new self-supervised objective. In PEGASUS, important sentences are removed/masked from an input document and are generated together as one output sequence from the remaining sentences, similar to an extractive summary. We evaluated our best PEGASUS model on 12 downstream summarization tasks spanning news, science, stories, instructions, emails, patents, and legislative bills. Experiments demonstrate it achieves state-of-the-art performance on all 12 downstream datasets measured by ROUGE scores. Our model also shows surprising performance on low-resource summarization, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results on 6 datasets with only 1000 examples. Finally we validated our results using human evaluation and show that our model summaries achieve human performance on multiple datasets.

It removes important sentences from a document and trains a large Transformer encoder-decoder to generate those sentences together from the remaining text. The missing sentences form a summary-like target, linking pretraining more directly to the later summarization task.

summary.tldr: PEGASUS pretrains summarizers by reconstructing important missing sentences, achieving leading results across twelve summarization datasets.

title: PEGASUS: Pre-training with Extracted Gap-sentences for Abstractive Summarization

abstract: Co-part segmentation is an important problem in computer vision for its rich applications. We propose an unsupervised learning approach for co-part segmentation from images. For the training stage, we leverage motion information embedded in videos and explicitly extract latent representations to segment meaningful object parts. More importantly, we introduce a dual procedure of part-assembly to form a closed loop with part-segmentation, enabling an effective self-supervision. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with a host of extensive experiments, ranging from human bodies, hands, quadruped, and robot arms. We show that our approach can achieve meaningful and compact part segmentation, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches on diverse benchmarks.

paragraphs: Co-part segmentation seeks meaningful object parts across images. This paper proposes an unsupervised approach, using motion in videos during training to help discover those parts. The method explicitly extracts latent representations that support segmentation, drawing on information available from movement rather than relying on manually supplied part annotations.

Its central mechanism pairs segmentation with a complementary assembly procedure. Segmentation separates an object into parts, while assembly brings parts together, creating a closed learning loop. The authors use this relationship as self-supervision: the assembly task supplies a training signal for the decomposition. This connects the usefulness of a part representation to its role in forming the object.

Experiments span human bodies, hands, quadrupeds, and robot arms. The authors report meaningful, compact segmentations and improvements over state-of-the-art approaches across diverse benchmarks. The range of evaluated objects supports the approach’s usefulness beyond a single kind of articulated subject. The key contribution is the combination of motion-based training information with segmentation-and-assembly self-supervision for discovering parts from images.
summary.tldr: Video motion and a segmentation–assembly learning loop enable unsupervised discovery of meaningful object parts across several evaluated object types.

title: Unsupervised Co-part Segmentation through Assembly

abstract: The recent breakthrough achieved by contrastive learning accelerates the pace for deploying unsupervised training on real-world data applications. However, unlabeled data in reality is commonly imbalanced and shows a long-tail distribution, and it is unclear how robustly the latest contrastive learning methods could perform in the practical scenario. This paper proposes to explicitly tackle this challenge, via a principled framework called Self-Damaging Contrastive Learning (SDCLR), to automatically balance the representation learning without knowing the classes. Our main inspiration is drawn from the recent finding that deep models have difficult-to-memorize samples, and those may be exposed through network pruning. It is further natural to hypothesize that long-tail samples are also tougher for the model to learn well due to insufficient examples. Hence, the key innovation in SDCLR is to create a dynamic self-competitor model to contrast with the target model, which is a pruned version of the latter. During training, contrasting the two models will lead to adaptive online mining of the most easily forgotten samples for the current target model, and implicitly emphasize them more in the contrastive loss. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and imbalance settings show that SDCLR significantly improves not only overall accuracies but also balancedness, in terms of linear evaluation on the full-shot and few-shot settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/SDCLR.

During training, contrasting the two models will lead to adaptive online mining of the most easily forgotten samples for the current target model, and implicitly emphasize them more in the contrastive loss. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and imbalance settings show that SDCLR significantly improves not only overall accuracies but also balancedness, in terms of linear evaluation on the full-shot and few-shot settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/SDCLR.

paragraphs: Unlabeled datasets often have long-tailed distributions, with some kinds of examples much more common than others. This paper investigates how to make contrastive representation learning more balanced without knowing the classes. Its starting hypothesis is that underrepresented examples may be harder for a model to learn well because they receive less support from the data.

Self-Damaging Contrastive Learning creates a changing competitor by pruning the target network. Comparing the target with this pruned version exposes examples that the current model most easily forgets. During training, the method adaptively mines these examples and implicitly gives them greater emphasis in the contrastive loss, using the model’s response to pruning as a learning signal.

Across multiple datasets and imbalance settings, the authors report significant improvements in overall accuracy and balancedness. These results are measured through linear evaluation in both full-shot and few-shot settings. The findings support using a pruned self-competitor to improve representations under class imbalance, while the proposed connection between long-tail examples and learning difficulty remains part of the method’s motivating hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Contrasting a network with its pruned version emphasizes easily forgotten examples and improves representation accuracy and balance on imbalanced datasets.

title: Self-Damaging Contrastive Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning in large action spaces is a challenging problem. This is especially true for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), which often requires tractable learning while respecting various constraints like communication budget and information about other agents. In this work, we focus on the fundamental hurdle affecting both value-based and policy-gradient approaches: an exponential blowup of the action space with the number of agents. For value-based methods, it poses challenges in accurately representing the optimal value function for value-based methods, thus inducing suboptimality. For policy gradient methods, it renders the critic ineffective and exacerbates the problem of the lagging critic. We show that from a learning theory perspective, both problems can be addressed by accurately representing the associated action-value function with a low-complexity hypothesis class. This requires accurately modelling the agent interactions in a sample efficient way. To this end, we propose a novel tensorised formulation of the Bellman equation. This gives rise to our method Tesseract, which utilises the view of Q-function seen as a tensor where the modes correspond to action spaces of different agents. Algorithms derived from Tesseract decompose the Q-tensor across the agents and utilise low-rank tensor approximations to model the agent interactions relevant to the task. We provide PAC analysis for Tesseract based algorithms and highlight their relevance to the class of rich observation MDPs. Empirical results in different domains confirm the gains in sample efficiency using Tesseract as supported by the theory.

paragraphs: In cooperative reinforcement learning, the number of joint action combinations grows exponentially with the number of agents. This makes action values difficult to represent accurately and can undermine the critic used by policy-gradient methods. Tesseract addresses this shared problem by seeking a compact representation that still captures interactions relevant to the task.

The paper reformulates the Bellman equation using tensors. It views the action-value function as a multidimensional array with one dimension corresponding to each agent's action space. Algorithms derived from this formulation decompose that array across agents and use low-rank approximations to represent their interactions with a lower-complexity model.

The authors connect accurate representation within a low-complexity hypothesis class to learning efficiency and provide a probably approximately correct analysis for Tesseract-based algorithms. They also discuss relevance to decision processes with rich observations. Experiments across different domains confirm gains in sample efficiency consistent with the theory, supporting tensor decomposition as a way to manage joint action complexity while modeling inter-agent dependencies.
summary.tldr: Tesseract represents joint action values with low-rank tensors to model agent interactions compactly and improve sample efficiency.

title: Tesseract: Tensorised Actors for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Semantic understanding of programs is a fundamental problem for programming language processing (PLP). Recent works that learn representations of code based on pre-training techniques in NLP have pushed the frontiers in this direction. However, the semantics of PL and NL have essential differences. These being ignored, we believe it is difficult to build a model to better understand programs, by either directly applying off-the-shelf NLP pre-training techniques to the source code, or adding features to the model by the heuristic. In fact, the semantics of a program can be rigorously defined by formal semantics in PL theory. For example, the operational semantics, describes the meaning of a valid program as updating the environment (i.e., the memory address-value function) through fundamental operations, such as memory I/O and conditional branching. Inspired by this, we propose a novel program semantics learning paradigm, that the model should learn from information composed of (1) the representations which align well with the fundamental operations in operational semantics, and (2) the information of environment transition, which is indispensable for program understanding. To validate our proposal, we present a hierarchical Transformer-based pre-training model called OSCAR to better facilitate the understanding of programs. OSCAR learns from intermediate representation (IR) and an encoded representation derived from static analysis, which are used for representing the fundamental operations and approximating the environment transitions respectively. OSCAR empirically shows the outstanding capability of program semantics understanding on many practical software engineering tasks. Code and models are released at: \url{https://github.com/pdlan/OSCAR}.

paragraphs: The paper argues that learning program meaning requires attention to how programs operate, beyond treating source code as language-like text. Programming-language theory provides an explicit account through operational semantics: a program changes an environment, such as memory contents, through operations including reads, writes, and conditional branches.

This motivates a learning paradigm with two sources of information. One represents fundamental operations in a form aligned with operational semantics. The other describes how the environment changes, which the authors regard as essential to understanding programs. Their model, OSCAR, implements this idea with hierarchical Transformer pretraining using intermediate representations and an encoding derived from static analysis.

The intermediate representation supplies the operational view, while static analysis approximates environment transitions. That approximation is part of the proposed approach, rather than a claim that all runtime behavior is directly observed. Across practical software engineering tasks, OSCAR empirically demonstrates strong program-semantics understanding. The contribution links the choice of pretraining information to a formal account of program meaning and supports that design through downstream task performance.
summary.tldr: OSCAR learns program representations from fundamental operations and approximated environment transitions inspired by operational semantics.

title: How could Neural Networks understand Programs?

abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) building blocks, i.e. $Q$-functions and policy networks, usually take elements from the cartesian product of two domains as input. In particular, the input of the $Q$-function is both the state and the action, and in multi-task problems (Meta-RL) the policy can take a state and a context. Standard architectures tend to ignore these variables’ underlying interpretations and simply concatenate their features into a single vector. In this work, we argue that this choice may lead to poor gradient estimation in actor-critic algorithms and high variance learning steps in Meta-RL algorithms. To consider the interaction between the input variables, we suggest using a Hypernetwork architecture where a primary network determines the weights of a conditional dynamic network. We show that this approach improves the gradient approximation and reduces the learning step variance, which both accelerates learning and improves the final performance. We demonstrate a consistent improvement across different locomotion tasks and different algorithms both in RL (TD3 and SAC) and in Meta-RL (MAML and PEARL).

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning networks often combine inputs with different roles. A Q-function takes a state and an action, while a multi-task policy may take a state and a task context. Standard architectures commonly concatenate these inputs. This paper argues that doing so can contribute to poor gradient estimates or high-variance learning steps.

The proposed alternative uses a hypernetwork: a primary network produces the weights of a conditional, dynamically specified network. This gives the architecture an explicit way to represent interactions between the different inputs. The authors show improvements in gradient approximation and reductions in learning-step variance, linking these changes to faster learning and better final performance.

Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across locomotion tasks and several algorithms. The evaluated reinforcement-learning methods are TD3 and SAC, and the meta-reinforcement-learning methods are MAML and PEARL. These results support the architectural proposal across the tested combinations. The main contribution is to reconsider how the inputs to familiar learning components are combined, rather than treating their different roles as interchangeable features.
summary.tldr: Hypernetwork architectures improve how reinforcement-learning components combine inputs, yielding better gradients and more stable learning in the reported evaluations.

title: Recomposing the Reinforcement Learning Building Blocks with Hypernetworks

abstract: We consider two key issues faced by many clustering methods when used for data summarization, namely (a) an unfair representation of "demographic groups” and (b) distorted summarizations, where data points in the summary represent subsets of the original data of vastly different sizes. Previous work made important steps towards handling separately each of these two issues in the context of the fundamental k-Center clustering objective through the study of fast algorithms for natural models that address them. We show that it is possible to effectively address both (a) and (b) simultaneously by presenting a clustering procedure that works for a canonical combined model and (i) is fast, both in theory and practice, (ii) exhibits a worst-case constant-factor guarantee, and (iii) gives promising computational results showing that there can be significant benefits in addressing both issues together instead of sequentially.

paragraphs: A clustering-based summary can misrepresent data in two different ways. It may represent demographic groups unfairly, and its representative points may stand for populations of very different sizes. The paper studies how to address these issues together when constructing a summary using the k-center clustering objective.

Earlier work had developed fast algorithms for natural models of each concern separately. The authors introduce a clustering procedure for a combined model, so demographic representation and the sizes of represented subsets enter the same problem. This matters because treating one concern after the other need not capture the benefits available when both influence the clustering procedure together.

The procedure is fast both in theoretical analysis and in practical evaluation. It also has a worst-case constant-factor guarantee, providing a bounded approximation under the combined model. Computational results are described as promising and show that joint treatment can offer significant benefits over sequential treatment. The claim is that such benefits are possible and observed in the reported evaluation, rather than that joint treatment must outperform sequential approaches on every dataset.
summary.tldr: A fast k-center procedure jointly addresses demographic representation and uneven summary sizes with a constant-factor worst-case guarantee.

title: Fair and Fast k-Center Clustering for Data Summarization

abstract: In this work, we study the effect of varying the architecture and training data quality on the data scaling properties of Neural Machine Translation (NMT). First, we establish that the test loss of encoder-decoder transformer models scales as a power law in the number of training samples, with a dependence on the model size. Then, we systematically vary aspects of the training setup to understand how they impact the data scaling laws. In particular, we change the following (1) Architecture and task setup: We compare to a transformer-LSTM hybrid, and a decoder-only transformer with a language modeling loss (2) Noise level in the training distribution: We experiment with filtering, and adding iid synthetic noise. In all the above cases, we find that the data scaling exponents are minimally impacted, suggesting that marginally worse architectures or training data can be compensated for by adding more data. Lastly, we find that using back-translated data instead of parallel data, can significantly degrade the scaling exponent.

paragraphs: This paper examines how neural machine translation improves as the amount of training data grows, and whether architecture or data quality changes that relationship. For encoder-decoder Transformers, the authors establish a power-law relationship between test loss and training sample count, with an additional dependence on model size.

They then vary the learning setup systematically. Architecture comparisons include a Transformer-LSTM hybrid and a decoder-only Transformer trained with a language modeling loss. Data-quality experiments include filtering and adding independent, identically distributed synthetic noise. Across these changes, the estimated data-scaling exponents change only slightly.

That result suggests that, in the studied settings, adding data can compensate for marginally worse architectures or training data. It does not imply that every data source supports the same improvement rate. The authors find a contrasting result when back-translated data replaces parallel data: the scaling exponent can degrade substantially. The distinction matters because data quantity and data source can affect the scaling relationship differently, even when several other changes leave its exponent largely intact.
summary.tldr: Translation scaling exponents change little under several architecture and noise variations, but can worsen substantially with back-translated data.

title: Data Scaling Laws in NMT: The Effect of Noise and Architecture

abstract: Active regression considers a linear regression problem where the learner receives a large number of data points but can only observe a small number of labels. Since online algorithms can deal with incremental training data and take advantage of low computational cost, we consider an online extension of the active regression problem: the learner receives data points one by one and immediately decides whether it should collect the corresponding labels. The goal is to efficiently maintain the regression of received data points with a small budget of label queries. We propose novel algorithms for this problem under $\ell_p$ loss where $p\in[1,2]$. To achieve a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate solution, our proposed algorithms only requires $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d/poly(\epsilon))$ queries of labels. The numerical results verify our theoretical results and show that our methods have comparable performance with offline active regression algorithms.

paragraphs: Active regression seeks to fit a linear model while requesting labels for only a small portion of the available examples. This paper studies the online version: examples arrive individually, and the learner must immediately decide whether to obtain each label. The objective is to maintain a good regression fit as data accumulate under a limited query budget.

The authors propose algorithms for losses in the ℓp family with p between one and two. To obtain a solution within a multiplicative factor of 1+ε of the target regression objective, their label-query bound is approximately d divided by a polynomial in ε, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here d describes the dimension of the regression problem.

The theoretical result ties label demand to dimension and desired accuracy while accommodating immediate decisions about incoming examples. Numerical results support the analysis and show performance comparable to offline active regression methods. This matters because the online learner must select labels incrementally, whereas an offline method can operate on the available collection together.
summary.tldr: Online active regression algorithms choose labels as examples arrive and obtain approximate fits with a dimension- and accuracy-dependent query budget.

title: Online Active Regression

abstract: Adversarial purification refers to a class of defense methods that remove adversarial perturbations using a generative model. These methods do not make assumptions on the form of attack and the classification model, and thus can defend pre-existing classifiers against unseen threats. However, their performance currently falls behind adversarial training methods. In this work, we propose DiffPure that uses diffusion models for adversarial purification: Given an adversarial example, we first diffuse it with a small amount of noise following a forward diffusion process, and then recover the clean image through a reverse generative process. To evaluate our method against strong adaptive attacks in an efficient and scalable way, we propose to use the adjoint method to compute full gradients of the reverse generative process. Extensive experiments on three image datasets including CIFAR-10, ImageNet and CelebA-HQ with three classifier architectures including ResNet, WideResNet and ViT demonstrate that our method achieves the state-of-the-art results, outperforming current adversarial training and adversarial purification methods, often by a large margin.

paragraphs: Adversarial purification uses a generative model to remove malicious changes from an input before classification. This approach can protect an existing classifier without assuming a particular attack form or classifier architecture. The paper introduces DiffPure to improve purification performance, which the authors describe as previously trailing defenses based on adversarial training.

DiffPure first adds a small amount of noise to an adversarial image through a forward diffusion process. It then applies the reverse generative process to recover a clean image. The defense therefore relies on a controlled noising-and-recovery procedure. For evaluation against strong adaptive attacks, the authors use an adjoint method to compute full gradients through the reverse process efficiently and at scale.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and CelebA-HQ, together with ResNet, WideResNet, and vision transformer classifiers. In these evaluations, DiffPure achieves state-of-the-art results and exceeds existing adversarial training and purification methods, often substantially. The findings support diffusion-based purification across the tested datasets and architectures, while the adaptive-attack procedure provides a way to assess attacks that account for the defense.
summary.tldr: DiffPure uses diffusion-based image recovery to remove adversarial perturbations and outperforms existing defenses in the reported evaluations.

title: Diffusion Models for Adversarial Purification

abstract: Of theories for why large-scale machine learning models generalize despite being vastly overparameterized, which of their assumptions are needed to capture the qualitative phenomena of generalization in the real world? On one hand, we find that most theoretical analyses fall short of capturing these qualitative phenomena even for kernel regression, when applied to kernels derived from large-scale neural networks (e.g., ResNet-50) and real data (e.g., CIFAR-100). On the other hand, we find that the classical GCV estimator (Craven and Wahba, 1978) accurately predicts generalization risk even in such overparameterized settings. To bolster this empirical finding, we prove that the GCV estimator converges to the generalization risk whenever a local random matrix law holds. Finally, we apply this random matrix theory lens to explain why pretrained representations generalize better as well as what factors govern scaling laws for kernel regression. Our findings suggest that random matrix theory, rather than just being a toy model, may be central to understanding the properties of neural representations in practice.

paragraphs: The paper examines which theoretical assumptions help explain generalization in highly overparameterized learning. Its test case is kernel regression using representations from large neural networks and real datasets. In this setting, the authors find that many existing theoretical analyses fail to capture even qualitative patterns in how prediction performance generalizes beyond training data.

A classical generalized cross-validation estimator, abbreviated GCV, performs much better in their empirical investigation: it accurately predicts generalization risk even in the overparameterized setting. The paper supports this observation with a conditional theorem. When a local random matrix law holds, the GCV estimator converges to the generalization risk. The condition is central to the guarantee, rather than a claim that convergence holds for arbitrary representations.

The authors then use the random-matrix perspective to explain benefits from pretrained representations and factors governing kernel-regression scaling laws. Together, the empirical evidence and conditional theory suggest that random matrix models can describe meaningful behavior of practical neural representations. The findings concern this representation-based kernel-regression setting and motivate the broader possibility that random matrix theory helps explain neural generalization.
summary.tldr: GCV predicts generalization for real neural representations, with a convergence guarantee when a local random matrix law holds.

title: More Than a Toy: Random Matrix Models Predict How Real-World Neural Representations Generalize

abstract: Contrastive Learning (CL) has emerged as a dominant technique for unsupervised representation learning which embeds augmented versions of the anchor close to each other (positive samples) and pushes the embeddings of other samples (negatives) apart. As revealed in recent studies, CL can benefit from hard negatives (negatives that are most similar to the anchor). However, we observe limited benefits when we adopt existing hard negative mining techniques of other domains in Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL). We perform both experimental and theoretical analysis on this phenomenon and find it can be attributed to the message passing of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Unlike CL in other domains, most hard negatives are potentially false negatives (negatives that share the same class with the anchor) if they are selected merely according to the similarities between anchor and themselves, which will undesirably push away the samples of the same class. To remedy this deficiency, we propose an effective method, dubbed \textbf{ProGCL}, to estimate the probability of a negative being true one, which constitutes a more suitable measure for negatives’ hardness together with similarity. Additionally, we devise two schemes (i.e., \textbf{ProGCL-weight} and \textbf{ProGCL-mix}) to boost the performance of GCL. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProGCL brings notable and consistent improvements over base GCL methods and yields multiple state-of-the-art results on several unsupervised benchmarks or even exceeds the performance of supervised ones. Also, ProGCL is readily pluggable into various negatives-based GCL methods for performance improvement. We release the code at \textcolor{magenta}\url{https://github.com/junxia97/ProGCL}.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning pulls related representations together and pushes designated negatives apart. Highly similar negatives can be useful training examples, but this paper finds limited benefits from importing existing hard-negative selection methods into graph learning. Its experimental and theoretical analysis attributes the problem to message passing in graph neural networks.

When candidates are selected only by similarity, many hard negatives may actually belong to the same class as the anchor. Pushing them away would then separate examples that should remain related. ProGCL estimates the probability that a candidate is a true negative and combines that estimate with similarity to judge hardness. The paper develops two associated schemes, ProGCL-weight and ProGCL-mix.

Experiments show consistent improvements over base graph contrastive methods, multiple leading results on unsupervised benchmarks, and performance exceeding supervised methods in some cases. The approach can also be inserted into various graph contrastive methods that use negatives. Its main lesson is that similarity alone can be misleading: selecting useful difficult examples also requires considering whether the negative assignment is plausible.
summary.tldr: ProGCL improves graph contrastive learning by judging hard negatives using both similarity and the estimated probability that they are truly negative.

title: ProGCL: Rethinking Hard Negative Mining in Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a privacy-preserving paradigm where multiple participants jointly solve a machine learning problem without sharing raw data. Unlike traditional distributed learning, a unique characteristic of FL is statistical heterogeneity, namely, data distributions across participants are different from each other. Meanwhile, recent advances in the interpretation of neural networks have seen a wide use of neural tangent kernels (NTKs) for convergence analyses. In this paper, we propose a novel FL paradigm empowered by the NTK framework. The paradigm addresses the challenge of statistical heterogeneity by transmitting update data that are more expressive than those of the conventional FL paradigms. Specifically, sample-wise Jacobian matrices, rather than model weights/gradients, are uploaded by participants. The server then constructs an empirical kernel matrix to update a global model without explicitly performing gradient descent. We further develop a variant with improved communication efficiency and enhanced privacy. Numerical results show that the proposed paradigm can achieve the same accuracy while reducing the number of communication rounds by an order of magnitude compared to federated averaging.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines information from participants without collecting their raw data in one place. A central difficulty is that participants can have different data distributions, so their local learning signals may differ substantially. This paper proposes changing what participants communicate to make the shared information more expressive in that heterogeneous setting.

Participants upload sample-wise Jacobian matrices instead of model weights or gradients. These matrices describe how model outputs respond to parameter changes for individual samples. Using the neural tangent kernel framework, the server constructs an empirical kernel matrix and updates a global model without explicitly running gradient descent. The paper also develops a variant intended to improve communication efficiency and privacy.

Numerical experiments show that the proposed paradigm can reach the same accuracy as federated averaging with an order-of-magnitude reduction in communication rounds. This result concerns the number of rounds needed in the reported experiments. It supports the value of richer update information for coordinating learning across participants with different data distributions.
summary.tldr: Sharing sample-wise Jacobians enables kernel-based federated updates that experimentally match federated averaging accuracy with far fewer communication rounds.

title: Neural Tangent Kernel Empowered Federated Learning

abstract: Non-linear state-space models, also known as general hidden Markov models (HMM), are ubiquitous in statistical machine learning, being the most classical generative models for serial data and sequences. Learning in HMM, either via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) or Markov Score Climbing (MSC) requires the estimation of the- smoothing expectation of some additive functionals. Controlling the bias and the variance of this estimation is crucial to establish the convergence of learning algorithms. Our first contribution is to design a novel additive smoothing algorithm, the Parisian particle Gibbs (PPG) sampler, which can be viewed as a PaRIS (Olsson, Westerborn 2017) algorithm driven by conditional SMC moves, resulting in bias-reduced estimates of the targeted quantities. We substantiate the PPG algorithm with theoretical results, including new bounds on bias and variance as well as deviation inequalities. We then establish, in the learning context, and under standard assumptions, non-asymptotic bounds highlighting the value of bias reduction and the implicit Rao–Blackwellization of PPG. These are the first non-asymptotic results of this kind in this setting. We illustrate our theoretical results with numerical experiments supporting our claims.

paragraphs: Learning nonlinear state-space models requires reasoning about hidden states from observed sequences. For maximum likelihood estimation and Markov Score Climbing, an important step is estimating smoothing expectations of additive quantities. Errors in these estimates matter because both bias and variance affect the convergence analysis of the learning procedure.

The paper introduces the Parisian particle Gibbs sampler, or PPG, as a new additive smoothing algorithm. It combines the PaRIS approach with conditional sequential Monte Carlo moves to produce estimates with reduced bias. The authors develop bounds on bias and variance, together with deviation inequalities that characterize estimation errors.

They then analyze PPG within learning algorithms and establish finite-computation bounds under standard assumptions. These results highlight benefits from bias reduction and the sampler's implicit Rao–Blackwellization, an averaging effect that improves estimation. Numerical experiments support the theoretical claims. The contribution links the design of a better smoothing estimator to explicit guarantees for learning states and parameters from sequential observations.
summary.tldr: Parisian particle Gibbs reduces smoothing-estimation bias and supports finite-computation learning guarantees for nonlinear state-space models.

title: State and parameter learning with PARIS particle Gibbs

abstract: Typical off-policy evaluation (OPE) and off-policy learning (OPL) are not well-defined problems under "truncation by death", where the outcome of interest is not defined after some events, such as death. The standard OPE no longer yields consistent estimators, and the standard OPL results in suboptimal policies. In this paper, we formulate OPE and OPL using principal stratification under "truncation by death". We propose a survivor value function for a subpopulation whose outcomes are always defined regardless of treatment conditions. We establish a novel identification strategy under principal ignorability, and derive the semiparametric efficiency bound of an OPE estimator. Then, we propose multiply robust estimators for OPE and OPL. We show that the proposed estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal even with flexible semi/nonparametric models for nuisance functions approximation. Moreover, under mild rate conditions of nuisance functions approximation, the estimators achieve the semiparametric efficiency bound. Finally, we conduct experiments to demonstrate the empirical performance of the proposed estimators.

paragraphs: Some outcomes are undefined after events such as death, creating a problem that ordinary missing-data handling does not resolve. Standard off-policy evaluation and learning can then target quantities that are not well defined or produce inconsistent estimates. This paper reformulates the problem using principal stratification.

The authors define a survivor value function for the subpopulation whose outcomes would remain defined under all treatment conditions. Under principal ignorability, they establish identification and derive a semiparametric efficiency bound. They then construct multiply robust estimators for both evaluating policies and learning improved ones.

The estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal while allowing flexible nuisance-function models. With additional rate conditions, they attain the efficiency bound, and experiments examine their empirical behavior. The contribution is a principled policy-analysis target for this difficult setting. Its interpretation depends on the survivor subpopulation and identification assumptions, rather than representing an unconditional value for everyone originally observed.
summary.tldr: A survivor-based policy value and multiply robust estimators make off-policy analysis well defined under truncation by death.

title: Multiply Robust Off-policy Evaluation and Learning under Truncation by Death

abstract: Visual and linguistic concepts naturally organize themselves in a hierarchy, where a textual concept "dog" entails all images that contain dogs. Despite being intuitive, current large-scale vision and language models such as CLIP do not explicitly capture such hierarchy. We propose MERU, a contrastive model that yields hyperbolic representations of images and text. Hyperbolic spaces have suitable geometric properties to embed tree-like data, so MERU can better capture the underlying hierarchy in image-text datasets. Our results show that MERU learns a highly interpretable and structured representation space while being competitive with CLIP’s performance on standard multi-modal tasks like image classification and image-text retrieval.

paragraphs: Visual and textual concepts often have hierarchical relationships: a broad word such as dog can describe many different images and more specific concepts. Standard contrastive vision-language models do not explicitly encode that structure. MERU uses the geometry of the representation space to make such relationships easier to express.

The model learns image and text representations in hyperbolic space through contrastive training. Hyperbolic geometry is well suited to tree-like organization, providing a way to represent broad concepts and more specific instances within one shared space. The approach changes the structure available to the embeddings rather than treating all relationships as flat similarity comparisons.

The reported representations are interpretable and organized, while remaining competitive with CLIP on image classification and image-text retrieval. The contribution is therefore a structured alternative to conventional multimodal embeddings without sacrificing the evaluated task performance. The abstract does not claim superiority on every benchmark or establish that all semantic relations in the learned space form a perfect hierarchy.
summary.tldr: MERU learns hyperbolic image-text embeddings that express hierarchy while remaining competitive with CLIP on standard multimodal tasks.

title: Hyperbolic Image-text Representations

abstract: The Johnson-Lindenstaruss lemma (Johnson & Lindenstrauss, 1984) is a cornerstone result in dimensionality reduction, stating it is possible to embed a set of $n$ points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space into optimal $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2} \ln n)$ dimensions, while preserving all pairwise distances to within a factor $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$. The seminal Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss (Fast JL) transform by Ailon and Chazelle (SICOMP’09) supports computing the embedding of a data point in $O(d \ln d +k \ln^2 n)$ time, where the $d \ln d$ term comes from multiplication with a $d \times d$ Hadamard matrix and the $k \ln^2 n$ term comes from multiplication with a sparse $k \times d$ matrix. Despite the Fast JL transform being more than a decade old, it is one of the fastest dimensionality reduction techniques for many tradeoffs between $\varepsilon, d$ and $n$. In this work, we give a surprising new analysis of the Fast JL transform, showing that the $k \ln^2 n$ term in the embedding time can be improved to $(k \ln^2 n)/\alpha$ for an $\alpha = \Omega(\min\{\varepsilon^{-1}\ln(1/\varepsilon), \ln n\})$. The improvement follows by using an even sparser matrix. We complement our improved analysis with a lower bound showing that our new analysis is in fact tight.

paragraphs: The Johnson-Lindenstrauss result allows high-dimensional points to be compressed while approximately preserving every pairwise distance. For n points and distortion tolerance epsilon, the target dimension can be O(epsilon^-2 log n). This paper revisits the Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform and shows that its sparse-matrix stage can be made cheaper.

The established per-point computation has two main terms: O(d log d) for a Hadamard transform and O(k log² n) for a sparse matrix multiplication. The new analysis supports using an even sparser matrix, reducing the second term by a factor alpha. The stated lower bound on that improvement factor is proportional to the minimum of epsilon^-1 log(1/epsilon) and log n.

The improvement targets the sparse multiplication term; the stated Hadamard term remains in the runtime expression. Consequently, the overall benefit depends on how those terms compare for the chosen dimensions and accuracy. A matching lower-bound analysis establishes tightness of the new analysis, giving both an improved construction and a characterization of its limits within the analyzed setting.
summary.tldr: A tight new analysis permits a sparser Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, reducing its sparse-multiplication cost while preserving dimensionality-reduction guarantees.

title: The Fast Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transform Is Even Faster

abstract: Optimization problems over dynamic networks have been extensively studied and widely used in the past decades to formulate numerous real-world problems. However, (1) traditional optimization-based approaches do not scale to large networks, and (2) the design of good heuristics or approximation algorithms often requires significant manual trial-and-error. In this work, we argue that data-driven strategies can automate this process and learn efficient algorithms without compromising optimality. To do so, we present network control problems through the lens of reinforcement learning and propose a graph network-based framework to handle a broad class of problems. Instead of naively computing actions over high-dimensional graph elements, e.g., edges, we propose a bi-level formulation where we (1) specify a desired next state via RL, and (2) solve a convex program to best achieve it, leading to drastically improved scalability and performance. We further highlight a collection of desirable features to system designers, investigate design decisions, and present experiments on real-world control problems showing the utility, scalability, and flexibility of our framework.

paragraphs: Controlling a dynamic network can require decisions over many interconnected elements. Traditional optimization approaches can struggle as networks grow, while effective heuristics often require extensive manual design. This paper frames network control as reinforcement learning and introduces a graph-network framework intended to handle a broad class of such problems.

Its key design divides each decision into two levels. A reinforcement learning component specifies a desired next state, and a convex optimization program determines how best to achieve it. This avoids asking the learned policy to directly produce a high-dimensional collection of actions over graph elements such as edges. Learning chooses the target, while optimization handles its realization.

The authors report substantially improved scalability and performance from this formulation. They investigate design choices and evaluate the framework on real-world control problems, finding evidence of utility, scalability, and flexibility. The approach matters because it provides a concrete way to combine learned decision-making with a structured optimization problem, reducing the burden placed on direct action prediction.
summary.tldr: A graph-based controller learns desired next states and uses convex optimization to realize them, improving network-control scalability and performance.

title: Graph Reinforcement Learning for Network Control via Bi-Level Optimization

abstract: We propose Banker Online Mirror Descent (Banker-OMD), a novel framework generalizing the classical Online Mirror Descent (OMD) technique in the online learning literature. The Banker-OMD framework almost completely decouples feedback delay handling and the task-specific OMD algorithm design, thus facilitating the design of new algorithms capable of efficiently and robustly handling feedback delays. Specifically, it offers a general methodology for achieving $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{T} + \sqrt{D})$-style regret bounds in online bandit learning tasks with delayed feedback, where $T$ is the number of rounds and $D$ is the total feedback delay. We demonstrate the power of Banker-OMD by applications to two important bandit learning scenarios with delayed feedback, including delayed scale-free adversarial Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) and delayed adversarial linear bandits. Banker-OMD leads to the first delayed scale-free adversarial MAB algorithm achieving $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{K}L(\sqrt T+\sqrt D))$ regret and the first delayed adversarial linear bandit algorithm achieving $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\text{poly}(n)(\sqrt{T} + \sqrt{D}))$ regret. As a corollary, the first application also implies $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{KT}L)$ regret for non-delayed scale-free adversarial MABs, which is the first to match the $\Omega(\sqrt{KT}L)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors and can be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Bandit learners make decisions using limited feedback, and delayed feedback makes those decisions harder because recent outcomes may still be unavailable. This paper introduces Banker Online Mirror Descent, a framework that extends online mirror descent to handle such delays. Its central contribution is to almost separate delay management from the design choices specific to a learning task.

The framework provides a general route to regret bounds that scale like √T + √D, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, T counts decision rounds and D measures total feedback delay. Regret expresses the learner’s accumulated disadvantage relative to a benchmark, so this form describes how the cost of learning grows with both time and delayed information.

The authors apply the framework to scale-free adversarial multi-armed bandits and adversarial linear bandits, obtaining the first stated bounds of their respective forms. The first application also yields a result without delays: its regret matches the corresponding lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Thus, the framework contributes both a reusable treatment of delays and an improvement for an ordinary, non-delayed bandit setting.
summary.tldr: Banker-OMD largely separates feedback-delay handling from bandit algorithm design while delivering improved regret guarantees.

title: Banker Online Mirror Descent: A Universal Approach for Delayed Online Bandit Learning

abstract: Clustering is a widely used unsupervised learning technique involving an intensive discrete optimization problem. Associative Memory models or AMs are differentiable neural networks defining a recursive dynamical system, which have been integrated with various deep learning architectures. We uncover a novel connection between the AM dynamics and the inherent discrete assignment necessary in clustering to propose a novel unconstrained continuous relaxation of the discrete clustering problem, enabling end-to-end differentiable clustering with AM, dubbed ClAM. Leveraging the pattern completion ability of AMs, we further develop a novel self-supervised clustering loss. Our evaluations on varied datasets demonstrate that ClAM benefits from the self-supervision, and significantly improves upon both the traditional Lloyd’s k-means algorithm, and more recent continuous clustering relaxations (by upto 60% in terms of the Silhouette Coefficient).

paragraphs: Clustering groups data without supplied labels, but deciding which group each item belongs to creates a discrete optimization problem. That discrete assignment is awkward to integrate into a fully differentiable learning system. The paper connects clustering assignments to associative memories, neural networks whose recursive dynamics support the recovery or completion of patterns.

Using this connection, the authors propose ClAM, an unconstrained continuous relaxation of the clustering problem. Replacing the discrete formulation with this relaxation allows clustering to participate in end-to-end gradient-based learning. They also develop a self-supervised clustering loss that draws on associative memories' pattern-completion ability, providing a training signal without externally supplied cluster labels.

Evaluations across varied datasets show that the self-supervised component helps ClAM. The authors report improvements over both Lloyd's k-means algorithm and more recent continuous relaxations, reaching up to 60% on the Silhouette Coefficient. This is a reported maximum improvement on that clustering-quality measure, while the broader contribution is the link between memory dynamics, continuous clustering, and self-supervised training.
summary.tldr: ClAM uses associative-memory dynamics and a self-supervised loss to make clustering differentiable and improve measured clustering quality.

title: End-to-end Differentiable Clustering with Associative Memories

abstract: Active learning is perhaps most naturally posed as an online learning problem. However, prior active learning approaches with deep neural networks assume offline access to the entire dataset ahead of time. This paper proposes VeSSAL, a new algorithm for batch active learning with deep neural networks in streaming settings, which samples groups of points to query for labels at the moment they are encountered. Our approach trades off between uncertainty and diversity of queried samples to match a desired query rate without requiring any hand-tuned hyperparameters. Altogether, we expand the applicability of deep neural networks to realistic active learning scenarios, such as applications relevant to HCI and large, fractured datasets.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should receive labels, making selective use of labeling effort. Many deep-learning approaches assume they can inspect the entire dataset before making those choices. This paper addresses a streaming setting, where examples arrive over time and decisions about requesting labels must be made as they are encountered.

The proposed algorithm, VeSSAL, performs batch active learning by sampling groups of incoming points. It balances uncertainty with diversity: the selection considers both where the model is uncertain and how varied the queried examples are. The method targets a desired query rate without requiring hand-tuned hyperparameters to manage this trade-off.

This changes the information-access requirements of deep active learning. Selection no longer depends on having an offline view of all examples in advance, which makes the approach relevant to human-computer interaction and large datasets spread across separate pieces. The paper's stated contribution is an algorithm suited to these streaming circumstances, with label selection organized around arrival-time decisions and a chosen query rate.
summary.tldr: VeSSAL selects examples for labeling as they arrive, balancing uncertainty and diversity while matching a desired query rate.

title: Streaming Active Learning with Deep Neural Networks

abstract: We propose causal isotonic calibration, a novel nonparametric method for calibrating predictors of heterogeneous treatment effects. Furthermore, we introduce cross-calibration, a data-efficient variant of calibration that eliminates the need for hold-out calibration sets. Cross-calibration leverages cross-fitted predictors and generates a single calibrated predictor using all available data. Under weak conditions that do not assume monotonicity, we establish that both causal isotonic calibration and cross-calibration achieve fast doubly-robust calibration rates, as long as either the propensity score or outcome regression is estimated accurately in a suitable sense. The proposed causal isotonic calibrator can be wrapped around any black-box learning algorithm, providing robust and distribution-free calibration guarantees while preserving predictive performance.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect predictors aim to describe how the effect of an intervention varies across individuals. This paper focuses on calibrating those predictions so that their reported effect sizes are reliable. It introduces causal isotonic calibration, a nonparametric adjustment that can be applied around any black-box learning algorithm.

The authors also propose cross-calibration to make better use of limited data. Instead of reserving a separate calibration set, it combines cross-fitted predictors into one calibrated predictor using all available observations. This addresses the data cost of calibration while retaining a single predictor for subsequent use.

Under weak conditions that do not require monotonicity, both methods achieve fast, doubly robust calibration rates. The guarantee requires either the propensity score or the outcome regression to be estimated accurately in the specified sense; it does not require both to be accurate. The proposed calibrator offers robust, distribution-free calibration guarantees while preserving predictive performance. The central contribution is therefore a broadly applicable calibration layer with explicit protection against certain estimation errors.
summary.tldr: Causal isotonic calibration adjusts treatment-effect predictions with doubly robust guarantees, while cross-calibration avoids a separate hold-out set.

title: Causal Isotonic Calibration for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects

abstract: Encoding constraints into neural networks is attractive. This paper studies how to introduce the popular positive linear satisfiability to neural networks. We propose the first differentiable satisfiability layer based on an extension of the classic Sinkhorn algorithm for jointly encoding multiple sets of marginal distributions. We further theoretically characterize the convergence property of the Sinkhorn algorithm for multiple marginals, and the underlying formulation is also derived. In contrast to the sequential decision e.g. reinforcement learning-based solvers, we showcase our technique in solving constrained (specifically satisfiability) problems by one-shot neural networks, including i) a neural routing solver learned without supervision of optimal solutions; ii) a partial graph matching network handling graphs with unmatchable outliers on both sides; iii) a predictive network for financial portfolios with continuous constraints. To our knowledge, there exists no one-shot neural solver for these scenarios when they are formulated as satisfiability problems. Source code is available at https://github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/LinSATNet.

paragraphs: Neural predictions often need to obey constraints as well as fit data. LinSATNet studies how to incorporate positive linear satisfiability into neural networks through a differentiable layer. Differentiability allows the constraint-handling component to participate in training, making feasibility part of the network’s computation.

The layer extends the Sinkhorn algorithm to jointly encode multiple sets of marginal distributions. The paper derives the underlying formulation and theoretically characterizes convergence for this multiple-marginal setting. This provides both a computational construction and an analysis of the procedure used to impose the constraints.

The authors demonstrate one-shot neural solvers in three applications: routing learned without optimal-solution supervision, partial graph matching with unmatchable outliers on both sides, and financial portfolio prediction with continuous constraints. These examples show how the same layer can support distinct satisfiability formulations. The contribution is a way to build constrained predictions into a neural solver, with demonstrations that do not require expressing the solution process as a sequence of reinforcement learning decisions.
summary.tldr: LinSATNet extends Sinkhorn scaling into a differentiable satisfiability layer for one-shot neural predictions subject to positive linear constraints.

title: LinSATNet: The Positive Linear Satisfiability Neural Networks

abstract: Interpretable policy learning seeks to estimate intelligible decision policies from observed actions; however, existing models force a tradeoff between accuracy and interpretability, limiting data-driven interpretations of human decision-making processes. Fundamentally, existing approaches are burdened by this tradeoff because they represent the underlying decision process as a universal policy, when in fact human decisions are dynamic and can change drastically under different contexts. Thus, we develop Contextualized Policy Recovery (CPR), which re-frames the problem of modeling complex decision processes as a multi-task learning problem, where each context poses a unique task and complex decision policies can be constructed piece-wise from many simple context-specific policies. CPR models each context-specific policy as a linear map, and generates new policy models on-demand as contexts are updated with new observations. We provide two flavors of the CPR framework: one focusing on exact local interpretability, and one retaining full global interpretability. We assess CPR through studies on simulated and real data, achieving state-of-the-art performance on predicting antibiotic prescription in intensive care units ($+22$% AUROC vs. previous SOTA) and predicting MRI prescription for Alzheimer’s patients ($+7.7$% AUROC vs. previous SOTA). With this improvement, CPR closes the accuracy gap between interpretable and black-box methods, allowing high-resolution exploration and analysis of context-specific decision models.

It treats each context as a separate task within a shared multi-task learning framework.

This lets the overall decision process vary while keeping its individual components intelligible. The authors provide two versions: one offers exact local interpretability, while the other retains full global interpretability.

Studies on simulated and real data include predicting antibiotic prescriptions in intensive care and MRI prescriptions for Alzheimer’s patients. The reported AUROC improvements over the previous state of the art are 22% and 7.7%, respectively. In these evaluations, CPR closes the accuracy gap between interpretable and black-box approaches. The resulting models support detailed examination of context-specific prescribing decisions, rather than requiring one universal policy to account for all observed behavior.
summary.tldr: CPR models medical decisions with adaptive, context-specific linear policies, improving prescription prediction while preserving local or global interpretability.

title: Contextualized Policy Recovery: Modeling and Interpreting Medical Decisions with Adaptive Imitation Learning

abstract: Large monolithic generative models trained on massive amounts of data have become an increasingly dominant approach in AI research. In this paper, we argue that we should instead construct large generative systems by composing smaller generative models together. We show how such a compositional generative approach enables us to learn distributions in a more data-efficient manner, enabling generalization to parts of the data distribution unseen at training time. We further show how this enables us to program and construct new generative models for tasks completely unseen at training. Finally, we show that in many cases, we can discover separate compositional components from data.

paragraphs: This position paper argues for building large generative systems by combining smaller generative models. Its starting point is the dominance of large, monolithic models trained on massive datasets. The proposed alternative makes composition a central design principle, so a system’s capabilities can emerge from how its constituent models are assembled.

The authors show how this approach can learn distributions more efficiently from data and generalize to regions of a distribution that were absent during training. The important connection is between reusable components and generalization: combining learned parts can provide a way to represent more than the particular data configurations encountered during learning.

The paper further shows how composition can support programming new generative models for tasks that were entirely unseen during training. It also reports that separate components can, in many cases, be discovered from data. These claims give composition two roles: a method for constructing new capabilities and a possible organizing structure for learning itself. The position encourages treating model assembly as a substantive part of generative-model design.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that composing smaller generative models can improve data efficiency and enable generalization to unseen data regions and tasks.

title: Position: Compositional Generative Modeling: A Single Model is Not All You Need

abstract: We present an algorithm for skill discovery from expert demonstrations. The algorithm first utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to propose an initial segmentation of the trajectories. Following that, a hierarchical variational inference framework incorporates the LLM-generated segmentation information to discover reusable skills by merging trajectory segments. To further control the trade-off between compression and reusability, we introduce a novel auxiliary objective based on the Minimum Description Length principle that helps guide this skill discovery process. Our results demonstrate that agents equipped with our method are able to discover skills that help accelerate learning and outperform baseline skill learning approaches on new long-horizon tasks in BabyAI, a grid world navigation environment, as well as ALFRED, a household simulation environment.
