paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for discovering reusable skills from expert demonstrations. The starting material is a collection of trajectories, which must be divided into meaningful pieces before those pieces can become useful skills. A large language model proposes the initial segmentation, supplying information that guides the subsequent learning process.

A hierarchical variational inference framework incorporates those proposed boundaries and discovers skills by merging trajectory segments. An additional objective based on the Minimum Description Length principle controls the trade-off between compression and reusability. This gives the method an explicit way to balance a compact description of demonstrations against the usefulness of the resulting skills across tasks.

The authors evaluate agents on new long-horizon tasks in BabyAI, a grid navigation environment, and ALFRED, a household simulation environment. The discovered skills accelerate learning and outperform the compared skill-learning baselines. These results support a staged approach in which language-model segmentation informs statistical skill discovery, with the compression objective helping shape skills that transfer to later tasks.
summary.tldr: Language-model trajectory segmentation guides a variational skill-discovery method that improves learning on new long-horizon tasks.

title: Language-guided Skill Learning with Temporal Variational Inference

abstract: Pre-trained vision-language models, e.g., CLIP, have been successfully applied to zero-shot semantic segmentation. Existing CLIP-based approaches primarily utilize visual features from the last layer to align with text embeddings, while they neglect the crucial information in intermediate layers that contain rich object details. However, we find that directly aggregating the multi-level visual features weakens the zero-shot ability for novel classes. The large differences between the visual features from different layers make these features hard to align well with the text embeddings. We resolve this problem by introducing a series of independent decoders to align the multi-level visual features with the text embeddings in a cascaded way, forming a novel but simple framework named Cascade-CLIP. Our Cascade-CLIP is flexible and can be easily applied to existing zero-shot semantic segmentation methods. Experimental results show that our simple Cascade-CLIP achieves superior zero-shot performance on segmentation benchmarks, like COCO-Stuff, Pascal-VOC, and Pascal-Context. Our code is available at https://github.com/HVision-NKU/Cascade-CLIP.

paragraphs: Zero-shot semantic segmentation uses language to help assign image regions to classes, including novel classes. Existing CLIP-based methods largely align text representations with visual features from the final layer. This paper argues that intermediate layers contain useful object detail, but finds that simply combining features across layers weakens performance on novel classes.

The difficulty is that features from different depths differ substantially, making a combined representation hard to align with text. Cascade-CLIP introduces independent decoders that align visual features at multiple levels with text embeddings in a cascade. This gives the different layers their own alignment components while bringing their information into the segmentation framework.

The authors describe the framework as flexible enough to apply to existing zero-shot segmentation methods. Experiments report superior zero-shot performance on COCO-Stuff, Pascal-VOC, and Pascal-Context. The central lesson from the approach is that access to more visual detail is not sufficient by itself: the method of aligning that detail with language matters for retaining the ability to recognize novel classes.
summary.tldr: Cascade-CLIP aligns visual features from multiple layers with text through separate cascaded decoders, improving zero-shot segmentation in reported experiments.

title: Cascade-CLIP: Cascaded Vision-Language Embeddings Alignment for Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Ad hoc teamwork poses a challenging problem, requiring the design of an agent to collaborate with teammates without prior coordination or joint training. Open ad hoc teamwork (OAHT) further complicates this challenge by considering environments with a changing number of teammates, referred to as open teams. One promising solution in practice to this problem is leveraging the generalizability of graph neural networks to handle an unrestricted number of agents with various agent-types, named graph-based policy learning (GPL). However, its joint Q-value representation over a coordination graph lacks convincing explanations. In this paper, we establish a new theory to understand the representation of the joint Q-value for OAHT and its learning paradigm, through the lens of cooperative game theory. Building on our theory, we propose a novel algorithm named CIAO, based on GPL’s framework, with additional provable implementation tricks that can facilitate learning. The demos of experimental results are available on https://sites.google.com/view/ciao2024, and the code of experiments is published on https://github.com/hsvgbkhgbv/CIAO.

paragraphs: Ad hoc teamwork requires an agent to cooperate with teammates without prior coordination or joint training. Open ad hoc teamwork adds another difficulty: the number of teammates can change. A learner must therefore handle variation in both who participates and how many agents are present.

Graph-based policy learning, or GPL, offers a practical approach because graph neural networks can accommodate varying numbers and types of agents. However, the paper identifies a gap in the explanation of GPL's joint Q-value representation over a coordination graph. This representation concerns the value of collective actions, making its justification central to understanding how the approach learns cooperation.

The authors develop a theory of that representation and its learning procedure using cooperative game theory. Building on this account, they introduce CIAO, an algorithm within the GPL framework that includes additional theoretically supported implementation techniques intended to facilitate learning. The contribution connects a practical architecture for changing teams to a clearer mathematical foundation and uses that foundation to motivate algorithmic changes.
summary.tldr: CIAO uses cooperative game theory to justify and improve graph-based policy learning for cooperation with unfamiliar, changing teams.

title: Open Ad Hoc Teamwork with Cooperative Game Theory

abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment efforts, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks that elicit harmful behavior. While existing studies predominantly focus on attack methods that require technical expertise, two critical questions remain underexplored: (1) Are jailbroken responses truly useful in enabling average users to carry out harmful actions? (2) Do safety vulnerabilities exist in more common, simple human-LLM interactions? In this paper, we demonstrate that LLM responses most effectively facilitate harmful actions when they are both actionable and informative—two attributes easily elicited in multi-step, multilingual interactions. Using this insight, we propose HarmScore, a jailbreak metric that measures how effectively an LLM response enables harmful actions, and Speak Easy, a simple multi-step, multilingual attack framework. Notably, by incorporating Speak Easy into direct request and jailbreak baselines, we see an average absolute increase of $0.319$ in Attack Success Rate and $0.426$ in HarmScore in both open-source and proprietary LLMs across four safety benchmarks. Our work reveals a critical yet often overlooked vulnerability: Malicious users can easily exploit common interaction patterns for harmful intentions.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether harmful model responses actually help ordinary users carry out harmful actions, alongside whether vulnerabilities appear in simple interactions. Its focus shifts evaluation toward the usefulness of an unsafe answer. The authors identify actionability and informativeness as two attributes that make such responses more enabling.

They introduce HarmScore to measure how effectively a response facilitates harmful actions. They also propose Speak Easy, a framework based on multi-step, multilingual interaction. The abstract reports that these interaction patterns can elicit the two response attributes, connecting a behavioral vulnerability with a metric intended to capture its practical significance.

They also show why evaluating whether a response is harmful and how enabling it is can provide complementary information.
summary.tldr: Speak Easy exposes safety weaknesses in simple multilingual interactions, while HarmScore measures how effectively harmful responses enable action.

title: Speak Easy: Eliciting Harmful Jailbreaks from LLMs with Simple Interactions

abstract: The Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model is a widely used model for the spread of information and infectious diseases, particularly non-immunizing ones, on a graph. Given a highly contagious disease, a natural question is how to best vaccinate individuals to minimize the disease’s extinction time. While previous works showed that the problem of optimal vaccination is closely linked to the NP-hard Spectral Radius Minimization (SRM) problem, they assumed that the graph is known, which is often not the case in practice. In this work, we consider the problem of minimizing the extinction time of an outbreak modeled by an SIS model where the graph on which the disease spreads is unknown and only the infection states of the vertices are observed. To this end, we split the problem into two: learning the graph and determining effective vaccination strategies. We propose a novel inclusion-exclusion-based learning algorithm and, unlike previous approaches, establish its sample complexity for graph recovery. We then detail an optimal algorithm for the SRM problem and prove that its running time is polynomial in the number of vertices for graphs with bounded treewidth. This is complemented by an efficient and effective polynomial-time greedy heuristic for any graph. Finally, we present experiments on synthetic and real-world data that numerically validate our learning and vaccination algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies vaccination decisions in a Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible model, where individuals can become susceptible again after infection. The objective is to shorten an outbreak's extinction time. Unlike approaches that assume the contact graph is known, this work considers an unknown graph and access only to observations of which vertices are infected.

The authors divide the problem into recovering the graph and choosing vaccination strategies. They introduce a graph-learning algorithm based on inclusion-exclusion and establish its sample complexity, quantifying the observations needed for recovery. For vaccination, they address spectral radius minimization, an optimization problem closely connected to effective outbreak control and known to be NP-hard in general.

Their exact algorithm solves spectral radius minimization optimally in polynomial time for graphs with bounded treewidth. For arbitrary graphs, they also provide a polynomial-time greedy heuristic. This distinguishes the conditional optimality result from the more broadly applicable heuristic. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data numerically validate both the graph-learning and vaccination components.
summary.tldr: The paper learns an unknown infection graph and develops vaccination algorithms, including an optimal polynomial-time method for bounded-treewidth graphs.

title: Learn to Vaccinate: Combining Structure Learning and Effective Vaccination for Epidemic and Outbreak Control

abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) as feature enhancers to optimize node representations, which are then used as inputs for graph neural networks (GNNs), has shown significant potential in graph representation learning. However, the fundamental properties of this approach remain underexplored. To address this issue, we propose conducting a more in-depth analysis of this issue based on the interchange intervention method. First, we construct a synthetic graph dataset with controllable causal relationships, enabling precise manipulation of semantic relationships and causal modeling to provide data for analysis. Using this dataset, we conduct interchange interventions to examine the deeper properties of LLM enhancers and GNNs, uncovering their underlying logic and internal mechanisms. Building on the analytical results, we design a plug-and-play optimization module to improve the information transfer between LLM enhancers and GNNs. Experiments across multiple datasets and models validate the proposed module.

paragraphs: Large language models can enrich node representations before those representations enter a graph neural network. Although this combination has shown promise, the paper asks how the two components interact internally. Its focus is the mechanism through which language-derived information becomes useful to graph learning, rather than performance alone.

The authors construct a synthetic graph dataset whose causal relationships can be controlled. This allows semantic relationships to be manipulated in a setting designed for causal analysis. They then apply interchange interventions to investigate the behavior of the language-model enhancer and the graph neural network, using controlled interventions to examine their underlying computations.

The analysis informs a plug-and-play optimization module intended to improve information transfer between the two components. Experiments across multiple datasets and models validate the proposed module. The contribution thus connects a controlled investigation with a practical modification: observations about internal interaction guide how enhanced node information is passed into graph learning. The supplied findings support the usefulness of that analysis-driven design across the evaluated model and dataset combinations.
summary.tldr: Controlled causal interventions reveal how LLM-enhanced node features interact with GNNs and inform a module that improves their information transfer.

title: LLM Enhancers for GNNs: An Analysis from the Perspective of Causal Mechanism Identification

abstract: The rapid advancement of Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech (ZS-TTS) technology has enabled high-fidelity voice synthesis from minimal audio cues, raising significant privacy and ethical concerns. Despite the threats to voice privacy, research to selectively remove the knowledge to replicate unwanted individual voices from pre-trained model parameters has not been explored. In this paper, we address the new challenge of speaker identity unlearning for ZS-TTS systems. To meet this goal, we propose the first machine unlearning frameworks for ZS-TTS, especially Teacher-Guided Unlearning (TGU), designed to ensure the model forgets designated speaker identities while retaining its ability to generate accurate speech for other speakers. Our proposed methods incorporate randomness to prevent consistent replication of forget speakers’ voices, assuring unlearned identities remain untraceable. Additionally, we propose a new evaluation metric, speaker-Zero Retrain Forgetting (spk-ZRF). This assesses the model’s ability to disregard prompts associated with forgotten speakers, effectively neutralizing its knowledge of these voices. The experiments conducted on the state-of-the-art model demonstrate that TGU prevents the model from replicating forget speakers’ voices while maintaining high quality for other speakers. The demo is available at https://speechunlearn.github.io/ .

paragraphs: Zero-shot text-to-speech systems can reproduce a voice from very little audio. This paper studies how to selectively remove a trained system’s ability to imitate designated speakers while preserving useful synthesis for others. The target is speaker identity knowledge within the model, making the task a form of machine unlearning.

The authors introduce unlearning frameworks for this setting, particularly Teacher-Guided Unlearning. Their methods incorporate randomness to prevent consistent reproduction of the speakers selected for forgetting. The intended change is selective: prompts associated with those speakers should no longer recover their identities, while speech generation for retained speakers should remain accurate.

The paper also proposes speaker-Zero Retrain Forgetting, an evaluation metric for whether the model disregards prompts tied to forgotten identities. Experiments on a state-of-the-art speech model show that Teacher-Guided Unlearning prevents replication of the designated voices while maintaining high quality for others. These findings establish an experimental approach to voice-specific removal and a corresponding way to evaluate whether identity prompts still influence synthesis.
summary.tldr: Teacher-Guided Unlearning selectively suppresses designated voice identities in zero-shot speech synthesis while preserving quality for other speakers.

title: Do Not Mimic My Voice : Speaker Identity Unlearning for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech

abstract: Despite recent advancements in offline multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) have harnessed the powerful capabilities of the Transformer architecture, most approaches focus on a limited number of tasks, with scaling to extremely massive tasks remaining a formidable challenge. In this paper, we first revisit the key impact of task numbers on current MTRL method, and further reveal that naively expanding the parameters proves insufficient to counteract the performance degradation as the number of tasks escalates. Building upon these insights, we propose M3DT, a novel mixture-of-experts (MoE) framework that tackles task scalability by further unlocking the model’s parameter scalability. Specifically, we enhance both the architecture and the optimization of the agent, where we strengthen the Decision Transformer (DT) backbone with MoE to reduce task load on parameter subsets, and introduce a three-stage training mechanism to facilitate efficient training with optimal performance. Experimental results show that, by increasing the number of experts, M3DT not only consistently enhances its performance as model expansion on the fixed task numbers, but also exhibits remarkable task scalability, successfully extending to 160 tasks with superior performance.

paragraphs: Offline multi-task reinforcement learning seeks to learn behavior for many tasks from existing data. Transformer-based approaches have advanced this goal, but performance can deteriorate as the number of tasks grows. The authors investigate this effect and find that simply adding model parameters does not adequately counteract the degradation.

Their M3DT framework adds a mixture of experts to a Decision Transformer. This architecture reduces the task load placed on individual parameter subsets, giving model expansion a more structured role. The method also introduces a three-stage training procedure to support efficient learning and strong performance, addressing optimization alongside the architecture.

In experiments with a fixed number of tasks, increasing the number of experts consistently improves performance. The framework also scales to 160 tasks with superior reported performance. These findings connect model capacity and task capacity: distributing work across experts can make additional parameters more useful as the task collection expands. The paper therefore addresses both how a multi-task agent is organized and how it is trained.
summary.tldr: M3DT combines expert-based Decision Transformers with three-stage training to improve offline multi-task learning and scale to 160 tasks.

title: Mastering Massive Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning via Mixture-of-Expert Decision Transformer

abstract: Generating accurate sounds for complex audio-visual scenes is challenging, especially in the presence of multiple objects and sound sources. In this paper, we propose an interactive object-aware audio generation model that grounds sound generation in user-selected visual objects within images. Our method integrates object-centric learning into a conditional latent diffusion model, which learns to associate image regions with their corresponding sounds through multi-modal attention. At test time, our model employs image segmentation to allow users to interactively generate sounds at the object level. We theoretically validate that our attention mechanism functionally approximates test-time segmentation masks, ensuring the generated audio aligns with selected objects. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that our model outperforms baselines, achieving better alignment between objects and their associated sounds.

paragraphs: An image containing several objects can imply several possible sound sources, making it difficult to generate audio for the object a user intends. This paper develops an interactive model that grounds sound generation in selected image objects. The user’s visual selection becomes the basis for deciding which object the generated audio should correspond to.

The model combines object-centric learning with conditional latent diffusion. Multimodal attention learns associations between image regions and their corresponding sounds. At test time, image segmentation supports object-level interaction, allowing the system to use the selected region when generating audio. This connects learning visual–audio relationships with a concrete mechanism for user control.

The authors provide theoretical validation that their attention mechanism functionally approximates the segmentation masks used at test time. This supports the connection between learned attention and object selection. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show better alignment between objects and generated sounds than the compared baselines. The stated result is more accurate object-grounded audio generation within scenes containing multiple potential sources.
summary.tldr: An object-aware diffusion model generates audio for user-selected image regions and improves alignment between selected objects and their sounds.

title: Sounding that Object: Interactive Object-Aware Image to Audio Generation

abstract: Nash equilibrium (NE) plays an important role in game theory. How to efficiently compute an NE in NFGs is challenging due to its complexity and non-convex optimization property. Machine Learning (ML), the cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, has demonstrated remarkable empirical performance across various applications including non-convex optimization. To leverage non-convex stochastic optimization techniques from ML for approximating an NE, various loss functions have been proposed. Among these, only one loss function is unbiased, allowing for unbiased estimation under the sampled play. Unfortunately, this loss function suffers from high variance, which degrades the convergence rate. To improve the convergence rate by mitigating the high variance associated with the existing unbiased loss function, we propose a novel surrogate loss function named Nash Advantage Loss (NAL). NAL is theoretically proved unbiased and exhibits significantly lower variance than the existing unbiased loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that the algorithm minimizing NAL achieves a significantly faster empirical convergence rates compared to other algorithms, while also reducing the variance of estimated loss value by several orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Computing a Nash equilibrium in a normal-form game is difficult, motivating approaches that turn equilibrium approximation into a non-convex optimization problem. When these methods use sampled play, the choice of loss function affects both what is estimated and how noisy that estimate becomes.

The paper identifies high variance in the existing unbiased loss as a barrier to convergence. It introduces Nash Advantage Loss, or NAL, as a surrogate designed to reduce that variance while preserving unbiasedness. The authors theoretically establish that NAL is unbiased and has significantly lower variance than the previous unbiased loss.

Experiments show that minimizing NAL converges substantially faster than the compared algorithms and reduces variance in estimated loss values by several orders of magnitude. These results connect a statistical property of the optimization objective to practical progress toward an approximate equilibrium. The contribution improves the loss used by stochastic optimization; the stated empirical speed advantage concerns the tested algorithms and games, while the unbiasedness and variance results receive theoretical support.
summary.tldr: Nash Advantage Loss preserves unbiased estimation while reducing variance, yielding substantially faster empirical convergence when approximating Nash equilibria.

title: Reducing Variance of Stochastic Optimization for Approximating Nash Equilibria in Normal-Form Games

abstract: Despite the impressive advancements in modern machine learning, achieving robustness in Domain Generalization (DG) tasks remains a significant challenge. In DG, models are expected to perform well on samples from unseen test distributions (also called domains), by learning from multiple related training distributions. Most existing approaches to this problem rely on single-valued predictions, which inherently limit their robustness. We argue that set-valued predictors could be leveraged to enhance robustness across unseen domains, while also taking into account that these sets should be as small as possible. We introduce a theoretical framework defining successful set prediction in the DG setting, focusing on meeting a predefined performance criterion across as many domains as possible, and provide theoretical insights into the conditions under which such domain generalization is achievable. We further propose a practical optimization method compatible with modern learning architectures, that balances robust performance on unseen domains with small prediction set sizes. We evaluate our approach on several real-world datasets from the WILDS benchmark, demonstrating its potential as a promising direction for robust domain generalization.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks models trained on several related distributions to perform well on previously unseen ones. This paper explores giving a set of possible predictions instead of committing to a single answer. The aim is to improve robustness while keeping prediction sets small enough to remain useful.

The authors define success in terms of meeting a specified performance criterion across as many domains as possible. Their theoretical framework examines conditions under which this form of generalization is achievable. This shifts attention to performance across domains while making the size of the returned set an explicit part of the problem.

They also introduce an optimization method compatible with modern learning architectures that balances robust performance against set size. Evaluations on several real-world WILDS datasets indicate that the approach is promising. The stated result supports set-valued prediction as a direction for domain generalization; the framework itself recognizes that achieving the desired behavior depends on conditions, and that enlarging prediction sets carries a cost.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework and practical optimizer use small prediction sets to pursue robustness across unseen domains.

title: Set Valued Predictions For Robust Domain Generalization

abstract: Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting (PTSF) plays a crucial role in decision-making across various fields, including economics, energy, and transportation. Most existing methods excell at short-term forecasting, while overlooking the hurdles of Long-term Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting (LPTSF). As the forecast horizon extends, the inherent nonlinear dynamics have a significant adverse effect on prediction accuracy, and make generative models inefficient by increasing the cost of each iteration. To overcome these limitations, we introduce $K^2$VAE, an efficient VAE-based generative model that leverages a KoopmanNet to transform nonlinear time series into a linear dynamical system, and devises a KalmanNet to refine predictions and model uncertainty in such linear system, which reduces error accumulation in long-term forecasting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $K^2$VAE outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both short- and long-term PTSF, providing a more efficient and accurate solution.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasting must represent uncertainty as well as predict future values. The paper focuses on long horizons, where nonlinear dynamics can undermine accuracy and increase the computational cost of generative forecasting. It introduces K²VAE, a variational autoencoder-based model designed to address both difficulties.

The model combines two components with distinct roles. KoopmanNet transforms nonlinear time series into a linear dynamical system, giving subsequent prediction a simpler form to work with. KalmanNet then refines forecasts and models uncertainty within that linear system. Their combination is intended to reduce the accumulation of errors as predictions extend farther into the future.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods for both short- and long-term probabilistic forecasting, alongside improved efficiency. The approach matters because it connects the representation of dynamics directly to the forecasting procedure: transformation makes the dynamics linear, and refinement operates in that transformed system. The stated findings support this combination as a way to improve forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency while retaining uncertainty modeling.
summary.tldr: K²VAE combines a learned linear dynamics transformation with prediction refinement and uncertainty modeling to improve probabilistic forecasting.

title: $K^2$VAE: A Koopman-Kalman Enhanced Variational AutoEncoder for Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting

abstract: DINO and DINOv2 are two model families being widely used to learn representations from unlabeled imagery data at large scales. Their learned representations often enable state-of-the-art performance for downstream tasks, such as image classification and segmentation. However, they employ many empirically motivated design choices and their training pipelines are highly complex and unstable — many hyperparameters need to be carefully tuned to ensure that the representations do not collapse — which poses considerable difficulty to improving them or adapting them to new domains. In this work, we posit that we can remove most such-motivated idiosyncrasies in the pre-training pipelines, and only need to add an explicit coding rate term in the loss function to avoid collapse of the representations. As a result, we obtain highly simplified variants of the DINO and DINOv2 which we call SimDINO and SimDINOv2, respectively. Remarkably, these simplified models are more robust to different design choices, such as network architecture and hyperparameters, and they learn even higher-quality representations, measured by performance on downstream tasks, offering a Pareto improvement over the corresponding DINO and DINOv2 models. This work highlights the potential of using simplifying design principles to improve the empirical practice of deep learning. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RobinWu218/SimDINO.

paragraphs: DINO and DINOv2 learn useful visual representations from unlabeled images, but their training depends on many carefully tuned design choices. A central concern is representation collapse, where learned features cease to provide useful distinctions. This paper asks whether an explicit training objective can replace much of the complexity used to prevent that outcome.

The authors add a coding-rate term to the loss and remove most of the empirically motivated peculiarities in the original pre-training pipelines. The resulting variants are called SimDINO and SimDINOv2. The proposed simplification puts collapse prevention directly into the objective, reducing dependence on a collection of interacting pipeline choices and hyperparameter settings.

The simplified models are reported to be more robust to architectural and hyperparameter choices while learning representations that perform better on downstream tasks. The authors describe this as a Pareto improvement over the corresponding DINO models: simplification accompanies improved representation quality. The broader finding is that making a training requirement explicit can, in this setting, improve both practical robustness and the usefulness of learned features.
summary.tldr: SimDINO replaces much of DINO’s training complexity with coding-rate regularization, improving robustness and downstream representation quality.

title: Simplifying DINO via Coding Rate Regularization

abstract: Diffusion models, which iteratively denoise data samples to synthesize high-quality outputs, have achieved empirical success across domains. However, optimizing these models for downstream tasks often involves nested bilevel structures, such as tuning hyperparameters for fine-tuning tasks or noise schedules in training dynamics, where traditional bilevel methods fail due to the infinite-dimensional probability space and prohibitive sampling costs. We formalize this challenge as a generative bilevel optimization problem and address two key scenarios: (1) fine-tuning pre-trained models via an inference-only lower-level solver paired with a sample-efficient gradient estimator for the upper level, and (2) training diffusion model from scratch with noise schedule optimization by reparameterizing the lower-level problem and designing a computationally tractable gradient estimator. Our first-order bilevel framework overcomes the incompatibility of conventional bilevel methods with diffusion processes, offering theoretical grounding and computational practicality. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing fine-tuning and hyperparameter search baselines.

Our first-order bilevel framework overcomes the incompatibility of conventional bilevel methods with diffusion processes, offering theoretical grounding and computational practicality. paragraphs: Improving a diffusion model for a particular task can require optimizing two linked decisions: how the model is trained or adapted, and which settings make that process work best. The paper formulates this dependency as generative bilevel optimization. Conventional approaches encounter difficulties because diffusion processes involve probability distributions in an infinite-dimensional space and can require expensive repeated sampling.

The authors develop a first-order framework for two settings. For adapting a pretrained model, they combine a lower-level solver that uses inference only with an upper-level gradient estimator designed to use samples efficiently. For training from scratch, they reformulate the lower-level problem and construct a tractable gradient estimator to optimize the noise schedule.

These contributions make the nested optimization structure explicit while providing different computational solutions for adaptation and initial training. The framework has theoretical support, and the reported experiments outperform existing fine-tuning and hyperparameter-search baselines. The findings support treating these settings as connected optimization problems whose dependencies can be handled directly.
summary.tldr: A first-order bilevel framework makes diffusion-model adaptation and noise-schedule optimization computationally tractable, with reported improvements over existing baselines.

title: A First-order Generative Bilevel Optimization Framework for Diffusion Models

abstract: We introduce a new tool, Transductive Local Complexity (TLC), to analyze the generalization performance of transductive learning methods and motivate new transductive learning algorithms. Our work extends the idea of the popular Local Rademacher Complexity (LRC) to the transductive setting with considerable and novel changes compared to the analysis of typical LRC methods in the inductive setting. While LRC has been widely used as a powerful tool in the analysis of inductive models with sharp generalization bounds for classification and minimax rates for nonparametric regression, it remains an open problem whether a localized version of Rademacher complexity based tool can be designed and applied to transductive learning and gain sharp bound for transductive learning which is consistent with the inductive excess risk bound by (LRC). We give a confirmative answer to this open problem by TLC. Similar to the development of LRC, we build TLC by first establishing a novel and sharp concentration inequality for supremum of empirical processes for the gap between test and training loss in the setting of sampling uniformly without replacement. Then a peeling strategy and a new surrogate variance operator are used to derive the following excess risk bound in the transductive setting, which is consistent with that of the classical LRC based excess risk bound in the inductive setting. As an application of TLC, we use the new TLC tool to analyze the Transductive Kernel Learning (TKL) model, and derive sharper excess risk bound than that by the current state-of-the-art. As a result of independent interest, the concentration inequality for the test-train process is used to derive a sharp concentration inequality for the general supremum of empirical process involving random variables in the setting of sampling uniformly without replacement, with comparison to current concentration inequalities.

paragraphs: The paper develops Transductive Local Complexity, or TLC, to study how training performance relates to test performance in transductive learning. Its central question is whether localized complexity tools that give sharp guarantees in inductive learning can provide similarly strong guarantees in the transductive setting. The authors give an affirmative answer through a new analysis.

The foundation is a concentration inequality for the gap between test and training losses when sampling is uniform and without replacement. This sampling structure requires substantial changes to the usual Local Rademacher Complexity argument. The authors combine the inequality with a peeling strategy and a new surrogate variance operator to obtain an excess risk bound consistent with its classical inductive counterpart.

Applied to Transductive Kernel Learning, TLC yields a sharper excess risk bound than the existing state of the art. The work also derives a broader concentration inequality for empirical processes under the same sampling scheme. These are theoretical improvements: they strengthen the tools available for analyzing generalization and motivating transductive algorithms.
summary.tldr: A new concentration inequality enables sharper theoretical guarantees for transductive learning through Transductive Local Complexity.

title: A New Concentration Inequality for Sampling Without Replacement and Its Application for Transductive Learning

abstract: Neural networks are famously nonlinear. However, linearity is defined relative to a pair of vector spaces, $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$. Leveraging the algebraic concept of transport of structure, we propose a method to explicitly identify non-standard vector spaces where a neural network acts as a linear operator. When sandwiching a linear operator $A$ between two invertible neural networks, $f(x)=g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x))$, the corresponding vector spaces $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are induced by newly defined addition and scaling actions derived from $g_x$ and $g_y$. We term this kind of architecture a Linearizer. This framework makes the entire arsenal of linear algebra, including SVD, pseudo-inverse, orthogonal projection and more, applicable to nonlinear mappings. Furthermore, we show that the composition of two Linearizers that share a neural network is also a Linearizer. We leverage this property and demonstrate that training diffusion models using our architecture makes the hundreds of sampling steps collapse into a single step. We further utilize our framework to enforce idempotency (i.e. $f(f(x))=f(x)$) on networks leading to a globally projective generative model and to demonstrate modular style transfer.

Leveraging the algebraic concept of transport of structure, we propose a method to explicitly identify non-standard vector spaces where a neural network acts as a linear operator. When sandwiching a linear operator $A$ between two invertible neural networks, $f(x)=g_y^{-1}(A g_x(x))$, the corresponding vector spaces $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are induced by newly defined addition and scaling actions derived from $g_x$ and $g_y$. We term this kind of architecture a Linearizer. This framework makes the entire arsenal of linear algebra, including SVD, pseudo-inverse, orthogonal projection and more, applicable to nonlinear mappings. Furthermore, we show that the composition of two Linearizers that share a neural network is also a Linearizer. We leverage this property and demonstrate that training diffusion models using our architecture makes the hundreds of sampling steps collapse into a single step. We further utilize our framework to enforce idempotency (i.e. $f(f(x))=f(x)$) on networks leading to a globally projective generative model and to demonstrate modular style transfer.

paragraphs: Linearity depends on the vector spaces used to describe a mapping, including their definitions of addition and scaling. This paper constructs non-standard vector spaces in which a particular neural architecture acts linearly. The construction uses invertible neural networks to transport those operations between representations.

A Linearizer places a linear operator between an invertible input network and the inverse of an invertible output network. The resulting mapping can be nonlinear in ordinary coordinates while linear under the induced operations. This makes tools such as singular-value decomposition, pseudo-inverses, and orthogonal projection applicable within the framework. Two Linearizers that share a neural network also compose into another Linearizer.

The authors use that composition property in a diffusion architecture where hundreds of sampling steps collapse into one. They also enforce idempotency, meaning applying a mapping twice gives the same result as applying it once, to build a globally projective generative model, and demonstrate modular style transfer. These applications show how architectural algebra can impose useful structure on learned nonlinear mappings.
summary.tldr: Linearizers make structured neural mappings linear in induced vector spaces, enabling algebraic composition, single-step diffusion sampling, and projective generative models.

title: Who Said Neural Networks Aren’t Linear?

abstract: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF) has emerged as a promising paradigm for eliciting the latent capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) without external supervision. However, current methods rely on heuristic intrinsic rewards, which often lack a well-defined theoretical optimization target and are prone to degenerative biases. In this work, we introduce PowerFlow, a principled framework that reformulates unsupervised fine-tuning as a distribution matching problem. By casting GFlowNet as an amortized variational sampler for unnormalized densities, we propose a length-aware Trajectory-Balance objective that explicitly neutralizes the structural length biases inherent in autoregressive generation. By targeting $\alpha$-power distributions, PowerFlow enables the directional elicitation of the dual nature of LLMs: sharpening the distribution ($\alpha > 1$) to intensify logical reasoning, or flattening it ($\alpha < 1$) to unlock expressive creativity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PowerFlow consistently outperforms existing RLIF methods, matching or even exceeding supervised GRPO. Furthermore, by mitigating over-sharpening in aligned models, our approach achieves simultaneous gains in diversity and quality, shifting the Pareto frontier in creative tasks.

paragraphs: PowerFlow studies how to elicit language-model capabilities without external supervision. Existing reinforcement learning from internal feedback often uses heuristic rewards whose optimization target is unclear and whose biases can produce undesirable behavior. The paper instead specifies a target distribution and trains the model to match it.

The framework interprets a GFlowNet as an amortized variational sampler for unnormalized densities. It introduces a length-aware trajectory-balance objective to neutralize structural length biases in autoregressive generation. Its target is an alpha-power distribution: alpha above one sharpens probabilities toward favored outputs, while alpha below one flattens probabilities to encourage a broader range of outputs.

The authors use sharpening to strengthen logical reasoning and flattening to promote creativity. Experiments report consistent improvements over existing internal-feedback methods, sometimes matching or exceeding supervised GRPO. For aligned models, reducing excessive sharpening also improves both diversity and quality on creative tasks. The reported gains show how an explicit distributional target can guide different behaviors within the same unsupervised fine-tuning framework.
summary.tldr: PowerFlow fine-tunes language models toward explicit probability distributions to strengthen reasoning or broaden creative output without external supervision.

title: PowerFlow: Unlocking the Dual Nature of LLMs via Principled Distribution Matching

abstract: Many scientific problems are underdetermined: multiple distinct hypotheses are equally consistent with the same observations. In such settings, effective inference requires not only producing valid explanations, but also systematically exploring and covering the admissible hypothesis set. We introduce HypoSpace, a benchmark that treats large language models (LLMs) as samplers over finite hypothesis spaces and evaluates them on three metrics: Validity, Uniqueness, and Recovery. HypoSpace spans three structured domains (causal graph inference, gravity-constrained 3D voxel reconstruction, and Boolean genetic interaction modeling) with deterministic validators and exactly enumerable solution spaces, plus real-world anchored case studies. Empirically, HypoSpace reveals a capability- and scale-dependent coverage failure: models can maintain high Validity while exhibiting reduced Uniqueness and Recovery as admissible hypothesis spaces become larger or more combinatorial. We further show that the analysis on stratified decoding partially mitigates this collapse, demonstrating HypoSpace’s utility as a diagnostic benchmark for set-valued inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/CTT-Pavilion/_HypoSpace.

paragraphs: When observations admit several equally valid explanations, producing one correct answer does not demonstrate broad understanding of the possibilities. HypoSpace evaluates language models as samplers from a finite set of admissible hypotheses. It measures whether their answers are valid, how distinct those answers are, and how much of the solution space they recover.

The benchmark covers causal graph inference, gravity-constrained three-dimensional voxel reconstruction, and Boolean genetic interaction modeling. Each structured domain has deterministic checks and an exactly enumerable solution space. This makes it possible to compare generated hypotheses against the full set of valid possibilities. The benchmark also includes case studies anchored in real-world problems.

Experiments reveal a coverage failure that depends on model capability and problem scale. Models can continue producing valid answers while uniqueness and recovery decline as the space grows or becomes more combinatorial. Analysis of stratified decoding shows partial mitigation. The findings distinguish correctness from breadth and make HypoSpace useful for diagnosing whether a model explores alternatives or repeatedly returns a narrow subset.
summary.tldr: HypoSpace reveals that LLMs can generate valid hypotheses while covering only a shrinking share of the admissible alternatives.

title: HypoSpace: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Set-Valued Hypothesis Generation under Underdetermination and Sublinear Coverage Bounds

abstract: Regional climate prediction presents unique challenges for time series foundation models, which typically process temporal patterns through single-pass inference. Expert climatologists, in contrast, employ multi-scale temporal analysis and iterative refinement based on systematic error diagnosis. We present RGMR (Residual-Guided Multi-Resolution Refinement), an inference-time framework that adapts pre-trained foundation models to perform structured coarse-to-fine refinement for climate forecasting without updating backbone parameters. Applied to drought forecasting using the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), RGMR is architecture-agnostic across the three TSFM backbones evaluated per site (TimesFM, TimeGPT, TabPFN) and consistently lowers test-set MSE on three South Australian sites and three additional regions outside South Australia. Applied to TimesFM, the wrapper reduces one-month-ahead SPEI MSE by up to 18.9% across the three South Australian sites (mean reduction $\approx$18.7%). Overall, RGMR provides a practical route for deploying frozen TSFMs in regional climate forecasting workflows.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models typically produce forecasts in a single pass, while regional climate forecasting can benefit from examining several temporal scales and diagnosing systematic errors. RGMR introduces an inference-time framework that brings this structured refinement process to pretrained models. It leaves the backbone parameters frozen, adapting how predictions are refined rather than retraining the underlying model.

The framework uses residual-guided, coarse-to-fine refinement for drought forecasting with the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index. The evaluation covers TimesFM, TimeGPT, and TabPFN at each site, testing whether the approach can work across different backbones. It includes three South Australian sites and three additional regions outside South Australia.

RGMR consistently lowers test-set mean squared error across the evaluated settings. For TimesFM, one-month-ahead prediction error falls by up to 18.9% across the South Australian sites, with an average reduction of approximately 18.7%. The findings support using iterative, multi-resolution refinement as a practical wrapper for frozen forecasting models, with demonstrated architecture independence across the three tested backbones.
summary.tldr: RGMR improves drought forecasts by applying residual-guided, coarse-to-fine refinement to frozen time-series foundation models.

title: Residual-Guided Multi-Resolution Refinement of Foundation Models: A Case Study in Drought Forecasting

abstract: We investigate how to make small tabular foundation models effective for High-Dimensional, Low-Sample Size (HDLSS) tabular prediction without retraining large backbones. We introduce Graph-guided Ordering with Local Refinement (GO-LR), show its equivalence to weighted Minimum Linear Arrangement, and interpret the practical solver as a TSP-path-style surrogate. We propose GOTabPFN,which builds on GO-LR, and a Neuro-Inspired Subunit Compression (NSC) unit to pool locally adjacent ordered features into meta-features, yielding a compact representation that makes TabPFN-style prediction practical in HDLSS regimes. Across tabular benchmarks, GOTabPFN improves stability and accuracy under tight token budgets.
originalAbstract: We investigate how to make small tabular foundation models effective for High-Dimensional, Low-Sample Size (HDLSS) tabular prediction without retraining large backbones. We introduce Graph-guided Ordering with Local Refinement (GO-LR), show its equivalence to weighted Minimum Linear Arrangement, and interpret the practical solver as a TSP-path-style surrogate. We propose GOTabPFN,which builds on GO-LR, and a Neuro-Inspired Subunit Compression (NSC) unit to pool locally adjacent ordered features into meta-features, yielding a compact representation that makes TabPFN-style prediction practical in HDLSS regimes. Across tabular benchmarks, GOTabPFN improves stability and accuracy under tight token budgets.

paragraphs: Tables with many features but few examples pose a difficult setting for small tabular foundation models, especially when the available token budget is tight. This paper investigates how to make those models useful without retraining large backbones. Its approach changes how the input features are arranged and compressed before prediction.

The first component, Graph-guided Ordering with Local Refinement, places features into an order informed by a graph. The authors establish its equivalence to weighted Minimum Linear Arrangement and interpret the practical solver as a surrogate resembling a traveling-salesperson path problem. This provides an optimization perspective on feature ordering rather than treating the column sequence as arbitrary.

GOTabPFN then uses a Neuro-Inspired Subunit Compression unit to pool neighboring features in that order into compact meta-features. Ordering therefore determines the local groups available to compression. Across tabular benchmarks, the resulting representation improves stability and accuracy under tight token budgets. The findings support coordinating feature arrangement with compression to make TabPFN-style prediction practical in high-dimensional, low-sample settings.
summary.tldr: GOTabPFN combines graph-guided feature ordering and local compression to improve tabular prediction under tight token budgets without retraining large backbones.

title: GOTabPFN: From Feature Ordering to Compact Tokenization for Tabular Foundation Models on High-Dimensional Data

abstract: In large vision-language models, visual tokens typically constitute the majority of input tokens, leading to substantial computational overhead. To address this, recent studies have explored pruning redundant or less informative visual tokens for image understanding tasks. However, these methods struggle with pixel grounding tasks, where token importance is highly contingent on the input text. Through an in-depth analysis of CLIP, we observe that visual tokens within referent regions often exhibit low similarity to their textual representation. Motivated by this insight, we introduce LiteLVLM, a training-free, text-guided token pruning strategy for efficient pixel grounding inference. By reversing the ranking of CLIP’s visual-text similarity, LiteLVLM effectively retains visual tokens covering the referent regions, while recovering context tokens to enable clear foreground-background separation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiteLVLM significantly outperforms existing methods by over 5% across diverse token budgets. Without any training or fine-tuning, LiteLVLM maintains 90% of the original performance with a 22% speedup and a 2.3$\times$ memory reduction. Our code is available at https://github.com/sejong-rcv/LiteLVLM.
originalAbstract: In large vision-language models, visual tokens typically constitute the majority of input tokens, leading to substantial computational overhead. To address this, recent studies have explored pruning redundant or less informative visual tokens for image understanding tasks. However, these methods struggle with pixel grounding tasks, where token importance is highly contingent on the input text. Through an in-depth analysis of CLIP, we observe that visual tokens within referent regions often exhibit low similarity to their textual representation. Motivated by this insight, we introduce LiteLVLM, a training-free, text-guided token pruning strategy for efficient pixel grounding inference. By reversing the ranking of CLIP’s visual-text similarity, LiteLVLM effectively retains visual tokens covering the referent regions, while recovering context tokens to enable clear foreground-background separation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiteLVLM significantly outperforms existing methods by over 5% across diverse token budgets. Without any training or fine-tuning, LiteLVLM maintains 90% of the original performance with a 22% speedup and a 2.3$\times$ memory reduction. Our code is available at https://github.com/sejong-rcv/LiteLVLM.

paragraphs: Pixel grounding requires a vision-language model to locate the image region described by text. Reducing the number of visual tokens can save computation, but the tokens worth keeping depend heavily on the requested object or region. The authors find a counterintuitive pattern in CLIP: tokens inside the referenced region often have low similarity to the corresponding text representation.

LiteLVLM uses this observation to reverse the usual visual-text similarity ranking when selecting tokens. That reversal helps retain image information covering the requested region. The method also recovers context tokens so the model can distinguish the foreground from the background. It operates during inference without training or fine-tuning.

Across different token budgets, the authors report improvements of over 5% compared with existing methods. LiteLVLM also retains 90% of the original performance while delivering a 22% speedup and a 2.3-fold memory reduction. These findings show why token selection for precise localization benefits from a task-specific interpretation of similarity, together with enough surrounding context to identify boundaries.
summary.tldr: LiteLVLM reverses CLIP similarity rankings and restores context to accelerate pixel grounding without training.

title: CLIP Tricks You: Training-free Token Pruning for Efficient Pixel Grounding in Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: In batch multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO), it is often desirable to identify the whole Pareto optimal set, especially when considering the complicated interplay between different design criteria and constraints. This poses unique challenges in acquiring batches of both high quality and diversity to cover the Pareto front. We propose a novel acquisition strategy, Probability of Matching (POM), which evaluates both batch candidate quality and diversity by explicitly capturing the likelihood that all batch points are Pareto optimal, and the probability that they collectively cover the full Pareto set. To estimate the coverage probability and promote diversity, we incorporate non-replacement sampling principles, resulting in our new POM-guided batch MOBO method. Across synthetic benchmarks and real-world tasks, our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on standard MOBO metrics as well as a new design-space coverage metric, Expected Minimum Distance (EMD), with comparable computational efficiency.

paragraphs: When optimizing several competing objectives, a useful outcome is a collection of designs expressing different optimal trade-offs. Batch selection must therefore consider both the quality of individual candidates and how widely they cover the Pareto set. Choosing several strong but similar candidates can leave other desirable designs unexplored.

Probability of Matching evaluates these two requirements together. It considers the likelihood that every candidate in a batch is Pareto optimal and the probability that the batch collectively covers the full Pareto set. To estimate coverage and encourage diversity, the method incorporates principles of sampling without replacement. This makes collective coverage an explicit part of selecting the next batch.

Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world tasks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with comparable computational efficiency. Evaluation includes standard multi-objective optimization measures and Expected Minimum Distance, a new measure of coverage in design space. The findings support judging batches by how well their candidates complement one another as well as by their individual quality.
summary.tldr: Probability of Matching selects optimization batches by jointly assessing Pareto quality and collective design-space coverage.

title: Probability of Matching for Batch Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Personalization has become a pivotal field of study in contemporary intelligent systems. Federated learning enables privacy-preserving collaborative training, but highly heterogeneous client data remain challenging, especially in graph federated learning where clients possess structurally diverse graphs. Existing personalized federated learning (PFL) methods ignore the intrinsic geometric properties of diverse graph structures. We propose FlatLand, a novel personalized Federated learning method that embeds different clients’ data in tailored Lorentz space of hyperbolic geometry. Our key insight is that hyperbolic geometry naturally accommodates the intrinsic negative curvature prevalent in real-world graphs, while the time-like dimension in Lorentz space provides a principled way to encode client-specific heterogeneity. We develop a parameter decoupling strategy that separates heterogeneous information (captured in time-like parameters) from common knowledge (preserved in space-like parameters), enabling direct aggregation without requiring client similarity estimation and extra calculation modules. Empirical results on diverse federated graph learning tasks demonstrate that FlatLand achieves superior performance, particularly in low-dimensional settings. Code is available in our GitHub repository.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning brings together clients whose graph structures may differ substantially. Personalization must preserve those differences while still allowing useful knowledge to be shared. FlatLand argues that existing approaches overlook the geometry inherent in these graphs and develops a way to represent client-specific variation within the embedding space itself.

Each client’s data is embedded in a tailored Lorentz space, a representation of hyperbolic geometry. The motivation is that negative curvature naturally accommodates structure prevalent in real-world graphs. FlatLand uses the time-like dimension to encode client heterogeneity, separating those parameters from space-like parameters intended to preserve common knowledge across clients.

This separation enables direct aggregation without an additional client-similarity estimation procedure or extra calculation modules. Across diverse federated graph-learning tasks, the authors report superior empirical performance, especially with low-dimensional representations. The result suggests that choosing and organizing the representation geometry can help reconcile personalization with collaboration. Here, the division between local differences and shared information is built into how parameters are structured.
summary.tldr: FlatLand separates client-specific and shared graph information within Lorentz-space parameters to improve personalized federated learning.

title: FlatLand: Personalized Graph Federated Learning via Tailored Lorentz Space

abstract: Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) enables trustworthy multi-view classification, yet suffers from a critical vulnerability: the Scale Mismatch Problem. We theoretically demonstrate that existing evidential fusion rules erroneously equate logit magnitude with semantic confidence, rendering them susceptible to semantic hijacking by inflated but uninformative views. To resolve this, we propose Scale-Invariant Evidential Fusion (SAEF), a framework utilizing instance-wise standardization to strictly decouple confidence from scale. Instead of relying on magnitude dominance, SAEF aggregates views based on statistical consensus. Theoretically, SAEF guarantees invariance to global scaling and robustness to asymmetric dominance. Experiments on four diverse datasets confirm that SAEF outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy and robustness to semantic conflicts and noise, ensuring stability against severe scale perturbations.

paragraphs: When a classifier combines several views of an example, it needs to decide how much evidence each view contributes. This paper identifies a scale mismatch in existing evidential fusion rules: large numerical prediction scores can be treated as strong semantic confidence. Consequently, a view with inflated but uninformative scores can dominate the combined prediction.

Scale-Invariant Evidential Fusion, or SAEF, standardizes scores separately for each instance to separate their scale from their confidence contribution. It then combines views through statistical consensus instead of allowing raw magnitude to determine influence. The central idea is that changing how large a view’s scores are should not, by itself, make that view more persuasive.

The authors theoretically establish invariance to global scaling and robustness to asymmetric dominance. Experiments on four datasets report better accuracy and robustness than leading baselines when views contain noise or conflicting semantic information, together with stability under severe scale changes. These findings connect a specific mathematical property of the fusion rule to the observed reliability of combined predictions.
summary.tldr: SAEF standardizes evidence before combining views, preventing inflated score magnitudes from dominating classification.

title: Beyond Magnitude: Scale-Invariant Evidential Fusion for Multi-View Classification

abstract: Continuous ECG monitoring is clinically valuable, but scaling it beyond electrodes to comfortable long-term use motivates contactless mmWave sensing. In practice, mmWave-to-ECG reconstruction is severely constrained by the scarcity of high-quality synchronized recordings. Therefore, we propose Cardio-mmFlow, a Gaussian-prior-free physics-informed flow matching framework that synthesizes mmWave radar signals from clinical ECG. It learns a direct transport trajectory between the latent manifolds of ECG and radar. Considering subject-dependent propagation differences, we incorporate a simplified mass–spring–damper inspired modulation and inject it into the flow dynamics via feature-wise linear modulation for personalization. Extensive experiments show that our system generates high fidelity radar data in both signal and latent domains. It significantly improves zero-shot downstream mmWave to ECG task, and enable Atrial Fibrillation classification with synthetic data. Further analyses evaluate the model interpretability.

paragraphs: Cardio-mmFlow addresses a data shortage in contactless cardiac sensing. Reconstructing ECG from millimeter-wave radar is constrained by limited high-quality synchronized recordings. The paper approaches that shortage by synthesizing radar signals from clinical ECG, creating data intended to help the downstream task of recovering ECG from radar measurements.

To account for differences in signal propagation between people, it incorporates a simplified modulation inspired by a mass–spring–damper system. These findings support the proposed synthesis method as a way to strengthen data-constrained sensing models; the reported contribution centers on generated data and downstream modeling performance.
summary.tldr: Cardio-mmFlow synthesizes personalized radar signals from ECG to improve data-constrained contactless cardiac modeling.

title: Cardio-mmFlow: A Gaussian-Prior-Free Physics-Informed Flow Matching Framework for Electrocardiogram to mmWave Radar Synthesis

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently memorize sensitive training data thereby creating significant privacy and copyright risks. Addressing these risks, i.e., removing such knowledge from an existing model checkpoint, has proven challenging as many unlearning methods lead to catastrophic utility loss or are ineffective for complex queries. We introduce Divergence Decoding (DD), a mechanism that uses small auxiliary models to steer the logits of the LLM away from specific data during inference. Training these models is straight forward, i.e., we use standard pre-training and fine-tuning setups. We find the method decisively outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines on unlearning benchmarks across a variety of model and training dataset scales consistent with DD being an effective and inexpensive solution to unlearning. We then demonstrate that this steered distribution can be trivially distilled back into the base model. Since the method is generally applicable to any probabilistic model, we explore its efficacy outside of text generation and find evidence of generalization to the domain of images.

paragraphs: Language models can memorize sensitive or copyrighted training material, creating a need to suppress specific learned information. Existing unlearning methods can damage general usefulness or struggle with complex queries. Divergence Decoding approaches this problem by changing the model's output behavior during inference using smaller auxiliary models.

These auxiliary models steer the main model's logits, the scores underlying its output probabilities, away from targeted data. They are trained using standard pretraining and fine-tuning procedures. This places the initial intervention in the generation process. The authors also demonstrate that the resulting steered distribution can be distilled back into the base model.

Across unlearning benchmarks involving different model and dataset scales, Divergence Decoding decisively outperforms the stated leading baselines. The authors interpret this as evidence for an effective, inexpensive approach. They also explore image generation because the mechanism is generally applicable to probabilistic models, finding evidence of transfer beyond text. That image result supports broader applicability without establishing effectiveness in every probabilistic modeling domain.
summary.tldr: Divergence Decoding uses small auxiliary models to steer generation away from targeted data and can distill that behavior into the base model.

title: Divergence Decoding: Inference-Time Unlearning via Auxiliary Models

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) based Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved superior performance, yet the massive memory overhead caused by storing multiple expert networks severely hinders their practical deployment. Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based compression has emerged as a promising post-training technique; however, most existing methods apply uniform rank allocation or rely solely on static weight properties. This overlooks the substantial heterogeneity in expert utilization observed in MoE models, where frequent routing patterns and intrinsic information density vary significantly across experts. In this work, we propose RFID-MoE, an effective framework for MoE compression by exploiting heterogeneous Routing Frequency and Information Density. We first introduce a fused metric that combines expert activation frequency with effective rank to measure expert importance, adaptively allocating higher ranks to critical expert groups under a fixed budget. Moreover, instead of discarding compression residuals, we reconstruct them via a parameter-efficient sparse projection mechanism to recover lost information with minimal parameter overhead. Extensive experiments on representative MoE LLMs (e.g., Qwen3, DeepSeekMoE) across multiple compression ratios demonstrate that RFID-MoE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods like MoBE and $\mathbf{D}^2$-MoE. Notably, RFID-MoE achieves a perplexity of 16.92 on PTB with the Qwen3-30B model at a 60% compression ratio, reducing perplexity by over 8.0 compared to baselines, and improves zero-shot accuracy on HellaSwag by approximately 8%.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models require substantial memory to store their expert networks. Compressing every expert equally overlooks differences in how often experts are used and how much information their weights contain. RFID-MoE uses both properties to decide where a limited compression budget should preserve more capacity.

title: Effective MoE-based LLM Compression by Exploiting Heterogeneous Inter-Group Experts Routing Frequency and Information Density

abstract: LLM-driven agents excel at sequential decision-making but often rely on on-the-fly reasoning, re-deriving solutions even in recurring scenarios. This insufficient experience reuse leads to computational redundancy and instability. To bridge this gap, we propose Skill-Pro, a framework enabling agents to autonomously learn reusable procedural skills from interaction experiences without parameter updates. By formalizing a Skill-MDP, Skill-Pro transforms passive episodic narratives into executable Skills defined by activation, execution, and termination conditions to ensure executability. To achieve reliable reusability without capability degradation, we introduce Non-Parametric PPO, which leverages semantic gradients for high-quality candidate generation and a PPO Gate for robust Skill verification. Through score-based maintenance, Skill-Pro sustains compact, high-quality procedural memory. Experimental results across in-domain, cross-task, and cross-agent scenarios demonstrate that Skill-Pro achieves superior reuse rates and significant gains with extreme memory compression. Visualized evolutionary trajectories and Skill distributions further reveal how Skill-Pro transparently accumulates, refines, and reuses procedural knowledge to facilitate long-term autonomy.

title: Skill-Pro: Learning Reusable Skills from Experience via Non-Parametric PPO for LLM Agents

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer energy-efficient, biologically plausible computation but suffer from non-differentiable spike generation, necessitating reliance on heuristic surrogate gradients. This paper introduces UltraLIF, a principled framework that replaces surrogate gradients with ultradiscretization, a mathematical formalism from tropical geometry providing continuous relaxations of discrete dynamics. The central insight is that the max-plus semiring underlying ultradiscretization naturally models neural threshold dynamics: the log-sum-exp function serves as a differentiable soft-maximum that converges to hard thresholding as a learnable temperature parameter $\varepsilon \to 0$. Two neuron models are derived from distinct dynamical systems: UltraLIF from the LIF ordinary differential equation (temporal dynamics) and UltraDLIF from the diffusion equation modeling gap junction coupling across neuronal populations (spatial dynamics). Both yield fully differentiable SNNs trainable via standard backpropagation with no forward-backward mismatch. Theoretical analysis establishes pointwise convergence to tropical LIF dynamics with quantitative error bounds and bounded non-vanishing gradients. Experiments on six benchmarks spanning static images, neuromorphic vision, and audio demonstrate improvements over surrogate gradient baselines, with gains most pronounced in the ultra-low latency regime ($T{=}1$) on neuromorphic and temporal datasets. An optional sparsity penalty enables significant energy reduction while maintaining competitive accuracy.

UltraLIF instead derives differentiable neuron dynamics through ultradiscretization, connecting continuous relaxations with discrete threshold behavior using the max-plus algebra of tropical geometry.

Gains are strongest in the single-step, ultra-low-latency setting on neuromorphic and temporal datasets. An optional sparsity penalty also reduces energy use while preserving competitive accuracy, linking the differentiable formulation to both predictive and efficiency benefits in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: UltraLIF derives differentiable spiking dynamics that approach hard thresholds, improving reported accuracy and enabling energy reductions through optional sparsity.

title: UltraLIF: Fully Differentiable Spiking Neural Networks via Ultradiscretization and Max-Plus Algebra

abstract: Existing scaling laws for Large Language Models (LLMs), predominantly monotonic power laws, fail to explain emerging non-monotonic phenomena such as catastrophic overtraining and quantization-induced degradation, where performance deteriorates despite increased compute. We propose the Shannon Scaling Law, a unified theoretical framework that models LLM training as information transmission over a noisy channel, grounded in the Shannon–Hartley theorem. By mapping model parameters to channel bandwidth and training tokens to signal power, our formulation explicitly captures the interaction between learning signal and intrinsic noise. This perspective reveals a fundamental Shannon capacity for LLMs: scaling model size or data without preserving a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) inevitably amplifies noise, inducing a transition from monotonic improvement to U-shaped performance degradation. We validate our theory through experiments on Pythia and OLMo2 under perturbations, including Gaussian noise, quantization and supervised fine-tuning on math, QA and code tasks. The Shannon Scaling Law consistently outperforms classical scaling laws and recent perturbation-aware laws, achieving strong $R^2$ scores and accurately capturing loss basins missed by prior approaches. It also extrapolates: fitted on $\leq$6.9B Pythia models with $\leq$180B tokens, it predicts the unseen 12B model up to 307B tokens at pooled $R^2{=}0.847$, while monotonic baselines collapse.

This paper addresses cases where that pattern reverses, including catastrophic overtraining and degradation associated with quantization. It proposes a Shannon Scaling Law that treats training as information transmission through a noisy channel, explicitly representing the interaction between useful learning signal and intrinsic noise.

title: LLMs as Noisy Channels: A Shannon Perspective on Model Capacity and Scaling Laws

abstract: We aim to improve the reasoning capabilities of diffusion language models (DLMs). While SFT is a popular post-training recipe for autoregressive models, its use in DLMs faces challenges and can even hurt performance, though the underlying causes remain understudied. Our analysis reveals that vanilla SFT overlooks learnability, namely, what and when tokens are learned. Specifically, rare tokens are difficult to learn when most of the input is masked, whereas it is straightforward and thus of little value to learn common tokens when most of the input is unmasked. Motivated by our analysis, we propose LIFT, an efficient SFT-based post-training algorithm for DLMs. LIFT learns easy tokens when most of the input is masked and hard tokens when more context is available, thereby aligning training with the information available at different diffusion time steps. Our results show that LIFT outperforms existing SFT baselines across six reasoning benchmarks, achieving up to a 3x relative gain on AIME’24 and AIME’25. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/divelab/LIFT.
