Specifically, rare tokens are difficult to learn when most of the input is masked, whereas it is straightforward and thus of little value to learn common tokens when most of the input is unmasked. Motivated by our analysis, we propose LIFT, an efficient SFT-based post-training algorithm for DLMs. LIFT learns easy tokens when most of the input is masked and hard tokens when more context is available, thereby aligning training with the information available at different diffusion time steps. Our results show that LIFT outperforms existing SFT baselines across six reasoning benchmarks, achieving up to a 3x relative gain on AIME’24 and AIME’25. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/divelab/LIFT.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning can improve autoregressive language models, but applying it directly to diffusion language models can sometimes hurt performance. This paper links that problem to learnability: the difficulty of predicting a token depends on how much surrounding text is visible at a particular diffusion step. A uniform training approach can overlook that relationship.

The analysis finds that rare tokens are difficult to learn when most input tokens are masked. Common tokens, meanwhile, can become too easy to provide much learning value when most context is visible. LIFT adjusts supervision accordingly, emphasizing easy tokens under heavy masking and harder tokens when more context is available.

This aligns what the model is asked to learn with the information it has at each stage. Across six reasoning benchmarks, LIFT outperforms existing supervised fine-tuning baselines, with relative gains reaching up to threefold on AIME’24 and AIME’25. The results support making token difficulty and diffusion timing part of the fine-tuning design when improving reasoning in diffusion language models.
summary.tldr: LIFT improves diffusion-language-model reasoning by matching token difficulty to the amount of context available during fine-tuning.

title: Learnability-Informed Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional, non-log-concave distributions with unnormalized densities remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning, particularly in black-box settings where gradient information is inaccessible or computationally prohibitive. While Langevin dynamics provides a principled framework for sampling when gradients are accessible, its extension to the black-box settings suffers from high variance and lacks non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for non-log-concave sampling. To address these limitations, we propose a variance-reduced zeroth-order Langevin sampling method. Our method employs a gradient estimator that substantially reduces the variance of the classical batched zeroth-order estimator and eliminates the unfavorable dimensional dependence of the batch size required for accurate estimation, enabling practical and stable sampling. We establish the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for zeroth-order non-log-concave sampling in terms of $\varepsilon$-relative Fisher information, and, under a Poincaré inequality assumption, squared total variation distance. We further propose ZO-APMC, a posterior sampling algorithm for black-box inverse problems with pre-trained score-based generative priors, establishing the first non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for such methods. We validate our theory through synthetic experiments and demonstrate strong empirical performance on practical linear and nonlinear inverse problems.

paragraphs: Sampling from complicated high-dimensional distributions is difficult when gradients are unavailable or too expensive to compute. The paper studies this black-box setting for non-log-concave distributions whose densities are known only up to normalization. It develops a zeroth-order Langevin method, using density evaluations to estimate the gradient information needed to guide sampling.

The proposed estimator reduces variance relative to the classical batched zeroth-order estimator and removes an unfavorable dependence of the required batch size on dimension. The authors establish the first reported non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for this sampling setting using relative Fisher information. They also obtain guarantees in squared total variation distance under a Poincaré inequality assumption, making that additional distributional condition explicit.

Synthetic experiments validate the theory, while linear and nonlinear inverse-problem experiments show strong empirical performance. summary.tldr: A variance-reduced gradient-free Langevin sampler gains finite-run convergence guarantees and supports posterior sampling for black-box inverse problems.

title: Zeroth-Order Non-Log-Concave Sampling with Variance Reduction and Applications to Inverse Problems

abstract: Differentiable optimization layers are traditionally integrated in predict-then-optimize frameworks where a neural model estimates parameters that subsequently serve as fixed inputs to downstream decision-making optimization problems. In this work, we introduce the concept of a "fairness layer": a differentiable optimization layer appended to a model’s output layer that guarantees a chosen notion of output parity is satisfied when integrated into a neural network. Additionally, we introduce an online primal-dual inference algorithm that provides provable aggregate fairness guarantees for streaming predictions with arbitrarily small batch sizes, where traditional per-batch constraints become overly restrictive. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the fairness layer and associated algorithm, and theoretical analysis characterizes the layer’s differentiability and stability properties during model training and backpropagation. Our code for these experiments is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/dtroxell19/FairDL-ICML-2026.git and our public Python package documentation can be found online: https://dtroxell19.github.io/fairness_training/.

paragraphs: A model can be trained to favor fair predictions without necessarily guaranteeing that its outputs satisfy a specified parity rule. This paper introduces a fairness layer: a differentiable optimization problem appended to the network’s output. When integrated into the network, the layer guarantees the chosen notion of output parity, making that requirement part of the prediction mechanism.

Differentiability matters because the optimization layer participates in training through backpropagation. The authors analyze both its differentiability and stability, addressing how an explicit constraint-enforcing component can work within a neural network. The guarantee concerns the selected output-parity definition, so its meaning is tied to the fairness criterion being enforced.

The paper also addresses streaming predictions, where enforcing fairness separately on very small batches can be overly restrictive. An online primal-dual algorithm instead provides provable aggregate fairness guarantees with arbitrarily small batches. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the layer and streaming algorithm, offering complementary approaches for enforcing parity within model outputs and maintaining fairness across a stream of predictions.
summary.tldr: A differentiable fairness layer guarantees a chosen output-parity criterion, while an online algorithm provides aggregate fairness for streaming predictions.

title: Differentiable Optimization Layers for Guaranteed Fairness in Deep Learning

abstract: Bridging the gap between visual realism and physical understanding is a core challenge for video-based world models. We study the structural identifiability of continuous-time physical laws from raw pixels, focusing on whether an encoder-only pipeline can uniquely recover the parameters of second-order linear ODEs. We prove that a level-set slope-coverage condition ensures the learned latent space is locally affine to the true physical state, enabling exact parameter recovery. Our theory provides the first characterization of minimal data requirements across damping regimes, establishing that underdamped systems are identifiable from a single video clip, whereas other regimes require three diverse trajectories. We further introduce a variance-floor regularizer to stabilize the decoder-free objective and prevent latent collapse. Validated on synthetic and real-world data, our approach demonstrates that interpretable physical constants can be reliably estimated from video without the need for compute-intensive pixel reconstruction, ensuring both physical correctness and transparency. Code is available at https://github.com/wenjiewang3/PhysicsFromVideo.

Their theory also distinguishes data requirements across damping regimes. These claims belong to the stated model class and theoretical conditions.

Together, the theory and experiments support extracting physical parameters directly from visual representations, avoiding the computational expense of a pixel-reconstruction objective.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for recovering second-order linear physical laws from video using an encoder without pixel reconstruction.

title: Physics from Video: Identifiability of Time-Invariant Second-Order ODEs under Minimal Trajectory Conditions

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has equipped LLM agents with a strong ability to solve complex tasks. However, existing RL methods normally use a single policy network, causing simplicity bias where simple tasks occupy most parameters and dominate gradient updates, leaving insufficient capacity for complex tasks. A plausible remedy could be employing the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture in the policy network, as MoE allows different parameters (experts) to specialize in different tasks, preventing simple tasks from dominating all parameters. However, a key limitation of traditional MoE is its token-level routing, where the router assigns each token to specialized experts, which fragments phase-consistent patterns into scattered expert assignments and thus undermines expert specialization. In this paper, we propose Phase-Aware Mixture of Experts (PA-MoE). It first features a lightweight phase router that learns latent phase boundaries directly from the RL objective without pre-defining phase categories. Then, the phase router allocates temporally consistent assignments to the same expert, allowing experts to preserve phase-specific expertise. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed PA-MoE. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PA-MoE-576C/.

paragraphs: When an agent learns through a single policy network, simple tasks can dominate parameter use and training updates, leaving less capacity for complex tasks. Mixture-of-experts architectures offer a possible remedy by allowing different parameter groups to specialize. However, assigning experts independently at the token level can split a coherent phase of activity across several experts.

Phase-Aware Mixture of Experts introduces a lightweight router that learns latent phase boundaries directly from the reinforcement-learning objective. It does not require predefined phase categories. Within the learned phases, routing produces temporally consistent assignments to the same expert, helping preserve specialization across a meaningful stretch of agent behavior.

The paper reports experiments demonstrating the method’s effectiveness. Its central contribution is to align the duration of an expert assignment with the structure of the task being performed. This addresses a specific obstacle to using expert specialization for agents: capacity allocation needs continuity over time if experts are to develop phase-specific expertise, rather than receiving fragments scattered across different phases.
summary.tldr: PA-MoE learns task-phase boundaries and routes coherent stretches of agent behavior to the same expert to support specialization.

title: Phase-Aware Mixture of Experts for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern vision-language models achieve strong performance in static perception, but remain limited in the complex spatiotemporal reasoning required for embodied, egocentric tasks. A major source of failure is their reliance on temporal priors learned from passive video data, which often leads to spatiotemporal hallucinations and poor generalization in dynamic environments. To address this, we present EgoTSR, a curriculum-based framework for learning task-oriented spatiotemporal reasoning. EgoTSR is built on the premise that embodied reasoning should evolve from explicit spatial understanding to internalized task-state assessment and finally to long-horizon planning. To support this paradigm, we construct EgoTSR-Data, a large-scale dataset comprising 46 million samples organized into three stages: Chain-of-Thought supervision for explicit reasoning, weakly supervised tagging for internalizing reasoning, and long-horizon sequences composed of orthogonal atomic subtasks. We further introduce a Reasoning-Enhanced Task Decomposition mechanism that explicitly models causal dependencies between actions and objects, enabling controllable planning from high-level task descriptions. To rigorously validate our approach, we establish a Dual-Level Evaluation Framework that covers both atomic spatial perception and logical planning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoTSR effectively eliminates chronological biases, achieving 92.4% accuracy on long-horizon logical reasoning tasks while maintaining 88.2% fine-grained perceptual precision, significantly outperforming existing open-source and closed-source state-of-the-art models.

title: From Perception to Planning: Evolving Ego-Centric Task-Oriented Spatiotemporal Reasoning via Curriculum Learning

abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) has driven their success, yet dense Transformers couple capacity and computation: every parameter is activated for every token, making training and inference costs grow linearly with model size—a critical bottleneck as models approach trillion-parameter regimes. We aim to scale capacity through MoE-style mixture throughout the LLM pipeline rather than only the FFN. Prior pipeline-level approaches include ParaScale, which introduces virtual tokens and parallel streams but incurs substantial overhead and suffers from homogenized routing and gradient collapse, and AltUp, which uses an auxiliary prediction branch but offers limited adaptivity and slow convergence. We establish that MoE-style mixture layers can be reformulated as variable-kernel dynamic convolutions, where each expert corresponds to a $1{\times}1$ convolutional kernel and routing implements input-conditioned kernel aggregation. Building on this equivalence, we introduce cMoLLM: a convolutionally gated mixture-of-LLMs that routes over end-to-end streams through fully differentiable dynamic convolution. In GPT-2-style models trained on FineWeb, cMoLLM improves language modeling perplexity and downstream GLUE and SQuAD accuracy under matched compute, with better stream utilization, more stable optimization, and favorable scaling compared to ParaScale- and AltUp-style baselines.

paragraphs: Dense language models increase computational cost as they grow because every parameter participates in processing every token. This paper explores increasing capacity through mixtures of complete processing streams across the language-model pipeline. The aim is to extend mixture-style scaling beyond its usual concentration in feed-forward modules.

title: cMoLLM at Scale: Horizontal Scaling Laws for Convolutionally-Gated Mixture-of-LLMs

abstract: A long-term goal of language agents is to learn and improve through their own experience, ultimately outperforming humans in complex, real-world tasks. However, training agents from experience data with reinforcement learning remains difficult in many environments, which either lack verifiable rewards (e.g., websites) or require inefficient long-horizon rollouts (e.g., multi-turn tool use). As a result, most current agents rely on supervised fine-tuning on expert data, which is challenging to scale and generalizes poorly. This limitation stems from the nature of expert demonstrations: they capture only a narrow range of scenarios, and expose the agent to limited environment diversity. We address this limitation with a middle-ground paradigm we call early experience: interaction data generated by the agent’s own actions, where the resulting future states serve as supervision without reward signals. Within this paradigm, we study two strategies of using such data: (1) implicit world modeling, which uses collected states to ground the policy in environment dynamics; and (2) self-reflection, where the agent learns from its suboptimal actions to improve reasoning and decision-making. Evaluation across eight diverse environments and multiple model families shows that our approaches consistently improve effectiveness and out-of-domain generalization, highlighting the value of early experience. Moreover, in environments with verifiable rewards, our results provide promising signals that early experience offers a strong foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning, making it a practical bridge between imitation learning and fully experience-driven agents.

This paper explores an intermediate approach: agents collect experience through their own actions and use the resulting future states as supervision, without needing reward signals.

The authors study two ways to use this early experience. Implicit world modeling teaches the policy about environment dynamics through the states it encounters. Self-reflection uses the agent’s suboptimal actions to improve its reasoning and decisions. Both approaches make the consequences of the agent’s own behavior a source of training information.

Across eight environments and multiple model families, the approaches consistently improve effectiveness and generalization beyond the training domain. In environments with verifiable rewards, the results also offer promising evidence that early experience can prepare agents for later reinforcement learning. The contribution is a practical way to learn from interaction before reliable reward-based training becomes available.
summary.tldr: Agents improve by learning from the future states produced by their own actions, even without reward signals.

title: Agent Learning via Early Experience

abstract: Existing multimodal reasoning approaches predominantly follow two paradigms: converting visual inputs into text prior to reasoning, or performing end-to-end reasoning within a unified vision–language representation space. Despite their empirical progress, both paradigms suffer from fundamental structural limitations. The former relies on static visual-to-text conversion, which tends to compress and lose fine-grained visual details. The latter is prone to linguistic dominance induced by joint optimization and attention mechanisms, leading to systematically weakened faithfulness to visual evidence during reasoning. In this work, we argue that a central challenge is how and when visual evidence is introduced into the reasoning process. Motivated by this insight, we propose CSMR, a multimodal reasoning framework in which a language model controls the reasoning process by deciding when to invoke an independent visual perception module to acquire task-relevant visual evidence. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that CSMR consistently outperforms representative baseline methods in accuracy under a zero-shot setting. Further experimental analysis confirms that these advantages primarily arise from the proposed cognitive scheduling mechanism.

paragraphs: Multimodal reasoning can lose contact with the image it is supposed to explain. Converting an image to text before reasoning may discard fine details, while joint vision-language processing can allow language to dominate the visual evidence. This paper focuses on when and how the reasoning process obtains visual information.

CSMR places a language model in control of reasoning and lets it decide when to call an independent visual perception module. Those calls acquire evidence relevant to the current task. The approach makes visual inspection a scheduled part of reasoning, so evidence acquisition can respond to what the reasoning process currently needs instead of being settled entirely by an initial image description.

Across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks, CSMR consistently improves zero-shot accuracy over representative baselines. Further analysis attributes the advantages primarily to the scheduling mechanism. The findings support treating the timing of visual evidence collection as a substantive design choice, alongside the capabilities of the language and perception components themselves.
summary.tldr: CSMR lets a language model request visual evidence when needed during reasoning, improving zero-shot accuracy across tested multimodal benchmarks.

title: Look on Demand: A Cognitive Scheduling Framework for Visual Evidence Acquisition in Multimodal Reasoning

abstract: As large language models evolve into tool-augmented agents, a central question remains unresolved: when is external tool use actually justified? Existing agent frameworks typically treat tools as ordinary actions and optimize for task success or reward, offering little principled distinction between epistemically necessary interaction and unnecessary delegation. This position paper argues that agents should invoke external tools only when epistemically necessary. Here, epistemic necessity means that a task cannot be completed reliably via the agent’s internal reasoning over its current context, without any external interaction. We introduce the Theory of Agent (ToA), a unified framework that reconceives agents as tool-use decision makers under epistemic uncertainty to decide whether remaining uncertainty should be resolved internally or delegated externally. From this perspective, common agent failure modes (e.g., overthinking and overacting) arise from miscalibrated decisions under uncertainty rather than deficiencies in reasoning or tool execution alone. We further discuss implications for training, evaluation, and agent design, highlighting that unnecessary delegation not only causes inefficiency but can impede the development of internal reasoning capability. Our position provides a normative and fundamental criterion for tool use that complements existing decision-theoretic models and is essential for building agents that are not only correct, but increasingly intelligent.

paragraphs: The paper asks when an agent actually needs to use an external tool. Its proposed criterion is epistemic necessity: external interaction is justified when the agent cannot reliably complete the task through internal reasoning over its existing context. This is a normative position about tool use, extending beyond the common practice of treating tool calls as ordinary actions selected for reward or task success.

The authors introduce the Theory of Agent, a framework that treats agents as decision makers about tool use under uncertainty. The key decision is whether remaining uncertainty can be resolved internally or requires external interaction. From this perspective, excessive reasoning and excessive action can both reflect poorly calibrated judgments about uncertainty.

This reframing connects tool decisions to training, evaluation, and agent design. The authors argue that unnecessary delegation can waste resources and impede the development of internal reasoning ability. Their proposal complements existing decision-theoretic approaches by making the reliability of context-based reasoning central to deciding when a tool call is warranted.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes that agents use external tools only when reasoning over their current context cannot reliably complete the task.

abstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) have recently been proposed as an alternative to partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) for representing the state of a dynamical system (Littman et al., 2001). We present a learning algorithm that learns a PSR from observational data. Our algorithm produces a variant of PSRs called transformed predictive state representations (TPSRs). We provide an efficient principal-components-based algorithm for learning a TPSR, and show that TPSRs can perform well in comparison to Hidden Markov Models learned with Baum-Welch in a real world robot tracking task for low dimensional representations and long prediction horizons.
originalAbstract: Predictive state representations (PSRs) have recently been proposed as an alternative to partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) for representing the state of a dynamical system (Littman et al., 2001). We present a learning algorithm that learns a PSR from observational data. Our algorithm produces a variant of PSRs called transformed predictive state representations (TPSRs). We provide an efficient principal-components-based algorithm for learning a TPSR, and show that TPSRs can perform well in comparison to Hidden Markov Models learned with Baum-Welch in a real world robot tracking task for low dimensional representations and long prediction horizons.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn a representation of a dynamical system from observational data. It builds on predictive state representations, an alternative to partially observable Markov decision processes for describing system state. The aim is to obtain a learned representation that supports prediction while remaining low dimensional, making the choice of state representation central to the learning problem.

The algorithm produces transformed predictive state representations, or TPSRs. It uses a principal-components-based procedure that the authors describe as efficient. The contribution therefore includes both a variant of the representation and a concrete method for learning it from observations, connecting the representational idea to an implementable learning process.

The evaluation concerns a real-world robot tracking task and compares TPSRs with hidden Markov models trained using Baum-Welch. The reported result is that TPSRs can perform well in that comparison when representations are low dimensional and prediction horizons are long. This supports their usefulness under those tested conditions, with the comparison focused on compact representations and predictions extending further into the future.
summary.tldr: An efficient principal-components-based method learns compact predictive representations that perform well in a robot tracking comparison at long prediction horizons.

title: Learning low dimensional predictive representations

abstract: The l-bfgs limited-memory quasi-Newton method is the algorithm of choice for optimizing the parameters of large-scale log-linear models with L2 regularization, but it cannot be used for an L1 -regularized loss due to its non-differentiability whenever some parameter is zero. Efficient algorithms have been proposed for this task, but they are impractical when the number of parameters is very large. We present an algorithm OrthantWise Limited-memory Quasi-Newton (owlqn), based on l-bfgs, that can efficiently optimize the L1 -regularized log-likelihood of log-linear models with millions of parameters. In our experiments on a parse reranking task, our algorithm was several orders of magnitude faster than an alternative algorithm, and substantially faster than lbfgs on the analogous L2 -regularized problem. We also present a proof that owl-qn is guaranteed to converge to a globally optimal parameter vector.

paragraphs: Large log-linear models need optimization methods that can handle many parameters. Limited-memory quasi-Newton optimization, particularly L-BFGS, works well with L2 regularization, but L1 regularization introduces a problem: the objective is not differentiable when a parameter is zero. The paper addresses this obstacle while targeting models with millions of parameters.

The proposed Orthant-Wise Limited-memory Quasi-Newton algorithm, OWL-QN, builds on L-BFGS to optimize an L1-regularized log-likelihood efficiently. The authors also prove that OWL-QN converges to a globally optimal parameter vector. This combines a method designed for large parameter spaces with a stated convergence guarantee for the optimization problem.

In parse-reranking experiments, OWL-QN is several orders of magnitude faster than an alternative algorithm. It is also substantially faster than L-BFGS on the analogous L2-regularized problem. These runtime findings come from the reported task and accompany the separate theoretical convergence result. Together, they establish the paper's contribution as both a scalable training algorithm and a mathematically supported way to handle the nondifferentiability introduced by L1 regularization.
summary.tldr: OWL-QN efficiently trains L1-regularized log-linear models with millions of parameters and has a global-optimum convergence guarantee.

title: Scalable training of L1-regularized log-linear models

abstract: A number of updates for density matrices have been developed recently that are motivated by relative entropy minimization problems. The updates involve a softmin calculation based on matrix logs and matrix exponentials. We show that these updates can be kernelized. This is important because the bounds provable for these algorithms are logarithmic in the feature dimension (provided that the 2-norm of feature vectors is bounded by a constant). The main problem we focus on is the kernelization of an online PCA algorithm which belongs to this family of updates.
originalAbstract: A number of updates for density matrices have been developed recently that are motivated by relative entropy minimization problems. The updates involve a softmin calculation based on matrix logs and matrix exponentials. We show that these updates can be kernelized. This is important because the bounds provable for these algorithms are logarithmic in the feature dimension (provided that the 2-norm of feature vectors is bounded by a constant). The main problem we focus on is the kernelization of an online PCA algorithm which belongs to this family of updates.

paragraphs: The paper studies matrix update rules derived from relative entropy minimization, concentrating on an online principal component analysis algorithm. These rules update density matrices using a softmin calculation involving matrix logarithms and exponentials. The main contribution is to show that this family of updates can be kernelized.

Kernelization matters here because it connects the update procedure with a feature representation whose dimension affects the theoretical bounds. The authors emphasize that the provable bounds depend logarithmically on feature dimension. This dependence comes with an explicit condition: feature vectors must have their Euclidean norm bounded by a constant.

The central application is therefore an online kernel PCA method built from these entropy-motivated matrix updates. The result links a particular style of matrix optimization to kernel-based learning while preserving the relevance of its dimension-dependent analysis. Its stated significance is theoretical and algorithmic: it makes kernelization available for this update family and explains why the associated bounds are attractive under the bounded-feature assumption.
summary.tldr: Entropy-based matrix updates can be kernelized for online PCA, with bounds logarithmic in feature dimension when feature norms are bounded.

title: Online kernel PCA with entropic matrix updates

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the policy gradient in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) with a special class of policies that are based on Predictive State Representations (PSRs). We compare PSR policies to Finite-State Controllers (FSCs), which are considered as a standard model for policy gradient methods in POMDPs. We present a general actor-critic algorithm for learning both FSCs and PSR policies. The critic part computes a value function that has as variables the parameters of the policy. These latter parameters are gradually updated to maximize the value function. We show that the value function is polynomial for both FSCs and PSR policies, with a potentially smaller degree in the case of PSR policies. Therefore, the value function of a PSR policy can have less local optima than the equivalent FSC, and consequently, the gradient algorithm is more likely to converge to a global optimal solution.

We compare PSR policies to Finite-State Controllers (FSCs), which are considered as a standard model for policy gradient methods in POMDPs. We present a general actor-critic algorithm for learning both FSCs and PSR policies. The critic part computes a value function that has as variables the parameters of the policy. These latter parameters are gradually updated to maximize the value function. We show that the value function is polynomial for both FSCs and PSR policies, with a potentially smaller degree in the case of PSR policies. Therefore, the value function of a PSR policy can have less local optima than the equivalent FSC, and consequently, the gradient algorithm is more likely to converge to a global optimal solution.

paragraphs: This paper examines policy-gradient learning in partially observable Markov decision processes. It focuses on a class of policies based on predictive state representations and compares them with finite-state controllers, a standard policy representation in this setting. The central question is how the choice of representation affects the optimization problem faced during learning.

The authors introduce a general actor-critic algorithm for both representations. The critic computes a value function expressed in terms of the policy's parameters. Those parameters are then gradually updated to increase the value function. This gives the comparison a common learning framework rather than treating the two policy classes as unrelated algorithms.

The paper shows that the value function is polynomial for both classes, with potentially lower degree for predictive-state policies. Such policies can consequently have fewer local optima than equivalent finite-state controllers, making gradient learning more likely to reach a global optimum. The advantage is conditional: the argument identifies a possible improvement in the optimization landscape, not a guarantee of globally optimal learning.
summary.tldr: Predictive-state policies can yield simpler value-function landscapes than finite-state controllers, potentially improving policy-gradient optimization.

title: Predictive representations for policy gradient in POMDPs

abstract: A key aspect of semantic image segmenta- tion is to integrate local and global features for the prediction of local segment labels. We present an approach to multi-class seg- mentation which combines two methods for this integration: a Conditional Random Field (CRF) which couples to local image features and an image classification method which considers global features. The CRF follows the approach of Reynolds & Murphy (2007) and is based on an unsupervised multi scale pre-segmentation of the image into patches, where patch labels correspond to the ran- dom variables of the CRF. The output of the classifier is used to constraint this CRF. We demonstrate and compare the approach on a standard semantic segmentation data set.

We present an approach to multi-class seg- mentation which combines two methods for this integration: a Conditional Random Field (CRF) which couples to local image features and an image classification method which considers global features. The CRF follows the approach of Reynolds & Murphy (2007) and is based on an unsupervised multi scale pre-segmentation of the image into patches, where patch labels correspond to the ran- dom variables of the CRF. The output of the classifier is used to constraint this CRF. We demonstrate and compare the approach on a standard semantic segmentation data set.

paragraphs: Semantic image segmentation assigns class labels to local regions of an image. A region's own appearance provides useful evidence, while information about the image as a whole can also inform its label. This paper combines those two information sources through a conditional random field and a separate image classification method.

The image is first divided into patches through unsupervised pre-segmentation at multiple scales. Patch labels become the variables in the conditional random field, which is coupled to local image features. The image classifier considers global features, and its output constrains the conditional random field. This gives whole-image information an explicit role in determining local segment labels.

The authors demonstrate and compare the approach on a standard semantic segmentation dataset. The contribution described in the abstract is the integration mechanism: local structured labeling operates under constraints supplied by global classification. This design addresses the problem of combining evidence available at different spatial scopes within a single segmentation procedure.
summary.tldr: A global image classifier constrains a patch-based conditional random field to combine whole-image context with local evidence for semantic segmentation.

title: Multi-class image segmentation using conditional random fields and global classification

abstract: We examine maximum spanning tree-based methods for learning the structure of tree Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) P(Y|X). We use edge weights which take advantage of local inputs X and thus scale to large problems. For a general class of edge weights, we give a negative learn ability result. However, we demonstrate that two members of the class--local Conditional Mutual Information and Decomposable Conditional Influence--have reasonable theoretical bases and perform very well in practice. On synthetic data and a large-scale fMRI application, our methods outperform existing techniques.

We use edge weights which take advantage of local inputs X and thus scale to large problems. For a general class of edge weights, we give a negative learn ability result. However, we demonstrate that two members of the class--local Conditional Mutual Information and Decomposable Conditional Influence--have reasonable theoretical bases and perform very well in practice. On synthetic data and a large-scale fMRI application, our methods outperform existing techniques.

paragraphs: A conditional random field models relationships among output variables given an input. This paper studies how to learn a tree structure for such a model using maximum spanning tree methods. The challenge is to choose which output relationships belong in the tree while taking the conditioning input into account during structure learning.

The authors assign candidate edges weights that use local input information, allowing the approach to scale to large problems. They establish a negative learnability result for a general class of these weights. At the same time, they identify two members of the class with reasonable theoretical foundations: local Conditional Mutual Information and Decomposable Conditional Influence.

Both proposed choices perform very well in practice. On synthetic data and a large-scale fMRI application, the methods outperform existing techniques. The paper therefore pairs a theoretical caution about the broader class with positive evidence for particular members. Its findings support these specific ways of scoring edges without turning their practical success into a general learnability guarantee.
summary.tldr: Locally informed edge scores enable effective tree CRF structure learning despite a negative learnability result for their broader class.

title: Learning Tree Conditional Random Fields

abstract: We study an instance of high-dimensional statistical inference inwhich the goal is to use $N$ noisy observations to estimate a matrix$\Theta^* \in \real^{k \times p}$ that is assumed to be either exactlylow rank, or "near" low-rank, meaning that it can bewell-approximated by a matrix with low rank. We consider an$M$-estimator based on regularization by the trace or nuclear normover matrices, and analyze its performance under high-dimensionalscaling. We provide non-asymptotic bounds on the Frobenius norm errorthat hold for a general class of noisy observation models, and applyto both exactly low-rank and approximately low-rank matrices. We thenillustrate their consequences for a number of specific learningmodels, including low-rank multivariate or multi-task regression,system identification in vector autoregressive processes, and recoveryof low-rank matrices from random projections. Simulations showexcellent agreement with the high-dimensional scaling of the errorpredicted by our theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a large matrix from noisy observations when the matrix has low rank or can be closely approximated by one that does. Low rank expresses a form of shared structure across the matrix. Allowing approximate low rank broadens the analysis to cases where that structure is imperfect.

The estimator uses trace-norm, also called nuclear-norm, regularization. The authors derive finite-sample bounds on estimation error measured by the Frobenius norm, which summarizes error across matrix entries. These bounds cover a general class of noisy observation models and both exact and approximate low-rank targets, describing performance as the problem dimensions grow.

The paper applies the analysis to multivariate and multitask regression, identification of vector autoregressive systems, and matrix recovery from random projections. Simulations closely match the error scaling predicted by the theory. The contribution is a common statistical account of several matrix-estimation problems, with theoretical predictions that receive empirical support in the reported simulations.
summary.tldr: The paper derives finite-sample error bounds for nuclear-norm estimation of noisy low-rank and approximately low-rank matrices.

title: Estimation of (near) low-rank matrices with noise and high-dimensional scaling

abstract: Approximate dynamic programming has been used successfully in a large variety of domains, but it relies on a small set of provided approximation features to calculate solutions reliably. Large and rich sets of features can cause the existing algorithms to overfit because of the limited number of samples. We address this shortcoming using L_1 regularization in approximate linear programming. Because the proposed method can automatically select the appropriate richness of features, its performance does not degrade with an increasing number of features. These results rely on new and stronger sampling bounds for regularized approximate linear programs. We also propose a computationally efficient homotopy method. The empirical evaluation of the approach shows that the proposed method performs well on simple MDPs and standard benchmark problems.

Large and rich sets of features can cause the existing algorithms to overfit because of the limited number of samples. We address this shortcoming using L_1 regularization in approximate linear programming. Because the proposed method can automatically select the appropriate richness of features, its performance does not degrade with an increasing number of features. These results rely on new and stronger sampling bounds for regularized approximate linear programs. We also propose a computationally efficient homotopy method. The empirical evaluation of the approach shows that the proposed method performs well on simple MDPs and standard benchmark problems.

paragraphs: Approximate dynamic programming represents solutions using a supplied set of features. Richer feature sets can express more, but limited samples create a risk of overfitting. This paper addresses the resulting tension: providing many potentially useful features can make existing algorithms less reliable instead of improving their solutions.

The authors introduce L1 regularization into approximate linear programming for Markov decision processes. The method automatically controls the richness of the features used, rather than requiring a small feature set to be chosen beforehand. They report that performance does not deteriorate as the number of available features increases, with this result resting on new, stronger sampling bounds for the regularized formulation.

The paper also proposes a computationally efficient homotopy method, addressing how to solve the resulting problem in practice. Empirical evaluation shows good performance on simple Markov decision processes and standard benchmarks. The contribution combines feature selection, sampling theory, and computation, making larger collections of candidate features usable within the proposed approximate planning approach.
summary.tldr: L1-regularized approximate linear programming automatically controls feature richness, supported by stronger sampling bounds and an efficient homotopy method.

title: Feature Selection Using Regularization in Approximate Linear Programs for Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Structured prediction is the cornerstone of several machine learning applications. Unfortunately, in structured prediction settings with expressive inter-variable interactions, inference and hence exact learning is often intractable. We present a new way, Decomposed Learning (DecL), for performing efficient learning over structured output spaces. In DecL, we restrict the inference step to a limited part of the output space. We use characterizations based on the structure, target parameters, and gold labels to guarantee that DecL with limited inference is equivalent to exact learning. We also show that in real world settings, where our theoretical assumptions may not hold exactly, DecL-based algorithms are significantly more efficient and provide accuracies close to exact learning.
originalAbstract: Structured prediction is the cornerstone of several machine learning applications. Unfortunately, in structured prediction settings with expressive inter-variable interactions, inference and hence exact learning is often intractable. We present a new way, Decomposed Learning (DecL), for performing efficient learning over structured output spaces. In DecL, we restrict the inference step to a limited part of the output space. We use characterizations based on the structure, target parameters, and gold labels to guarantee that DecL with limited inference is equivalent to exact learning. We also show that in real world settings, where our theoretical assumptions may not hold exactly, DecL-based algorithms are significantly more efficient and provide accuracies close to exact learning.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs whose components interact, so learning often requires searching a large space of possible combinations. Expressive interactions can make this inference step, and consequently exact learning, computationally intractable. Decomposed Learning addresses this bottleneck by limiting the part of the output space examined during training.

The important question is when such a restricted search preserves the result of exact learning. The authors give characterizations involving the problem's structure, the target parameters, and the correct training labels. Under the stated theoretical conditions, Decomposed Learning with limited inference is equivalent to exact learning, despite searching only part of the output space.

The paper also evaluates settings where those conditions may hold only approximately. There, its algorithms are significantly more efficient while achieving accuracies close to exact learning. This separates two contributions: a conditional equivalence guarantee and empirical evidence of practical usefulness beyond exact satisfaction of the assumptions. Together, they explain why reducing inference during training can retain much of the value of structured learning.
summary.tldr: Decomposed Learning restricts training-time inference, matching exact learning under stated conditions and approaching its accuracy efficiently in experiments.

title: Efficient Decomposed Learning for Structured Prediction
